Research shows that dry, dense vegetation around buildings can cause wildfires to spread . In extreme conditions, high winds carry a deluge of tiny, burning embers far beyond the fire itself. When those embers get caught in vegetation, they can ignite, spreading flames to nearby buildings and homes.

Sponsor Message

Wednesday's vote by the California Board of Forestry and Fire Protection comes after years of debate and delays . The state originally considered rules that would have restricted all vegetation within five feet of a house, aside from well-maintained trees. That generated pushback from some communities, concerned about losing greenery in their gardens and the cost of yard maintenance.

California regulators ultimately struck a compromise about plants allowed within the five-foot zone, known as Zone Zero . Lawns, flowers and non-woody plants up to 18 inches tall will be allowed, unless they are located directly under the roofline of a house. Trees will be allowed, though branches must be trimmed five feet away from a structure. The rules will apply to new construction right away, but will be phased in for existing structures, affecting almost 2 million homes in high-risk areas.

State regulators say the rules reflect the new reality of more extreme wildfires, driven in part by rising temperatures from climate change. More than 57,000 homes and buildings have been destroyed in California in the last decade, according to state regulators.

"California's faced an existential crisis that has affected our health, that has affected our finances related to our ability to buy and sell homes, to insure homes and has put us in a very precarious place," testified Yana Valachovic of the University of California Cooperative Extension at Wednesday's hearing, who also advised the state on the new rules.

Sponsor Message

Growing tensions across Western states

California's debate reflects growing tensions across the Western U.S. about how communities should prepare for wildfires. Wildfire experts warn even fires that start in open, wildland areas can quickly become urban fires, destroying thousands of homes in neighborhoods that residents never thought were at risk , like in the 2025 Los Angeles fires. This summer, more than 800 homes were destroyed in Spokane, Wash., by three wildfires that burned through dense neighborhoods.

Across several states, homeowners in public meetings have said wildfire regulations threaten private property rights, reduce urban wildlife habitat and require costly maintenance.

"You are about to approve a set of regulations that will cost millions of California homeowners tens of billions of dollars," testified Dave Lefkowitz, president of the Mandeville Canyon Association, a community group in the Los Angeles hills. "The math is insuperable."

Vegetation management rules were recently defeated in both Oregon and Washington after strong public pushback, including misinformation that spread online. Some community groups wanted regulators to wait for more scientific research on wildfire spread.

Research shows plants can increase risk

In experiments, researchers have shown that even green plants can ignite in the dry, windy conditions of an extreme wildfire. Analyses of past California wildfires have also shown that homes with vegetation predominantly within six feet of the exterior walls were at higher risk of being lost . Managing vegetation also creates "defensible space" for firefighters, providing better access for defending a structure.

California has long been at the forefront of wildfire policy, pioneering regulations that other states have adopted. For almost 20 years, California's wildfire building codes have required homes to use fire-resistant materials for construction. A handful of other states recently adopted similar codes . Research shows that while there are no guarantees a house will survive a fire, protections are strongest when homeowners address both building materials and vegetation. Even in some of the most severe wildfires in recent years, some homes made it through .

Sponsor Message

California regulators say the widespread regulations are needed because voluntary measures don't provide enough protection. Communities are safest when all homeowners comply, since one home with dense, dry vegetation can spread fire to its neighbors. Insurance companies in California are also required to provide discounts to homeowners that make their homes more fire-resistant.

New rules depend on inspections

While California's new rules provide more flexibility for homeowners, some wildfire experts say they don't go far enough, given that any combustible material next to a house could pose a risk. The new vegetation rules will be enforced by local fire departments and state agencies that do home inspections every year. Those inspectors will bear the brunt of educating homeowners and ensuring compliance.

"I want the board to understand what this compromise asks of local inspection programs," Todd Lando of the Central Marin Fire Department testified at the hearing. "A clean Zone Zero is a five-minute inspection with one question: Is anything combustible within five feet? Easy for the homeowner to understand and take action on." Lando says the new rules will involve more conditional judgements by inspectors, opening up debate with homeowners that could affect compliance.

California regulators say inspectors will focus on educating homeowners at first, before compliance becomes mandatory. For existing homes, the new vegetation rules will go into effect in 2029 at the earliest.

World.title: Experts raise alarms over Census Bureau report Trump is touting on noncitizen voting
World.content:
Experts raise alarms over Census Bureau report Trump is touting on noncitizen voting

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

A highly unusual Census Bureau report that President Trump is using to reup dubious claims of widespread illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens has ties to a Trump-aligned think tank, NPR has learned.

In a social media post Tuesday, Trump claimed that the bureau's initial analysis of more than 128 million voter records "proves that over 24,000 Noncitizens voted illegally" in the 2020 presidential election and that the final number will "explode" after the statistical agency finishes checking over 32 million more voter records.

The unauthored, seven-page report says it draws on a 2020 commercial voter file and various federal administrative records, but data and election experts say the report is questionable in its methodology and conclusions.

Sponsor Message

Work on the analysis was not conducted by career civil servants at the Census Bureau, and the team behind it included individuals affiliated with the America First Policy Institute, a think tank started by officials from Trump's first administration, according to a Census Bureau employee who NPR has agreed not to name because they fear retaliation at work.

Spokespeople for the bureau, the America First Policy Institute and the White House did not respond to NPR's requests for comment.

But AFPI highlighted the analysis in a social media post Tuesday, saying that the think tank "maintains that maximizing transparency is a critical step to restoring confidence in our elections."

The report is the latest attempt by Trump officials to push baseless claims of widespread voter fraud

Trump continues to falsely claim the 2020 election was rigged, and in the final stretch before this fall's midterm election has urged his Republican allies in Congress to pass sweeping new voting restrictions.

The numbers from the Census Bureau report join a growing list of figures the Trump administration has released in recent months. The figures use disputed or unknown methodology in an attempt to quantify noncitizen voting in federal races, a problem many studies and audits show is incredibly rare.

Sponsor Message

Last month, the Department of Homeland Security announced it had found 250,000 noncitizens on public voter rolls in California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, but it has yet to publicly disclose how it made those calculations. And election officials in those states expressed doubts about the accuracy of the claims.

The latest numbers from the Census Bureau report have also drawn pushback from election experts.

"This analysis is laughable. Census data cannot reliably be matched to voter data," David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said in a text exchange with NPR. "That said, it's good to see the president admit these numbers are so small that they couldn't have changed the outcome in 2020."

Using figures from the initial analysis, some 24,000 votes out of 128 million is just shy of 0.02%.

Michael Morse, an assistant professor at the University of Pennsylvania's law school who has researched voter registration files, echoed Becker's criticism over email, writing: "I'd expect that the Census data matching [exercise] is plagued by the lack of unique identifiers in voter records and outdated or incomplete naturalization records. But the brief's lack of transparency makes it difficult to pin down each problem or trust any explanation. Regardless, the estimated rate of apparent non-citizen voting is both a tiny fraction of total votes … and entirely consistent with both types of error."

The report threatens the Census Bureau's reputation as a nonpartisan statistical agency

Former employees of the Census Bureau are also raising alarms about the report.

"My biggest concern would be there's no author attached to the report, which is not common practice within the Census Bureau," says Misty Heggeness, a former bureau economist whose work is cited in the report. "Usually there are layers and layers of rigor and testing because the Census Bureau is a neutral statistical agency. They want to make sure that they're getting it right and understanding the data. The fact that there's no author on this report leads me to wonder whether or not that did happen."

Sponsor Message

As a former chief of the bureau's Center for Administrative Records Research and Applications, Amy O'Hara points out the risk of generating an inflated number of noncitizen voters by mismatching voter files with citizenship records from other federal agencies.

"This brief lacks any sort of measures of variance or discussion of bias," says O'Hara, who now directs Georgetown University's Massive Data Institute. "While those matches were found, were they the same people between the voter file and the compilation of data from Homeland Security, or do you have people with the same names potentially living in the same state and representing a mismatch?"

O'Hara was also taken aback by the report's claim that the bureau is "uniquely capable of compiling and publishing statistics on election crime and other forms of fraud."

"I found that very surprising because even if they observed anomalies in the data, those anomalies aren't necessarily fraud," O'Hara says.

The report's release comes after a major brain drain of statisticians, economists and other career civil servants at the bureau following the Trump administration's slashing of the federal workforce.

The administration has also been signaling it's preparing to propose major changes to the 2030 census that are likely to put the bureau in the center of another major political and legal fight.

O'Hara sees the report as another threat to the bureau's reputation as a nonpartisan statistical agency.

"We are drawing in on the 2030 census that really requires the participation of everybody in the country. Anything that casts a negative light on the Census Bureau's motives or operations or transparency or lack of adherence to policy could be detrimental," O'Hara says.

With the report's title — "Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election, A Beginning Analysis" — suggesting similar reports are on their way, Heggeness, the former bureau economist, says the country should be vigilant.

Sponsor Message

"It's a confusing time for the public. I think it is really hard for the public to trust what's coming out of the administration, the data that they're seeing," says Heggeness, who is now a professor of public affairs and economics at the University of Kansas. "This document really does have a lack of a source and citations and explanation about methods. And if the public sees a document like this that lacks all of those really integral pieces that are generally put out with official statistics, that's a really good sign to question the validity of the document."

NPR correspondent Miles Parks contributed reporting.

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

World.title: Whistleblower Arturo Béjar leads testimony in landmark trial against Meta
World.content:
Whistleblower Arturo Béjar leads testimony in landmark trial against Meta

toggle caption KARL MONDON/AFP via Getty Images



Meta was infused with a culture in which employees obsessed over user numbers and consistently pushed safety to the side, according to Arturo Béjar, a former employee turned whistleblower, who testified today in the landmark child safety trial against the social media company. Only one man had the ability to change that, Béjar said: CEO Mark Zuckerberg. But he didn't.

"At the end of the day, it was the company culture that Mark had created that made it so that it was practically impossible to deliver features that addressed the wellbeing and safety issues that we've been talking about," he said.

Sponsor Message

Béjar is a linchpin witness for a consortium of states led by California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey that sued Meta, alleging violations of consumer and child data protection laws, and that the company lied to the public about risks its platforms posed. The attorneys for the states say Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to hook young users and to keep them on site longer thanks to features such as infinite scrolling and the "like" button.

Meta has denied the allegations. In his opening statement on Tuesday , attorney Paul Schmidt argued that the company was sensitive to the risks to teens, sought to address them and did not deceive the public about them.

The state attorneys have not yet said if they will call Zuckerberg as a witness.

Testifying in federal court in Oakland, California, for a second day on Wednesday, Béjar, who worked on safety issues at Meta for eight years, said he interacted with Zuckerberg dozens of times, and charged that Zuckerberg was not telling the truth when he made public denials that the company put profits over safety.

In particular, Béjar addressed a widely-shared Facebook post Zuckerberg made in 2021 after another whistleblower, Frances Haugen, shared internal documents with The Wall Street Journal that highlighted risks to the mental health of teens. In the post , Zuckerberg said it's "just not true" that Meta prioritizes profit over safety and wellbeing.

"Based on my experience at Meta, that is not an accurate statement," Béjar said.

On the stand, Béjar noted that he'd seen several internal Meta studies that highlighted risks for teens on Facebook and Instagram. The studies surveyed users, including teenagers, about their experiences with harmful content on the platforms and negative feelings associated with them.

Sponsor Message

But he said efforts to introduce or change features to effectively address those risks were difficult to implement. Instead, Béjar testified, at almost every turn the company chose policies that boosted usership and revenue over safety. Safety was "not a meaningful priority," he said.

Béjar worked at Facebook from 2009 to 2015, largely focusing on cyberbullying. He returned to the company from 2019 to 2021 as a consultant to work on Instagram's wellbeing team. He said one of the reasons for his return was seeing how his daughter was treated as a teen on Instagram.

This is not the first time Béjar has spoken out against his former employer. In 2023, he testified before a Senate committee alleging that Meta pushed content to teens that promoted bullying, drug abuse, eating disorders and self-harm. He also gave an extensive interview to The Wall Street Journal that year, describing his efforts to raise his concerns with his employer.

The current case, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, is a high-stakes test of efforts to hold Meta accountable, not for the content on its platforms, but for the features it built into its platforms. The states allege they were designed to encourage compulsive use, and that the company stood to financially benefit from keeping young users on site, because it makes its money through advertising. The more users scroll — and the better-targeted ads they see — the more Meta stands to profit.

It is one of thousands of lawsuits against social media companies alleging that their platforms are addictive and have fueled youth mental health problems .

On cross examination, Meta attorney Brian Stekloff asked Béjar about the quality of the people he worked with at Meta and whether or not he had "solved" any of the safety risks he had worked on, in an apparent effort to highlight the complexity and difficulty of these challenges.

Béjar said the teams he worked with were full of qualified people whom he respected, and that none of the risk issues had been solved.

Sponsor Message

He called features like video autoplay, "like" counters and infinite scroll "inherently unsafe for teenagers."

And when it came to safety features Meta has introduced to try to minimize some of the risks, Béjar said they were "designed to fail." Features like Instagram's "quiet mode," which can mute push notifications, are ineffective because they are optional settings rather than defaults, he said.

"Most people will not turn the setting on," he said. "It's like you have to turn on the air bag every time you get into the car."

The trial is expected to last about six weeks.

The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, which was founded by CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, is a financial supporter of NPR.

World.title: The U.S. debt tops a record-shattering $40 trillion. Yes, with a T
World.content:
The U.S. debt tops a record-shattering $40 trillion. Yes, with a T

toggle caption Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images

The federal debt topped $40 trillion Wednesday, a new high-water mark for red ink that shows no sign of receding.

The news, reported by the Treasury Department in its daily financial update, comes just five months after the debt surpassed $39 trillion. The government continues to pile up debt at a rapid clip, as spending outstrips revenue by more than $2 trillion a year.

"Our current fiscal trajectory is plainly unsustainable, and that's the best-case scenario," said Margaret Spellings, president of the Bipartisan Policy Center. "Even in the rosiest scenarios, we're speeding toward a cliff and refusing to turn the wheel."

The deficit widened further after the Supreme Court struck down many of President Trump's tariffs, forcing the Treasury to refund more than $100 billion in import taxes that were collected illegally.

Sponsor Message

Government spending continues to surge

The administration sought to blame the ballooning deficit on Democrats.

"President Trump pledged to clean up Joe Biden's fiscal mismanagement," White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement. "That's why the Trump administration has been focused on slashing waste, fraud, and abuse in federal spending while accelerating economic growth to get America's debt-to-GDP ratio trending in the right direction again."

Government revenues have grown 3% this fiscal year — but spending has grown even faster. And the debt-to-GDP ratio has worsened since Trump returned to the White House.

The government is spending more than a trillion dollars a year just to pay interest on the mounting debt. Interest is now the government's second-biggest expense, trailing only Social Security.

Interest costs in the first 10 months of this fiscal year were 15% higher than they were in the same period a year ago. That reflects not only the growing debt but also the higher interest rates that investors are now demanding in order to keep lending the government money.

Bond markets are reacting

The yield on 30-year Treasurys reached a 19-year high this week. That raises borrowing costs for everyone else, since mortgage rates and other interest rates often follow long-term Treasurys.

Sponsor Message

The average rate on a 30-year mortgage neared 6.7% last week, according to Freddie Mac.

"Federal debt is already raising the cost of living and choking out other spending and investment, threatening our economy and Americans' long-term prosperity," Spellings said.

So far, Congress has shown little appetite for tackling the problem.

"$40 trillion should be a wake-up call. But neither Congress nor the president have a credible plan to stop it from growing," said Carolyn Bourdeaux, executive director of Concord Action, a group that advocates for fiscal responsibility. "We owe the next generation better than this crushing debt and another hollow promise that someone else will deal with it later."

World.title: Former Fauci adviser Dr. David Morens pleads guilty to concealing COVID-related records
World.content:
Former Fauci adviser Dr. David Morens pleads guilty to concealing COVID-related records

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Dr. David Morens, a former senior adviser to Dr. Anthony Fauci during the COVID-19 pandemic, pleaded guilty in federal court Tuesday to a charge of conspiracy to defraud the United States.

Morens, who worked under Fauci at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, was accused of concealing federal records related to coronavirus research. He was indicted in April for allegedly trying to hide email exchanges about that research by using his personal email instead of his government email.

Sponsor Message

"By pleading guilty today, Dr. Morens has taken responsibility for what he did, and he will continue to do so," his legal counsel, Tim Belevetz, told NPR in an email Tuesday.

Morens has apologized in previous hearings for his handling of federal records.

The coronavirus research in question has come under fire by Sen. Rand Paul and other Republicans, who have claimed without proof that the coronavirus that caused the pandemic came from a lab in China, and have accused Fauci and Morens of covering that up. Both scientists have denied this. Many researchers agree that the weight of the available evidence suggests the virus emerged naturally.

Fauci, who played a leading role in the United States' pandemic response, was not charged with anything in connection with Morens. But earlier this month, Paul's Senate committee voted to hold him in contempt of Congress for invoking the Fifth Amendment against self-incrimination and refusing to answer questions at a hearing. It will ultimately be up to the Justice Department to decide whether to pursue a criminal prosecution of Fauci.

Some experts have said these moves are part of broader undermining of science and scientists in the United States.

Jennifer Jones, who runs the Center for Science and Democracy at the Union of Concerned Scientists, would not comment specifically about either Morens' or Fauci's situations. But she says the Trump administration has been attacking scientists in many ways.

Sponsor Message

"Criminal prosecution of scientists is a classic authoritarian tactic," she told NPR in an interview.

But Robert Fisher, a Boston attorney who is not involved in the Morens case, says the government's charges against Morens appear solid.

"When you're a government official you swear an oath, you're working for a federal agency, you're just held to a higher standard," Fisher said.

Morens, who is 78 years old, could face five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 when he is sentenced in November.

World.title: Who is Mohammad Ghamira and why has his death, alleged abuse ignited outcry in Syria?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Syrians took to the streets this week to call for justice over the death of Mohammad Ghamira, a Syrian man who died in hospital after alleged abuse by security forces while in detention — less than two years after the new government vowed to break away from the systemic, arbitrary detentions and abuse that was common under the ousted regime.

Ghamira's family said they told police that the 29-year-old father of two suffered from hemophilia, a rare genetic disorder that impairs the body's ability to make blood clots, which can lead to prolonged bleeding.

He was held in detention for three days before being released on Aug. 9 and taken immediately to hospital. He died a week later.

For Syria’s new government, Ghamira’s death has become somewhat of a litmus test of whether its promises of accountability will translate into action after the fall of the Assad's iron-fisted dynasty, which ruled the country for more than 50 years.

Ghamira's death sparked a series of peaceful sit-ins and protests in the country this week, but rights groups say his case is only one of many reports of alleged mistreatment at detention centres that have come out since the new government took power.

"The death of Mohammad Ghamira raises exactly the concerns we have been documenting since the transition began: detention practices that are not yet governed by a unified, judicially supervised system," Fadel Abdulghany, executive director of Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR), told CBC News.

"Syria’s transition will be judged on whether accountability for cases like this becomes systemic, not selective."

Family warned police of dire medical condition

Ghamira was a former volunteer with the White Helmets, also known as the Syria Civil Defence, which was formed in 2013 and operated during the war in opposition-held areas. The group's role shifted from an independent rescue group to part of the country's formal state emergency services after the collapse of the former regime in 2024.

The Latakia Internal Security Command said Ghamira was detained regarding an allegation "that he stole a sum of money." It did not provide any further details.

Members of the White Helmets carry the body of Ghamira, a former White Helmets volunteer who died shortly after his release from jail, before his burial in the village of al-Haffa, Latakia province, Syria, on Monday. (The Associated Press)

While in custody, his family was unable to visit or contact him, and was told only that he was “under investigation," according to the SNHR.

His uncle, Issam Ghamira, told state news agency SANA the family had informed the police chief in al-Haffah that his nephew had hemophilia and warned against hitting him. Despite that, he said, his nephew was hit while in custody.

Ghamira died at the Latakia University Hospital on Sunday after being released from jail.

Syria's Minister of Emergency and Disaster Management Raed al-Saleh mourned the death of his "brother, friend and young colleague."

Al-Saleh, who was previously head of the White Helmets, said on X that Ghamira had died of "complications from cerebral and gastrointestinal hemorrhaging" that "resulted from a beating he sustained after being detained at the al-Haffah police station."

"I affirm to his family and all Syrians that the new Syria is a state of law and justice…. The Syrians have sacrificed throughout 14 years to reach a Syria that upholds their dignity and preserves their humanity, and there will be no impunity in the new Syria," Al-Saleh said.

Government launched investigation

Ghamira was buried Monday in his hometown of al-Haffah in Syria's coastal Latakia province.

Syria's Interior Ministry announced on Sunday an investigation into Ghamira's death. It said seven Interior Ministry personnel were detained for questioning but did not provide any other details.

SNHR's Abdulghany said anyone detained must be informed of the reasons for arrest, brought promptly before an independent judge and able to challenge the lawfulness of detention, in accordance with Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

Abdulghany questioned whether the internal investigation would be enough to provide accountability.

"What matters now is whether the case moves to an independent criminal investigation and prosecution, not an internal disciplinary process alone, and whether the outcome — and the forensic evidence behind it — is made available to the family and the public," Abdulghany said.

Mourners carry the coffin at Ghamira's funeral on Monday in al-Haffa. (The Associated Press)

Syria's Interior Ministry spokesperson Noureddine al-Baba acknowledged "shortcomings and deficiencies" in some of the country's police departments but said others were doing "exceptional" work.

"God willing, this painful incident will serve as a catalyst for positive change in the operations of the Ministry of Interior," he told reporters on Monday.

CBC News reached out to the Interior Ministry but did not receive a response.

Accountability 'not enough,' families say

Syrians whose loved ones disappeared or died in detention centres during Assad's rule say they were disturbed to hear of ongoing abuse.

"What happened to [Ghamira] reopens the wounds of torture and death in detention for thousands of Syrian families — practices that Syrians have struggled for years to end, and whose recurrence today cannot be tolerated," Families for Freedom, a group representing relatives of detainees, said in a statement written in Arabic on Monday.

The group said it is calling for an "independent and transparent" investigation, along with a publication of the investigation's findings and a formal apology to Ghamira's family.

The organization added that prosecuting abuses after they occur is "not enough," calling instead for systemic reforms to prevent mistreatment, strengthen oversight of detention facilities and ensure such abuses are not repeated.

"A new Syria cannot be built with the old tools of oppression."

Abuses persist in detention centres, rights groups say

When insurgents unseated Assad in December 2024 after a nearly 14-year conflict, they opened the country's notorious prisons. During Assad's rule, thousands of prisoners were killed in mass executions or died from injuries and disease. Detainees were subjected to torture, beatings and rape, according to rights groups that have documented the abuse.

When Syria's transitional government took over, it vowed to uphold the "rule of law" and ensure fair trials and proper judicial oversight during arrests.

Syrians carry the pictures of their relatives, who were killed following the Syrian revolution in March 2011, as they celebrate in front of the Palace of Justice in Damascus on Aug. 11. A Syrian court sentenced former ruler Bashar al-Assad to death after a trial in absentia, convicting him of atrocities committed during the country's nearly 14-year conflict. (Bakr AlKasem/AFP/Getty Images)

Officials with the government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa have promised accountability in Ghamira's case, but rights groups say it is not an isolated incident and that abuses persist in detention centres.

In a new report published last week , Syrians for Truth and Justice, a human rights organization that tracks abuses, said "severe beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, threats, deprivation of basic necessities, and deaths in custody continue to be common practices at the hands of multiple security and military actors."

The group concluded that the incidents were too widespread to treat as isolated incidents but there was not evidence of a "single centralized system equivalent in structure and direction to the torture apparatus entrenched by the Assad regime."

"It is somehow widespread, but it's not structured," Bassam Alahmad, the group's executive director, told The Associated Press on Monday. "For us, there is no evidence that these orders came from the commanders to torture people, but still [the authorities] have a responsibility to stop this behaviour."

In an earlier report released in March, the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic said it had documented "torture and ill-treatment" in 18 official detention facilities and 12 "makeshift facilities" in different areas of Syria between January and October 2025.

World.title: As Israel’s military advances its yellow line, Gazans fear they’re being pushed to the sea
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On a Gaza seaside that looks more like a beach resort than a battleground, Palestinians splash in the sun. This crowd is grateful for peaceful pauses in a war that’s dragged into its third summer.

But despite talk of peace negotiations and withdrawals, very few believe it’s over.

“This war has taught me to be afraid of hope,” said Tamer Al-Sheikh. “We’ve hoped a lot through four or five truces, but the conflict continues.”

With only a few pauses, Israeli airstrikes hit Gaza almost daily as Israel says it is targeting wanted Hamas militants.

At the same time, Israeli troops have continued creeping west, expanding their military footprint and squeezing two million Palestinians into an ever smaller area, forcing a scramble for survival toward the Mediterranean Sea.

Under the Gaza peace agreement last October, Israel accepted that it would pull back its troops behind what’s known as the “yellow line,” the edge of Israeli military control inside Gaza. That would amount to less than 50 per cent of the territory along its border. But Israel’s army now controls more than 60 per cent, saying the new boundary is necessary for “operational security”.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he’s told his generals to keep going to 70 per cent.

Earlier this month, he rejected a U.S. plan to phase out both Israeli military and Hamas militant control of Gaza, saying Israel “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed.” The militant group has agreed to give up weapons only in tandem with a phased Israeli pullback, leaving a deadlock.

CBC’s visual investigations team has verified the near constant forward movement of Israeli troops and expansion of the yellow line using satellite images. Eyewitness accounts and video captured by freelancers on the ground in Gaza have confirmed the military advances.

The impact on Gaza’s civilians has been profound.

Blocks move without warning

Palestinians regularly wake up to find the yellow cement markers sitting right next to their homes, nudged metres or hundreds of metres closer overnight. Israeli forces aren’t far behind.

“Suddenly, at 6 a.m. I saw the stones had moved,” said Hala Mustaha, pointing to bright yellow blocks in the middle of Salah al-Din Street in Gaza City. “My neighbours were already moving their things, but I have no idea where I can go.”

A yellow block demarcating what's known as the 'yellow line,' which has separated the Gaza Strip's Israeli-held and Palestinian zones since the October ceasefire, is visible in Jabalia, northern Gaza Strip. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

Essam Dawla had to transplant his family four times.

“The tanks came day after day to shoot at us,” he said, describing the days after the yellow blocks appeared. “Then came the Apache helicopters, with bullets flying into our house. You can’t imagine the panic.”

In the north, satellite images show how the yellow line has moved from October to July, with the nearby Halawa tent camp growing more than 20 times larger as displaced Palestinians are pushed here from their previous shelters.

In the camp, Ismail Al-Barsh sits in front of his tent with a grandson on his lap. He lost another grandson when the boy’s classroom was hit by an Israeli airstrike near the yellow line.

He’s afraid the same will happen here.

“Now even Halawa isn’t safe,” Al-Barsh said. “Every day, we see more gunfire, to advance the yellow line, again.”

Residents of Halawa Camp say they hear fighting and worry that the line will force them to displace again. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

More than 1,200 Palestinians have been killed here since the ceasefire started last fall, according to UN figures. That brings the total of Gazans who have died since this conflict started on Oct. 7, 2023 to more than 70,000, a figure compiled by Gaza officials and reportedly accepted by Israel .

‘Defensive measures’ says Israel

Israel insists its movement of the yellow line is consistent with the ceasefire deal.

In a written reply to questions from CBC News, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it is working “to clearly and visually mark the location of the Yellow Line on the ground in order to reduce friction” with Palestinians.

“Defensive measures,” it said, “are intended to prevent infiltrations and hostile activity, and to protect both the troops and surrounding communities” in Israel.

Those IDF measures include the construction of a berm — a dirt barrier piled high — that the UN says now stretches 23 kilometres, along or behind the yellow line. It towers in the distance over many of the tent camps.

And, increasingly, Israel is building fortified compounds that look like permanent Israeli military bases.

Gaza’s neighbourhoods flattened

Satellite images show one of those military compounds — well inside Gaza — about half way between Israel’s border and the sea. It has permanent guard posts, multiple structures and a paved parking lot — all protected by tanks. Another one, further south in Jabalia, is even larger, and seems more established. Several others are under construction.

Still, Israel isn’t just digging in. It is also tearing down.

Many of Gaza’s neighbourhoods were destroyed during active fighting between Israel and Hamas over two years of war. This came in response to the Oct. 7, 2023 attack on Israel which left approximately 1,200 Israelis dead.

But as satellite images show, many more homes have been systematically flattened by Israeli forces since last October, after most conflict stopped.

Near the Indonesian hospital in northern Gaza, buildings which were still standing last November are now gone. And in Shejaiya, next to Gaza City, entire swaths of housing that are seen in images from October were blown up or bulldozed by April — on both sides of the yellow line.

Between October 2025 and July 2026, neighbourhoods in Gaza have been completely destroyed because of the advancement of the yellow line. (CBC Visual Investigation Unit)

UN experts have denounced “the systematic detonation of residential buildings,” as “re-engineering the geography of illegally occupied Gaza” by Israel.

Palestinians who have watched their homes destroyed say there’s a plan.

“Israel is trying everything to push the people to leave Gaza,” said Alaa Hajjaj. “To make people’s lives miserable.”

Hajjaj is a teacher, now living with his family in a tent in northern Gaza. The rubble of his house sits well behind the yellow line, a place he’s not sure he will ever be able to reach again.

“But for myself, I am not going to leave Gaza, whatever happens,” Hajjaj said. “This is my home. This is my land. I was born on this land and I have memories here and I have everything in this land.”

‘Gaza is ours,’ Israeli groups claim

Officially, the Israeli government denies it is trying to push out Palestinians or annex Gaza.

But there is strong political pressure to do exactly that, including inside Netanyahu’s party and coalition cabinet.

Extremist settler groups like Nachala have repeatedly marched to the Gaza border, running public relations campaigns with videos underlining their demands.

“The people of Israel will cross this fence, and establish settlements here,” Nachala leader Daniella Weiss said, pointing through the barrier into Gaza.

The yellow line has moved westward since the October ceasefire. Here, a block is visible in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip. (Abdel Kareem Hana/AP)

They have been joined by cabinet members from far-right parties. National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir is seen yelling “Gaza is ours,” and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told supporters “there will be no victory” until Jewish settlements are established in Gaza.

Even prominent members of Netanyahu’s own party, Likud, support annexation.

“We are preparing to take hold of the northern part of Gaza,” said Economy Minister Nir Barakat at the border.

Netanyahu himself has skirted the issue, telling one supporter who asked why the IDF should control 70 per cent of Gaza and not all of it, “First 70 per cent. We’ll start with that.”

That may be just talk.

With Israeli elections two months away, and Israeli media predicting Netanyahu is in a tight fight to stay in power, some of that may be political rhetoric aimed to please his own base.

Israel may also be taking a hard line in international negotiations, to pressure Hamas militants to give up their weapons, a move the group has been slow to adopt despite agreeing to it in October’s ceasefire deal.

But for Palestinians moved by yellow markers — and menaced by the guns behind them — there’s a real fear they’re being pushed into the sea.

World.title: Invasive plants are available across Canada. Is federal regulation possible?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian cities are trying to stop invasive plants from being sold in local garden centres, as advocates push Ottawa to create a national approach to regulating the horticultural trade.

With invasive plants threatening biodiversity across the country, municipalities are increasingly trying to fill gaps in a regulatory system that varies by jurisdiction. Canada, meanwhile, has set a target of reducing the rate of introduction and establishment of known invasive species by at least 50 per cent by 2030.

The Canadian Coalition for Invasive Plant Regulation (CCIPR) wants the federal government to establish a regulatory body for the horticultural industry and create a national database identifying invasive plants and their risks in different regions.

"Even if we don't prohibit them, we need to let the public know when there is potential harm," said CCIPR co-founder Cathy Kavassalis. "We do this on other products, and we should do it on plants too. It's just common sense."

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency regulates some invasive plants , while provinces and territories have their own invasive species or weed-control legislation.

CBC News reached out to the Canadian Food Inspection Agency for comment but did not receive a response by publication time.

Goutweed, an invasive plant, in a garden in Clyde River, P.E.I. (Sara Fraser/CBC)

In July, Nanaimo council passed a motion to pursue a bylaw amendment restricting the sale of plants on a list maintained by the Invasive Species Council of B.C. A week later, Surrey moved to ban sales by businesses including nurseries, large retail chains and florists.

In May, London, Ont.'s, environmental committee recommended requiring retailers that sell invasive plants and animals to provide information to customers at the point of sale.

Kavassalis said a problem that could be addressed at higher levels of government is being pushed down to municipalities.

"These are all patchwork solutions that, in some ways, just waste a lot of resources," she said.

Kirsty MacDonald, Nanaimo's parks manager, said invasive plants are already affecting the local landscape, with some posing potential risks to human health.

Most local plant suppliers were aware of the problem, she said, though invasive species can still appear in plant mixes or popular varieties such as English ivy.

"Banning the sale of new introductions [of invasive plants] in backyards, especially, is one method," she said. "It's a many-pronged approach that we need to be looking at to make some headway."

"All levels of government really need to be part of the solution," she said.

A white trillium is surrounded by periwinkle, an invasive plant sold in some stores, in Inglis Falls Conservation Area in Ontario. (Photo by Andy Fyon, supplied by CCIPR)

What advocates want Ottawa to do

Kavassalis said meeting the federal government's 2030 target will require addressing the horticultural trade.

A 2021 study by University of Massachusetts Amherst researchers identified the sale of ornamental non-native plants as a "primary pathway" for introducing invasive plants in the United States. A 2023 study found plant nurseries could contribute about 80 per cent of invasive plant introductions there.

Kavassalis said the same problem exists in Canada.

"Our gardens are actually the source of a lot of harm being done to our environment and economy," she said.

The CCIPR says a national database could give provinces, territories, retailers and gardeners a shared source of information about which plants pose risks in different regions. Kavassalis also wants invasive plants removed from shelves or clearly labelled.

What would new rules mean for nurseries?

Jim Hole, a horticulture and agriculture expert who previously owned Hole Greenhouses and Gardens in St. Albert, Alta., said most garden centres would support efforts to prevent the spread of invasive plants.

When purple loosestrife was identified as invasive to wetlands, he said his greenhouse stopped selling it.

LISTEN | Invasive plants for sale in London, Ont.: London Morning 7:14 Should invasive plants come with warning labels? A group of Londoners are calling on city council to require garden centres to warn customers about buying invasive plants and pets. Brendon Samuels, a member of the city's environmental stewardship and action community advisory committee, joined London Morning with more details about the pitch.

With thousands of plants available, Hole said removing a species is unlikely to threaten a business.

"It's not like you think, 'Oh well, there goes my business. That was a plant that I made all the money off of,'" he said.

He said stronger research, regulation and public education could also help greenhouse owners and farmers who spend time and money controlling unwanted plants.

"The payback is huge if you can keep even one more invasive species out," he said.

Why gardeners still matter

Native plant advocate and author Lorraine Johnson said consumers often don't know which plants are invasive, while nurseries have significant influence over what people put in their gardens.

She said the horticultural industry is "deeply implicated" in biodiversity loss.

"Their main bread and butter is selling non-native plants, introduced plants that have not co-evolved with those insects that we want to support, [or] with the pollinators," she said.

Native plant gardens are beneficial for pollinators, like bees, that play a key role in ecosystems, said Lorraine Johnson, a native plant advocate and author. (Daniel Thomas/CBC/Radio-Canada)

Kavassalis said regulating garden centres can also help gardeners get past "plant blindness," where every green thing can seem equal.

"We need to help the public … treat the plants in their gardens not simply as garden decor, sort of outdoor living space, but as something that's connected to the greater living world."

World.title: Proposed changes to endangered species law would 'stab it to death,' says scientist
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Five former chairs of a panel that advises the federal government on endangered wildlife have published an open letter highlighting concerns over proposed changes to the Species At Risk Act, which they say could lead to the "wilful extinction" of endangered species in Canada.

More than 600 species are listed under the legislation. Changes the government is considering would render the act — and the protection it provides — "meaningless," according to a press release written by the scientists last week.

The scientists, former chairs of the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC), sent the letter to the federal government last month. COSEWIC is an independent advisory panel that assesses species at risk of extinction and makes recommendations to list them under endangered species law.

The scientists opted to make the letter public so that Canadians could avoid being "complicit in the wilful extinction of Canadian Wildlife Species," according to the press release.

The letter comes as the Carney government considers sweeping changes to environmental regulations, including the Species At Risk Act, it says would allow for quicker approval and construction of major projects.

The future of 'jeopardy tests'

In May, two federal discussion papers proposed the approval of major projects before review and exempting certain projects from the "jeopardy test" required under the law, if they're deemed to be in the national interest.

"This is a sledgehammer to the law. It's not necessary," said David Green, a biologist and professor emeritus at McGill University who is one of the former COSEWIC chairs behind the letter.

Jeopardy tests prohibit Ottawa from authorizing projects that would harm species listed under the act and their critical habitats if they would jeopardize their survival. These jeopardy tests are essential to protecting endangered species, according to Green.

"[Jeopardy tests] are the final hurdle. It's the last-ditch protection for things that really need to be protected."

The proposed changes would also give Carney and his cabinet the ability to establish "federal economic zones" where they could then pre-approve industrial development. Cabinet would also gain the power to pre-approve pipelines before a route is established and exempt them from federal impact assessments.

Bill C-5 currently allows projects deemed in the national interest to have their approval process, including environmental assessments, fast-tracked.

The letter mentions a new West Coast oil pipeline, which is currently being considered as a project of national interest, specifically. The proposed pipeline would carry approximately one million barrels of crude oil a day along roughly 1,250 kilometres using a corridor similar to the existing Trans Mountain pipeline, according to the Alberta government.

This would be detrimental to multiple species listed under the act, including the southern resident killer whale — also known as Orcas — and the Chinook salmon, the whale's main food source, according to the scientists.

Both species and their critical habitats exist in the Salish Sea, a network of coastal waterways in southern B.C., where the proposed West Coast pipeline would end.

A southern resident killer whale swims past a school of salmon near the Fraser River, B.C. Chinook salmon are a main food source of the southern resident. (Keith Holmes/The Canadian Press/Hakai Institute)

"If deemed in the national interest, the currently conceived West Coast pipeline could decimate the entire population of the imperilled killer whales through time both directly via increased tanker traffic noise and indirectly via significant destruction of habitat needed for the whales' main prey," the scientists wrote.

"Are Canadians willing to bet this unique population of killer whales against another oil pipeline?"

There are 75 southern resident killer whales in the world.

An 'extraordinary' precedent

Green said he's shocked the Liberal government is proposing these changes.

"It surprises me because the Species At Risk Act was such an important thing to do for a Liberal government 25 years ago.… And now we have a Liberal government that wants to, you know, stab it to death."

Kathryn Harrison, a UBC professor who specializes in climate and energy politics, believes that through Bill C-5 and other changes under consideration, the government is setting an "extraordinary" precedent.

"It's a pretty extraordinary thing to pass new legislation that not only allows the government to waive application of those laws, but gives the government a certain amount of authority to add new laws," she said.

"Rather than going through Parliament and amending those laws, they're passing a new law saying, 'we're not worried about that anymore.'"



The scientists hadn't received a government response to their letter at the time of this article's publication.

The Privy Council Office said the government is "committed to the conservation and recovery of species at risk and to meeting obligations under the Species at Risk Act," in an emailed statement to CBC News.

The federal government has justified the potential changes by arguing Canada needs to fast-track projects that strengthen the economy and diversify exports away from the U.S., amid the ongoing trade war between the two countries.

The Privy Council Office didn't confirm whether they've received the open letter, but said there's been no decision regarding changes to the Species At Risk Act. The email also said the government will release a report highlighting feedback from all Canadians before summer ends.

Following criticism from First Nations and environmental groups, the government extended the public engagement period, which ended last month.

Formal legislation is expected after Parliament resumes in September. Green is cautioning the government to reconsider.

"If you eliminate species from Canada, they're not coming back," he said.

World.title: Ex-defence minister's call for a wartime election puts pressure on Ukraine's Zelenskyy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is under renewed pressure to hold wartime elections, even though under the country's constitution they are not allowed while martial law is in effect.

Zelenskyy, who was elected to power in 2019, is facing a call to hold elections from Mykhailo Fedorov, the young, popular former defence minister who was recently dismissed from his role in government.

Without stipulating a timeline, Fedorov says Ukraine must find "a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of a long war."

Some observers say elections are not feasible at this moment, as the country continues to fight an all-out war with Russia that started in February 2022.

But the political considerations of the calls for change may be something that Zelenskyy cannot necessarily ignore, whether elections are on the immediate horizon or not.

WATCH | Fedorov was once a staunch ally of Zelenskyy: Zelenskyy faces election call from the popular defence minister he fired | Duration 2:05 In what many see as Ukrainian President Voldymyr Zelenskyy's biggest challenge since the 2022 Russian invasion, ousted defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has publicly called for a wartime presidential election. Federov's firing last month triggered protests across Ukraine.

Tymofiy Mylovanov, a former Ukrainian government minister, said Wednesday in a post on X that Fedorov had made the prospect of elections "a vibrant domestic political question," but had not moved forward the likelihood they would occur soon.

He predicted that Zelenskyy, if pressed enough by continued protests, could announce how Ukraine could stage a vote down the road, whether " after the war or under wartime conditions ."

A popular figure

Prior to his dismissal, the 35-year-old Fedorov was publicly seen as a reformer and tech-savvy member of Zelenskyy's government.

Born in 1991 — the year that Ukraine declared its independence from the Soviet Union — Fedorov had previously served as Ukraine's minister of digital transformation and been a vocal proponent of the use of drone warfare in the fight against Russia.

An image of former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov is seen at a rally held in Kyiv in July. The rally was held to denounce the decision by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to dismiss Fedorov after six months in the post. (Efrem Lukatsky/The Associated Press)

Fedorov was named defence minister in January. He was ousted from that role in July in a move that prompted a wave of protests in Ukraine, with calls for Zelenskyy to reverse the decision.

Fedorov said he declined offers to take a different position in the government and that he would not accept any position other than the defence job.

But Zelenskyy did not relent, naming Yevhenii Khmara to the defence role. The appointment was formalized by Ukrainian lawmakers on Wednesday.

Can elections truly be held?

Some question whether elections can truly be held at the moment, given the challenges the war with Russia poses.

That's the view of Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a veteran combat medic who had called for the original protests to reinstate ​Fedorov in July.

"I cannot imagine how to technically provide the possibility of a vote to thousands of service personnel currently serving at the front," he wrote on X, in a post in which he wished Khmara success and indicated that the protest is now over.

A man walks in a street market in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, which was damaged by a Russian drone strike. (Reuters)

Lesia Bidochko, a policy fellow at the European Policy Institute in Kyiv, likewise does not see any realistic procedure for organizing a vote, with millions of Ukrainians living as refugees overseas, displaced within the country, and serving in the military.

She believes Fedorov has veered into "the populist trajectory" in calling for elections.

"Currently, it looks like an elegant ‌way of occupying the opposition space without taking responsibility for the mechanics," she said of Fedorov.

WATCH | Why Russia's Wildberries is coming under attack: Why attack 'Russia's Amazon'? | About That | Duration 1:45 Andrew Chang explains why Ukraine is carrying out drone attacks on warehouses owned by Wildberries — Russia's most profitable online retailer. (Photo credits: Wildberries, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Ukrainian lawmaker Lesia Vasylenko says "it's unrealistic" to talk about an election at the moment.

"It would require a constitutional change," she told Times Radio, something that is a "difficult enough process to orchestrate at peace time and during the martial law regime, it's virtually impossible."

Zelenskyy has yet to respond directly to Fedorov's call, but the president's ​communications adviser Dmytro Lytvyn told reporters that "Russia's daily drone and missile strikes are the exhaustive answer to this question."

Orysia Lutsevych, the head of the Ukraine Forum at Chatham House, called any push to hold wartime elections "a very high-risk bet" that could erode national unity and potentially be exploited by Moscow.

"It will open up a gateway of interference by Russia to wage war by other means," she told Germany's Deutsche Welle broadcaster.

Russia has said Zelenskyy is illegitimate because his term ran out in May 2024 and so cannot sign peace deals on Ukraine's behalf. U.S. President Donald Trump criticized the lack of elections in an interview with Politico in December, saying it was time for a vote.

World.title: Prince Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, are moving back to the U.K. with their children, Buckingham Palace says. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will remain non-working royals and live as private citizens after leaving Britain and stepping back from royal duties in 2020.

Prince Harry and Meghan are moving back to the U.K. | Hanomansing Tonight

Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, ‌are moving back to the United Kingdom with their children, Buckingham Palace confirmed Wednesday.

The news was reported first by The Telegraph.

The Duke and Duchess of ⁠Sussex are relocating with Prince Archie, 7, ‌and Princess Lilibet, 5, but will continue to live as private citizens, the Palace said.

There was no confirmation of when the couple would be back in Britain, but media reports said it would be in time for the children to start school in September.

Harry and Meghan stepped down from full-time royal life and left the U.K. in March 2020. They moved to California later that month after a brief stay in Canada.

WATCH | A royal reconciliation?: Royal Commentator on when Prince Harry met King Charles - a royal reconciliation in the making? | Duration 6:58 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis

The move came as their relationship with the Royal Family deteriorated after they were publicly critical of the monarchy and the family itself.

Harry had some particularly barbed comments for his father and his elder ⁠brother, heir-to-the-throne Prince William, leading to a total breakdown in their relationship.

"It was a really difficult environment, which I think a lot of people saw," Harry said during an interview in February 2021 on The Late, Late Show with James Corden, "so I did what any father or husband would do and thought, how do I get my family out of here?"

Harry was also angry the British ⁠government changed his security arrangements and said the lack of automatic police protection meant he was unable ⁠to ⁠bring his children to Britain.

But he told Corden that he never "walked away" and would never do so.

Lawsuit loss

Harry was among several high-profile British figures ⁠who ‌lost their privacy ⁠lawsuits against the publisher of the British newspaper The Daily Mail's ‌in July that had alleged widespread ​unlawful behaviour.

Harry had testified that The Daily Mail had made Meghan's life "an absolute misery."

In a statement released to British media outlets following the loss, Harry called the decision "a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected."

"However, the lengths to which the court has gone to exonerate the Mail is as shocking as it is totally unwarranted," he said.

King Charles and Queen Camilla were joined by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, right, at the opening ceremony of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland in July. (Phil Noble/Reuters)

Thaw in relations

Relations ​with the King appeared to be starting to thaw last September when father and son met briefly for the first ​time in 20 months.

The entire family visited Britain in July, and King Charles met his grandchildren for the first time since 2022.

The Palace said the King learned of his son's plans to relocate the family on Sunday, and welcomed the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity.

Charles, 77, was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer in early 2024. After receiving treatment, a spokesperson for Buckingham Palace said last December that doctors would be shifting treatment to "a precautionary phase" because the King had "responded exceptionally well to treatment."

World.title: What Trump’s focus on an oil pipeline means for Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump says a Canada-U.S. oil pipeline project cancelled by two of his predecessors "may be awoken from the grave" under a new bilateral trade agreement between the neighbouring nations.

But a former executive involved with Keystone XL and other industry experts suggest the remark may have more to do with politics than petroleum.

In a social media post late Tuesday, less than two hours before punishing new levies on Canadian goods entering the U.S. were due to start, Trump announced a "deal" with Canada and a three-day halt on new tariffs.

"The great Keystone XL Pipeline, long ago killed by Sleepy Joe Biden, may be awoken from the grave!" he wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform, referring to his predecessor in the White House.

Prime Minister Mark Carney did not address this in a statement responding to Trump’s post.

WATCH | U.S. president pauses 50% tariffs on Canadian goods: Trump pauses 50% tariffs, saying new trade deal reached | Duration 6:27 U.S. President Donald Trump has paused 50 per cent tariffs on Canada, saying the two countries have reached a new trade deal that just needs to be finalized. In a statement, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'substantial progress has been made.'

For U.S., Keystone XL 'can be a nightmare'

"The fact that Trump has signalled that is something that he sees in the deal, I think is helpful to Carney [and] the trade-offs he's going to have to make over the next 72 hours," said Dennis McConaghy, former executive vice-president of corporate development at TransCanada Corporation, now called TC Energy.

From auto parts and lumber to steel and aluminum, the Republican president has targeted key sectors of Canada's economy since Feb. 1, 2025, when his administration announced sweeping tariffs on goods from Canada.

Since then, he has regularly stated that the U.S. does not need anything that Canada has, even as key items like oil, potash and critical minerals have stayed exempt from U.S. tariffs.

"In the context of a person who says we don't need anything from Canada, that [Keystone XL remark] was somewhat welcome," McConaghy said.

However, Carlo Dade, director of international policy at the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy, told CBC Radio's Calgary Eyeopener that a revival of the controversial project would face familiar political and environmental challenges today.

"Let's not get too excited about Keystone just yet," Dade said on Wednesday.

"Will it be done by the end of his term? Because we potentially have Democrats ... in the offing, which is going to make this extremely difficult," he said. "He looks at this as a rejection of the policies of previous administrations, Biden, Democrats, et cetera."

Valérie Beaudoin, a member of the federal government's Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, said greenlighting Keystone XL will be far easier for Carney than Trump.

"For them, it can be a nightmare," she said. "Even if Trump says, 'Oh, Keystone XL is back on track,' who is going to want to invest when we know in 2028, the next president can be a Democrat?"

"It's all definitely meant as a retort to Biden," Commodity Context founder Rory Johnston told CBC News in an email. "[It] would be completely out of the blue, and make little immediate sense, to literally reanimate KXL given the work done on the other projects thus far. [It's] also a much different market from when KXL was initially proposed."

Ottawa revives interest in Keystone XL

About 85 to 90 per cent of Canada's crude oil exports go directly to the U.S., down slightly since the 2024 expansion of the Trans Mountain pipeline, which ships to Asian and other non-U.S. markets from terminals on the West Coast.

Owned and operated by Calgary-based South Bow Corp., the 4,327-kilometre Keystone Pipeline System delivers Canadian and U.S. crude oil to American refining markets in Illinois, Oklahoma and Texas.

WATCH | Trump suggests Keystone XL pipeline could be revived: Trump hints Keystone XL pipeline may be 'awoken from the grave' | Duration 2:08 In a late-night post on his Truth Social account, U.S. President Donald Trump hinted at a possible rebirth of the cancelled Keystone XL pipeline. The post included an AI-generated image of Trump pulling the pipeline out of a grave.

South Bow did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

In 2008, TransCanada and ConocoPhillips, the owners of Keystone at the time, proposed a major extension to the network called Keystone XL. After years of political, legal and environmental opposition, including cancellation by the Obama and Biden administrations in the U.S., the project was effectively abandoned by its backers.

When he returned to the White House in 2025, Trump rescinded Biden's revocation order and granted approvals to revive sections of the project in the U.S. Since then, he's openly praised the project's merits on multiple occasions.

Last fall, CBC News reported that Carney raised the project with Trump, expressing his renewed interest in advancing Keystone XL. The project remains fully permitted by the Canadian government. By 2021, about 150 kilometres of pipe were installed in Alberta.

Prairie Connector project

South Bow was ‌created in 2024, when TC Energy spun off its oil pipeline business in a pivot toward natural gas. The company is currently working with Wyoming-based midstream firm Bridger Pipeline on a project called Prairie Connector using parts of the cancelled Keystone XL pipeline previously built on the Canadian side of the border.

If built, the Prairie Connector project could increase Canada's crude ​exports to the U.S. by more than 12 per cent.

"If this project were to be built, it adds substantial value," said former TransCanada executive McConaghy.

South Bow CEO Bevin Wirzba has touted brisk long-term U.S. demand for Canadian crude, citing the company’s recent open-season process for Prairie Connector.

The company says this yielded 20-year binding commitments from nine customers, totalling 465,000 barrels of oil per day of firm transportation service from Hardisty, Alta., to South Bow’s U.S. delivery points.

South Bow has yet to issue a final investment decision on the project.

"Disruptions to global crude oil trade drove increased demand for connectivity to refining and export markets,” Wirzba told stock market analysts on a post-earnings conference call on Aug. 5.

"And we've consistently said that the demand in the Gulf Coast for Canadian crude into that refining market was and is and will be resilient for decades to come."

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity. The duty of a leader is to bring the truth to the doorstep of justice and stop there, scrupulously respecting the independence and majesty of the judicial system. That moment has arrived. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president blamed the budget deficit on the “sacking” of the Petro administration rather than Congress’s failure to approve the legislation that allowed the previous government to carry out its 2026 budget.

De la Espriella previously said he would extradite Petro if the US Government asked him to.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.
