Almost one-quarter of respondents (23.5%) chose the “neutral” option in response to the question about the safety of their deposits in banks in Mexico.

Only 5% of respondents think their money is “unsafe” (4.5%) or “very unsafe” (less than 0.5%) in a bank in Mexico.

One factor that may have influenced people’s perceptions about the safety of their money in banks in Mexico is that federal Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora promptly reassured CIBanco and Intercam account holders that their money was “absolutely” safe after the U.S. Department of the Treasury last year accused the banks of laundering millions of dollars for drug cartels, prompting the government to take control of them. For the vast majority of CIBanco and Intercam customers that proved to be the case, although account holders who responded to a previous Mexico News Daily survey did face a range of inconveniences linked to the U.S. accusations.

8 in 10 respondents don’t have a Mexican credit card

Almost 37% of respondents don’t have a checking account based in Mexico, 58% don’t have a savings account with a bank in Mexico and a striking 79% don’t have a credit card issued by a Mexico-based bank.

A strong majority of respondents (72%) do, however, have a debit card issued by a Mexico-based bank.

The results suggest that many foreigners in Mexico use credit cards issued by banks in their countries of origin.

One possible reason why many foreigners opt not to get a credit card from a bank in Mexico is that credit card interest rates are typically very high.

8 of 10 respondents have made some kind of investment in Mexico

Only 21% of respondents have not invested in at least one of real estate, stocks, bonds or a business in Mexico. The remaining 79% of surveyed foreigners have invested in at least one of those assets.

The purchase of a home in Mexico was easily the most popular investment. Seven in 10 respondents (71%) own a home in Mexico, while 14% have a property in which they don’t currently live. Just over 12% of respondents receive rental income from a property they own in Mexico.

One in 10 respondents (10%) has invested in a business in Mexico, while 8% of surveyed foreigners have bought stocks and 9% have purchased bonds.

A strong majority of respondents have not had ‘money issues’ with contractors or other service providers in Mexico

Over eight in ten respondents (83%) of respondents have not had “money issues” with contractors in Mexico.

Almost nine in 10 surveyed foreigners (87%) have not had “money issues” with people who provide regular services to them in Mexico, such as landlords, cleaners or gardeners.

* Read about some of the money issues respondents have experienced with contractors and other service providers in the final section of this article.

Most respondents have not been a victim of a financial crime in Mexico

Over eight in ten respondents (82%) have not been a victim of a financial crime in Mexico, whereas 18% of survey respondents have been a victim of such an offense.

* Read about some of the financial crimes respondents have suffered in the final section of this article.

The vast majority of respondents have not borrowed money from a financial institution in Mexico

Almost 97% of respondents have not borrowed money from a financial institution in Mexico. Just over 3% of surveyed foreigners have borrowed money in Mexico.

This result suggests that the vast majority of respondents purchased real estate, vehicles and other assets in Mexico with their own funds or took out loans abroad.

As is the case with credit cards, the high cost of credit in Mexico is a deterrent to taking out loans in Mexico for many foreigners.

Rising prices in Mexico have negatively affected the lifestyles of 4 in 10 respondents

The increase in prices in Mexico in recent years has negatively affected the lifestyles of around four in ten (38%) respondents.

The lifestyles of the remaining 62% of surveyed foreigners have not been adversely affected by rising prices.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate fell to 3.12% in July, the lowest level in more than six years. However, inflation in Mexico was much higher in earlier years of this decade, peaking at an annual headline rate of 8.7% August and September of 2022.

Inflation, combined with other factors such as the strength of the peso, has made life in Mexico considerably more expensive in recent years.

Respondents are, on average, ‘somewhat concerned’ about fluctuations in the USD:MXN exchange rate

MND asked survey respondents to rate their concern over fluctuations in the value of the Mexican peso or the US dollar on a scale of 0 to 100.

On the scale, 0 meant “unconcerned”; 50 signified “somewhat concerned”; and 100 denoted “always concerned.”

The average response among respondents was 53, indicating that the surveyed foreigners are, collectively speaking, “somewhat concerned” about fluctuations in the USD:MXN exchange rate.

In general, fluctuations in the exchange rate are more of a concern now for foreigners in Mexico than in years gone by because, over a period spanning decades, the value of the peso against the US dollar trended down. However, in recent years the peso has bucked that trend, appreciating more than 10% against the greenback between 2021 and 2025, and continuing to strengthen this year.

A majority of respondents have loaned money in Mexico

Over half of the survey respondents have loaned money locally while living in Mexico.

Around 22% of respondents have loaned an amount under US $500, while 20% have lent between $500 and $3,000. About 11.5% of respondents have lent over $3,000 to someone in Mexico. Those three percentages add up to about 53.5%.

The remaining 46.5% of surveyed foreigners haven’t lent money to anyone while living in Mexico.

15% is the most common restaurant tip rate among respondents

Almost 48% of respondents typically tip “roughly 15%” of their total bill at restaurants in Mexico.

Almost 30% of surveyed foreigners usually tip “roughly 20%” when eating out, while 18.5% typically leave gratuities of “roughly 10%” of their total bill.

Just over 2% of respondents typically tip more than 20% of their total restaurant bill, while just under 2% usually tip less than 10%.

Your say

We asked survey respondents to provide additional information if they have experienced money issues with contractors and/or service providers in Mexico or if they have been a victim of a financial crime here. Many of the survey respondents who said they have been a victim of a financial crime recounted stories of being mugged, pickpocketed or having money stolen from their homes.

Below is a (lightly edited) selection of the comments we received.

Money issues with contractors

I paid for materials I didn’t get.

The price changed during the project due to the number of man-hours worked.

I had disagreements over what was included with certain construction costs. The disagreements arose from familiarity with what is typical in the U.S. versus what is typical in Mexico.

I paid for products and services I never received.

I didn’t receive reimbursement for a shoddy job.

I paid upfront for work that never happened or was executed poorly.

The contractor demanded more money than we agreed on.

The contractor failed to complete work and stole building materials.

Money issues with contractors and providers of regular services

A cleaning lady we had for eight years was stealing money from our purse and wallets during the whole time she was working for us.

A landlord kept my 20,000-peso security deposit without cause.

In order to continue having hot water in the apartment, I had to purchase equipment and pay for the installation because the landlord would not.

My rent increased above the agreed-upon rate. The increase was much higher than the standard rate increase in San Miguel de Allende.

The gardener wanted more money and simply stopped working until he got his raise.

I’m a former timeshare owner and the maintenance fee was immediately doubled after I was informed it was being adjusted because it was unfair. This was almost 20 years ago. It was extremely intimidating and I was threatened. Now that we know about cartel involvement in timeshares, I am so glad we got out even though we had to pay US $10,000.

My landlord insisted on me paying rent in US dollars, then stopped when the dollar weakened. The landlord greatly increased my rent, specifically saying, “My expenses have gone up because of inflation and the dollar isn’t worth as much.” She then converted the rent from dollars into pesos, increasing it by 20%.

I have had minor issues but have always been able to work them out. That’s life anywhere.

Financial crimes in Mexico

I was a victim of fraud when purchasing a car.

I was mugged. I lost my phone and wallet.

I was robbed of money, jewelry and a tablet by a “nurse” taking care of me.

Someone hacked my virtual HSBC card and ran up unauthorized charges.

I was the victim of the fraudulent sale of a timeshare.

An employee of a Mexican bank was siphoning funds and using new deposits to cover withdrawals. She was caught. I had to testify against her in exchange for the bank honoring my account balance.

I was coerced into a timeshare purchase.

A vacation rental that I paid for in advance was not owned or managed by the guy who rented it to me.

I was a victim of a credit card scam in a taxi.

A fruit vendor gave me counterfeit money.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Peso punches below 17 to the US dollar for the second time in a week
World.content:
Listen to this article

Buoyed by a weaker greenback, the Mexican peso appreciated on Wednesday morning to trade below 17 to the US dollar.

At midday Mexico City time, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 16.97, according to Bloomberg.

Earlier on Wednesday, the peso reached 16.95 to the dollar, its strongest position since June 2024. Compared to the Bank of Mexico’s closing USD:MXN rate of 17.06 on Tuesday, the peso appreciated 0.65% to reach 16.95 to the dollar.

Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, wrote on X that the peso appreciated on Wednesday morning due to “the weakness of the dollar” as a result of the U.S. Treasury Department’s announcement that it was increasing a bond buyback operation. The dollar weakened after the Treasury Department announced in a statement that it was “increasing, by at least double, the size of liquidity support buyback operations for longer-dated nominal coupon securities (the 10-year to 20-year sector and the 20-year to 30-year sector).”

At midday, the US Dollar Index, which measures the greenback against a basket of foreign currencies, was down 0.7% compared to the closing level on Tuesday.

Janneth Quiroz, director of economic analysis at the Monex financial group, said that the peso benefited from “the retreat of the dollar” and from the United States’ decision on Tuesday to pause planned 50% tariffs on almost $30 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The appreciation of the peso on Wednesday morning came after the currency broke the 17-unit-per-dollar floor last Friday morning. However, the peso closed at 17.03 to the dollar on Friday, according to the Bank of Mexico, and was also above 17 at the end of trading on Monday and Tuesday.

The peso has appreciated around 6% against the dollar so far this year after ending 2025 at 18.00 to the greenback.

In the most recent MND Peso Index™ analysis, which was conducted in early August when the USD:MXN rate was 17.22, the peso was found to be overvalued against the dollar by 2.4%.

With reports from El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Nigeria Cement Prices Probed as Regulator Summons the Biggest Producers
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

NIGERIA · MARKETS

Key Facts —The action: The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission has opened a formal inquiry into Nigeria cement prices, issuing a Notice of Commencement of Investigation and Summons to Produce to the country’s major cement manufacturers. It was announced on Tuesday 18 August. —The price path: A 50kg bag sold for NGN 9,300 to NGN 9,700 in January 2026, about US$7. It reached NGN 10,500 to NGN 13,000 by mid-year and NGN 13,000 to NGN 15,000 in some regions by July, up to about US$11. —The paradox: Installed capacity is put at around 65 million tonnes a year against domestic consumption of 25 to 30 million tonnes. The commission says Nigeria is a net exporter of cement to neighbouring markets. —The comparison: The commission cites a bag at about US$5.40 in Kenya and US$4.80 in Tanzania. Togo, which has no limestone deposits of its own, is put at about US$6.75. —Who is named: The commission’s own statement names no company and refers only to “key players”. Business Post named Dangote Cement, BUA Cement and HBM Nigeria, formerly Lafarge Africa. The Nation listed the same three as the producers behind more than 90% of national capacity. —One holdout: ThisDay reports that every major manufacturer cooperated with the underlying study except one. The commission has not identified that company. —No finding yet: The commission says the preliminary findings are not a final determination of wrongdoing. Executive vice chairman and chief executive Tunji Bello says the aim is not to dictate commercial decisions. None of the three companies had responded publicly at the time of reporting.

Nigeria cement prices are now the subject of a formal competition investigation. The country’s antitrust regulator summoned the dominant producers on Tuesday 18 August, demanding pricing methods, capacity utilisation rates, export volumes and distribution agreements after a three-month cross-border study.

Why Nigeria cement prices drew the regulator in

The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission built its case on a 40-page industry-wide field report and a three-month cross-border study by its Anticompetitive Practices Department. The work began after complaints about the cost of cement.

The question it set out to answer is uncomfortable for the industry. Nigeria has abundant limestone, more plant capacity than it can absorb, and retail cement prices well above the other African markets the commission examined.

A 50kg bag moved from NGN 9,300 to NGN 9,700 in January, to NGN 10,500 to NGN 13,000 by mid-year, and to between NGN 13,000 and NGN 15,000 in parts of the country by July, according to the commission’s figures. At about 1,350 naira to the dollar in mid-August, that is a move from roughly US$7 a bag to as much as US$11.

The commission’s own regional comparison is the sharper point. It puts a bag at roughly US$5.40 in Kenya, or NGN 7,344, and US$4.80 in Tanzania, or NGN 6,528. Those conversions imply a rate of 1,360 naira to the dollar, which the commission does not state outright. Both countries used about 9.3 million tonnes of cement in 2025.

The Togo test

The most awkward benchmark in the commission’s file is Togo. The commission notes that Togo has no limestone deposit of its own, yet a bag there is put at about US$6.75, or NGN 9,180.

That comparison is designed to close off the usual defences. Energy costs, logistics and the price of imported inputs are real pressures, but they do not obviously explain a gap of this size against a country with no domestic raw material at all.

Nigerian producers have historically pointed to gas supply, diesel for haulage and the cost of imported spares. Those arguments will now be tested against documents rather than in public.

What the summons actually demands

Under the notice, the recipients must produce detailed records of their pricing methods, factory capacity utilisation rates, export volumes and distribution network agreements. Each of those four categories is chosen with care.

Pricing methods and capacity utilisation together show whether plants are being run below capacity while prices rise. Export volumes reveal how much output is leaving a market said to be short of supply.

Distribution agreements are the least discussed and often the most revealing. Competition authorities elsewhere have found that pricing discipline is enforced at the depot and dealer level rather than in the boardroom.

Three companies, one market

The commission’s statement, signed by its director of corporate affairs Ondaje Ijagwu, names no company at all. It refers to “key players in the cement industry”. Business Post went further and named Dangote Cement, BUA Cement and HBM Nigeria, the former Lafarge Africa, in its headline. The Nation listed the same three as the producers behind more than 90% of national output. ThisDay carried the statement in full and named none of them.

Publicly available estimates put their combined share above 90% of installed capacity: about 35.3 million tonnes a year for Dangote Cement in Nigeria, 17 million for BUA Cement and 10.5 million for HBM Nigeria. All three are listed on the Nigerian Exchange, where the former Lafarge Africa now trades as HBMNG after dropping the old WAPCO ticker.

One detail has drawn less attention than it deserves. ThisDay reports that all major manufacturers cooperated with the underlying investigation except one, and the commission has not said which.

A refusal to cooperate with a preliminary study is not itself evidence of anything. It does tend to shape how a regulator approaches the formal stage.

The timing is not neutral

The summons lands while the Dangote group is marketing its refinery to investors. Dangote Petroleum Refinery filed for a listing with Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission on 4 August, seeking about US$5 billion, and on 18 August it secured a US$1 billion underwriting programme. Attention on the wider group’s pricing power is not welcome in that window.

It also cuts against a central claim of the current reform programme. Removing fuel subsidies and unifying the exchange rate were meant to restore price discipline, and cement is a visible test of whether that has happened.

For anyone holding Nigerian equities, the read-across is straightforward enough. Cement has been one of the most reliably profitable sectors on the exchange, and a regulator now wants to know why.

What happens next, and what has not happened

Nothing has been proven. The commission has stated plainly that the preliminary findings are not a final determination of wrongdoing, and executive vice chairman and chief executive Tunji Bello says competition law does not stop firms earning a return on their investments.

The companies must now produce the documents, after which the commission decides whether to escalate. The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 gives the commission its summons power under section 33, and failing to produce documents without sufficient cause carries up to three years in prison or a fine of up to NGN 20 million, about US$15,000. Proven abuse of a dominant position exposes a company to a fine of at least 10% of its turnover in the preceding business year. No case has yet been brought.

None of the three named producers had responded publicly at the time of reporting. Their answers, when they come, will be the next real development in this story.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Nigeria investigating cement prices? The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission found indications of possible price manipulation after a three-month cross-border study. It has summoned the country’s major manufacturers to produce pricing and capacity records. How much has cement risen in Nigeria in 2026? A 50kg bag sold for NGN 9,300 to NGN 9,700 in January 2026, about US$7. By July it reached NGN 13,000 to NGN 15,000 in some regions, or as much as US$11, according to the commission’s figures. Which companies received the summons? The commission named no company, referring only to “key players”. Business Post named Dangote Cement, BUA Cement and HBM Nigeria, the former Lafarge Africa, and The Nation listed the same three as the producers behind more than 90% of capacity. ThisDay carried the statement without naming any of them. Has any wrongdoing been established? No. The commission says the preliminary findings are not a final determination of wrongdoing, and none of the companies had responded publicly at the time of reporting.

World.title: Argentina Just Told Banks How to Lend Dollars to Companies That Do Not Earn Them
World.content:
Argentina · Banking

Key Facts What changed Banks may now lend dollars to companies that do not earn foreign currency, which was previously barred.

Banks may now lend dollars to companies that do not earn foreign currency, which was previously barred. The legal instrument DNU 736/2026, published on 14 August, amending Article 23 of Decree 905/2002.

DNU 736/2026, published on 14 August, amending Article 23 of Decree 905/2002. The cap Lending under the new regime cannot exceed 15% of each bank’s foreign-currency deposits.

Lending under the new regime cannot exceed 15% of each bank’s foreign-currency deposits. The capital cost Banks must hold 125% of the capital a comparable loan would require, and count the exposure at 1.25 times.

Banks must hold 125% of the capital a comparable loan would require, and count the exposure at 1.25 times. The stress test Lenders must assess borrowers under different exchange-rate scenarios before approving.

Lenders must assess borrowers under different exchange-rate scenarios before approving. The currency rule If the money is spent domestically, borrowers must sell the dollars through the official market.

If the money is spent domestically, borrowers must sell the dollars through the official market. The governor’s view Santiago Bausili says the central bank does not expect a lending boom.

The decree opened the door last week. This week the central bank explained how narrow the doorway is.

For most of the last two decades an Argentine company that did not export could not borrow dollars from an Argentine bank. The rule existed because of what happens when a devaluation meets a peso-earning borrower with a dollar debt. That rule has now gone — and this week the central bank published the Argentina dollar lending rules that replace it, which turn out to be considerably tighter than the headline suggested.

The Banco Central in Buenos Aires, which published the fine print this week. (Photo internet reproduction)

What the Argentina dollar lending rules actually say

The opening came through DNU 736/2026, published on 14 August, which amended Article 23 of Decree 905/2002 — the post-2001 rule that confined dollar lending to companies with dollar income. The central bank then issued the implementing regulations.

Four constraints matter. First, a ceiling: lending under the new regime cannot exceed 15% of each bank’s foreign-currency deposits. Second, capital: banks must hold 125% of what a comparable loan would require. Third, exposure: the loan counts at 1.25 times normal weighting against concentration limits. Fourth, a repayment test under varying exchange-rate scenarios.

And if the borrower spends the money in Argentina, the dollars must be sold through the official exchange market rather than held.

Taken together those are not the terms of a credit expansion. They are the terms of a controlled experiment.

How much money this could actually be

Estimates vary by roughly a factor of two. One reading puts the immediately lendable amount near US$5.2 billion, about a fifth of the existing stock of dollar loans. Another puts the eventual scope at US$6 billion to US$10 billion.

The reason the range is wide is that the binding constraint is deposits, and deposits have moved fast. Dollar deposits in the Argentine system rose from around US$23 billion to about US$40 billion before the rule changed, largely on the back of the tax amnesty that pulled savings out of mattresses and safe deposit boxes.

Fifteen per cent of a growing number is a moving target. That is presumably the point of expressing the cap as a ratio.

Why the governor is playing it down

Santiago Bausili, who runs the central bank, has said plainly that he does not expect a boom. He has framed the change as flexibility with prudence.

That is not false modesty. Argentina has run this experiment before, and the 2001 crisis is the reference everyone in the room is thinking about: companies borrowed in dollars, earned in pesos, and were destroyed when the peg broke. The prudential loading in these rules exists precisely to make banks price that risk rather than assume it away.

There is also a separate strand of debt management running alongside. The Treasury and the central bank have been swapping dollar-denominated instruments to push maturities further out, which is housekeeping rather than policy but tells you where the attention is.

Why this matters if you run a business in Argentina

If your company earns pesos and buys imported inputs, dollar credit at a bank rate is cheaper than the alternatives you have been using. That is a genuine improvement, and it is the first time it has been available to you since 2002.

The caution is the one the central bank has written into the rules. A dollar loan is a bet that the peso will not move sharply against you before you repay. Argentine businesses have taken that bet before, and the history is not encouraging. The stress-test requirement means your bank will now make you demonstrate you have thought about it.

For the wider economy, the number to watch is not how much is lent. It is whether the dollars stay in the banking system. The rule requiring domestic spending to route through the official market is what stops this becoming a channel for capital flight, and it is the provision most likely to be tested.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the new Argentina dollar lending rules? Banks may now lend dollars to companies that do not generate foreign-currency income, which Decree 905/2002 had prohibited. The opening came via DNU 736/2026, published on 14 August 2026, and the central bank has since issued the implementing regulations. Lending under the regime is capped at 15% of each bank’s foreign-currency deposits. What conditions apply? Banks must hold 125% of the capital a comparable loan would require and count the exposure at 1.25 times normal weighting. They must assess borrowers under different exchange-rate scenarios. And if the borrower spends the funds inside Argentina, the dollars must be sold through the official exchange market. How much new credit could this unlock? Estimates range from about US$5.2 billion — roughly a fifth of the existing stock of dollar loans — to between US$6 billion and US$10 billion. The cap is a share of deposits, and dollar deposits in the system had risen from around US$23 billion to about US$40 billion before the change. Does the central bank expect a lending boom? No. Governor Santiago Bausili has said the central bank does not expect one, describing the change as flexibility with prudence. The capital and exposure loadings in the regulations are designed to make banks price currency risk rather than assume it away.

World.title: Brazil’s Top Court Extends Its Domestic-Violence Protections Beyond the Home
World.content:
Brazil · Law

Key Facts The ruling A majority of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court held that Maria da Penha protective measures can be applied where there is no domestic or family link.

A majority of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court held that Maria da Penha protective measures can be applied where there is no domestic or family link. When The majority formed on 19 August 2026.

The majority formed on 19 August 2026. What changes A woman attacked by a stranger, a colleague or an acquaintance can seek the same urgent orders as one attacked at home.

A woman attacked by a stranger, a colleague or an acquaintance can seek the same urgent orders as one attacked at home. What the orders do They can bar an aggressor from approaching, from contact, and from the victim’s home or workplace, at speed.

They can bar an aggressor from approaching, from contact, and from the victim’s home or workplace, at speed. Why it matters These measures are the fastest instrument Brazilian law offers, obtainable in days rather than months.

These measures are the fastest instrument Brazilian law offers, obtainable in days rather than months. The original law Lei Maria da Penha, 11.340/2006, named after a woman whose husband shot her and left her paraplegic.

Lei Maria da Penha, 11.340/2006, named after a woman whose husband shot her and left her paraplegic. What it is not This is not a new criminal offence. It extends who can obtain an existing protective remedy.

The 2006 law was written for violence inside the household. The court has now said the restraining orders do not have to stop at the front door.

Brazil’s Maria da Penha law has been the country’s main answer to violence against women for twenty years, and the Maria da Penha protective measures are the fastest thing in Brazilian law: a judge can bar a man from coming near a woman in a matter of days. The catch was always that the law was built around the household. On 19 August the Supreme Federal Court said that limit no longer holds.

Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court extended the law’s protective measures on 19 August. (Photo internet reproduction)

What the court decided about Maria da Penha protective measures

A majority of the Supreme Federal Court held that the urgent protective measures created by the Maria da Penha law can be granted in cases of violence against women where there is no domestic, family or intimate relationship between the woman and the man.

In practical terms that covers a great deal of ordinary life: a woman harassed by a neighbour she has never spoken to, stalked by a colleague, threatened by a customer, followed by a stranger. Until now those cases had to travel through slower general-purpose procedures, or lean on protective instruments that were harder to obtain.

It is worth being precise about what has changed. No new crime has been created. What the court extended is access to a remedy — the order that keeps a man away while everything else is decided.

Why the speed is the point

Protective measures under the Maria da Penha law can be requested at a police station and granted by a judge within days, sometimes within hours. They can prohibit approach within a set distance, prohibit contact by any means, and bar the aggressor from the woman’s home, workplace or usual places.

That timescale is the entire value of the instrument. Ordinary Brazilian civil and criminal procedure moves in months. Violence against women does not.

Extending that speed to cases without a domestic link closes a gap that women’s organisations and prosecutors have been pointing at for years: the law was most powerful exactly where the relationship was closest, and weakest where the man was a stranger.

Where the law came from

The law carries the name of Maria da Penha Maia Fernandes, a pharmacist from Ceará whose husband shot her while she slept in 1983, leaving her paraplegic, and later attempted to electrocute her. He remained free for nearly two decades.

Her case went to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which found in 2001 that Brazil had failed in its duty to act. Lei 11.340 followed in 2006 and is regarded internationally as one of the stronger legal frameworks on domestic violence.

Its enforcement has always been the weaker half. Brazil records among the highest absolute numbers of femicides in the world, and the distance between what the law provides and what a woman actually receives at a police counter is the country’s persistent problem.

Why this matters if you live in Brazil

If you are a woman living in Brazil, the practical change is what you can ask for and where. You no longer need a domestic or family relationship with the man in question to seek an urgent protective order.

Foreign residents should know these measures are not conditional on nationality or immigration status. Any woman in Brazil can request them, and specialised women’s police stations — delegacias da mulher — exist in most cities and are the place to start.

The wider point is about how Brazilian law changes. A great deal of it moves through the Supreme Court reinterpreting statutes rather than through Congress passing new ones. If you follow Brazilian legal developments as a resident or an investor, that is the mechanism to watch.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Supreme Court decide about Maria da Penha protective measures? On 19 August 2026 a majority of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court held that the urgent protective measures created by the Maria da Penha law can be granted in cases of violence against women even where there is no domestic, family or intimate relationship between the woman and the aggressor. Does this create a new crime? No. It extends access to an existing remedy. The protective measures are court orders that can bar an aggressor from approaching a woman, contacting her, or going near her home or workplace. The ruling widens who can obtain them; it does not change the criminal code. How fast are these measures? They are the fastest instrument in Brazilian law for this purpose. A request can be made at a police station and granted by a judge within days, sometimes hours, well ahead of any criminal or civil proceeding. Can foreign residents use them? Yes. The measures are not conditional on nationality or immigration status. Any woman in Brazil can request them. Specialised women’s police stations, known as delegacias da mulher, operate in most cities and are the usual starting point.

World.title: Rio’s Former Assembly Speaker Goes on Trial Over a Tipped-Off Police Raid
World.content:
Brazil · Justice

Key Facts Who Rodrigo Bacellar, former president of Rio de Janeiro’s state assembly, the Alerj.

Rodrigo Bacellar, former president of Rio de Janeiro’s state assembly, the Alerj. What happened The Supreme Federal Court’s First Chamber accepted the charges in mid-August, making him a defendant.

The Supreme Federal Court’s First Chamber accepted the charges in mid-August, making him a defendant. The charge Obstruction of a federal investigation into the Comando Vermelho. Not membership of it.

Obstruction of a federal investigation into the Comando Vermelho. Not membership of it. The alleged chain A federal appeals judge, Macário Ramos Júdice Neto, is accused of leaking details of Operation Zargum.

A federal appeals judge, Macário Ramos Júdice Neto, is accused of leaking details of Operation Zargum. Where it went Prosecutors say the information reached Bacellar, who warned the former state deputy known as TH Joias.

Prosecutors say the information reached Bacellar, who warned the former state deputy known as TH Joias. The consequence alleged Evidence removed and the target evading the operation before police moved.

Evidence removed and the target evading the operation before police moved. The political note Bacellar is described in Brazilian coverage as an ally of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

The allegation is not that he belonged to a gang. It is that a warning travelled from a courthouse to a target before the police arrived.

The Rodrigo Bacellar trial is about something narrower than the headlines suggest, and more troubling. Nobody is alleging that Rio de Janeiro’s former assembly speaker joined a criminal faction. The allegation is that a confidential police operation against the Comando Vermelho leaked out of a courthouse, travelled through him, and reached its target in time.

The Supreme Federal Court, whose First Chamber accepted the charges. (Photo internet reproduction)

What the Rodrigo Bacellar trial is about

The First Chamber of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court accepted the prosecution’s complaint in mid-August, which converts Bacellar from an investigated person into a defendant. The charge is obstruction of a criminal investigation.

According to the complaint filed by the prosecutor-general’s office, a federal appeals judge, Macário Ramos Júdice Neto, leaked confidential information about Operation Zargum — a federal operation targeting Comando Vermelho structures in Rio de Janeiro.

Prosecutors allege that information passed to Bacellar, then president of the Alerj, and from him to the former state deputy known as TH Joias, who was able to remove evidence and avoid the operation.

If that account is proved, the offence is not corruption in the ordinary sense. It is the transmission of state secrets through the political system to the people the state was moving against.

Why the distinction matters

Rio’s political scandals usually involve militias — the paramilitary groups, often built from serving and former police, that control territory and extract payments. Coverage of any Rio case tends to reach for that frame.

This is a different shape. The Comando Vermelho is a drug-trafficking faction, not a militia, and the accusation here is about a leak rather than membership or protection payments.

That matters legally, because obstruction and criminal association carry different penalties and different proof requirements. It also matters journalistically, because a case described loosely as “gang ties” is a different allegation from the one actually before the court.

The institutional problem underneath

The most serious element is the alleged first link in the chain. A leak from a legislature is a political failure. A leak from a federal appeals judge is a failure of the institution that is supposed to authorise and supervise operations of this kind.

Federal police operations against factions in Rio depend on judicial confidentiality holding for the days between authorisation and execution. If it does not hold, the operations do not work, and everyone involved knows it.

Bacellar is entitled to the presumption of innocence, and acceptance of a complaint is a decision that there is enough to hold a trial — not a finding of guilt.

Why this matters if you live in Rio

Anyone living in Rio has watched police operations in the city’s favelas produce casualties and headlines with limited durable effect on who controls what. This case offers one explanation that is rarely visible: some of those operations may have been compromised before they began.

It also lands in an election year, and Bacellar’s description in Brazilian coverage as an ally of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro guarantees the case will be read politically by everybody, whatever the evidence turns out to show.

The practical read for residents is narrower and more useful. Watch what happens to Operation Zargum’s underlying targets. That, rather than the political noise, is the measure of what the alleged leak cost.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Rodrigo Bacellar trial about? Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court accepted a prosecution complaint in mid-August 2026 making Rodrigo Bacellar, the former president of Rio de Janeiro’s state assembly, a defendant on a charge of obstructing a federal investigation into the Comando Vermelho criminal faction. Is he accused of belonging to a criminal organisation? No. The charge is obstruction of a criminal investigation. Prosecutors allege that confidential details of Operation Zargum were leaked and reached a target in time for evidence to be removed. That is a different offence from membership of, or association with, a criminal organisation. Who else is named? The complaint alleges that a federal appeals judge, Macário Ramos Júdice Neto, leaked the operational information, that it passed to Bacellar, and that Bacellar warned the former state deputy known as TH Joias. Does accepting the complaint mean he has been convicted? No. Accepting a complaint means the court considers there is sufficient basis to proceed to trial. Bacellar retains the presumption of innocence and the case has not been decided.

Sources: Procuradoria-Geral da República case coverage via Brazilian outlets

World.title: Venezuela’s Oil Minister Went to Houston and Signed Two Deals
World.content:
Venezuela · Energy

Key Facts Who Paula Henao, Venezuela’s oil minister, in Houston on 18 and 19 August.

Paula Henao, Venezuela’s oil minister, in Houston on 18 and 19 August. Deal one A hydrocarbons production participation agreement with Hunt Oil covering two oil fields, aimed at recovering production.

A hydrocarbons production participation agreement with Hunt Oil covering two oil fields, aimed at recovering production. Deal two A framework agreement with SLB, the oilfield services company formerly called Schlumberger, for integrated reservoir studies.

A framework agreement with SLB, the oilfield services company formerly called Schlumberger, for integrated reservoir studies. The pitch “Ready to sign oil deals”, she told Houston investors, seeking production-sharing contracts.

“Ready to sign oil deals”, she told Houston investors, seeking production-sharing contracts. Her invitation “The invitation is that we can sit down, we can evaluate, what is the opportunity in Venezuela?”

“The invitation is that we can sit down, we can evaluate, what is the opportunity in Venezuela?” Chevron, separately Its finance chief said on 31 July that output across its Venezuelan joint ventures should rise 50% by end-2028, to about 420,000 barrels a day.

Its finance chief said on 31 July that output across its Venezuelan joint ventures should rise 50% by end-2028, to about 420,000 barrels a day. Where it happened The Venezuela Energy Week Houston Showcase.

Two contracts, a sales pitch and a promise of legal security, delivered in the capital of the American oil industry.

The most striking thing about this week’s Venezuela oil deals is not their size. It is the venue. Venezuela’s oil minister spent two days in Houston, signed two agreements with American companies, and told a room of investors that the country with the world’s largest crude reserves is open and offering legal security.

PDVSA in Caracas. Two agreements were signed with American companies in Houston. (Photo internet reproduction)

The two Venezuela oil deals

Paula Henao, Venezuela’s oil minister, said on Tuesday 18 August that the country had signed contracts with SLB and Hunt Oil.

The Hunt Oil agreement is a hydrocarbons production participation agreement covering two oil fields, which Henao described as intended to recover production. The SLB agreement is a framework arrangement for integrated reservoir studies — the technical groundwork that establishes what is actually recoverable before anyone commits capital.

The sequence matters. Reservoir studies come first because Venezuelan fields have been run hard with limited investment for a decade, and nobody signs a production contract on numbers they have not verified themselves.

The pitch, and the word that matters

Speaking to investors in Houston on 19 August, Henao said Venezuela is ready to sign oil deals and wants production-sharing contracts to raise output. At the Venezuela Energy Week Houston Showcase she put it as an invitation: “The invitation is that we can sit down, we can evaluate, what is the opportunity in Venezuela?”

The word doing the work in that pitch is security — legal security, guaranteed. It is the specific thing Venezuela cannot simply assert, because the country expropriated foreign oil assets in 2007 and spent the following fifteen years in arbitration over it. Every company in that Houston room knows the history, and several were parties to it.

Which is why the contracts signed are modest and technical rather than large and capital-committing. Reservoir studies and field-level participation are how you rebuild a commercial relationship that ended badly.

Chevron’s number, and where it came from

The figure circulating alongside this week’s news — Venezuelan output up 50% by 2028 — is Chevron’s, and it is older than the Houston meetings. Chevron’s chief financial officer, Eimear Bonner, said on 31 July that production across the company’s Venezuelan joint ventures is expected to rise by half by the end of 2028, reaching roughly 420,000 barrels a day.

That is a company forecast about its own joint ventures, made three weeks ago, not a statement by the Venezuelan government this week. The two have been conflated in some coverage and are worth keeping apart.

Chevron matters here because it never left. It held a licence through the sanctions period and is the reference point for what an American major can actually achieve in Venezuela.

Why this matters if you live in Latin America

Venezuela sits on the largest proven crude reserves in the world and produces a fraction of what it could. Every barrel that comes back changes the arithmetic for the region: refining flows in the Caribbean, freight rates, and the price of the diluent that heavy Venezuelan crude needs to move at all.

It also changes the politics. An American oil industry with contracts in Venezuela is an American oil industry with an interest in stability there, and that interest tends to outlast individual administrations in both countries.

The caution is the one the minister was trying to answer. Legal security in Venezuela has been promised before. Contracts signed in Houston in August are worth what they are worth in five years, and the companies signing them have priced that.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Venezuela oil deals were signed in Houston? Two. A hydrocarbons production participation agreement with Hunt Oil covering two oil fields, aimed at recovering production, and a framework agreement with SLB — the oilfield services company formerly known as Schlumberger — for integrated reservoir studies. Oil minister Paula Henao announced them on Tuesday 18 August 2026. What did the minister say to investors? Speaking in Houston on 19 August, Paula Henao said Venezuela is ready to sign oil deals and wants production-sharing contracts to raise output from the world’s largest crude reserves. At the Venezuela Energy Week Houston Showcase she said: “The invitation is that we can sit down, we can evaluate, what is the opportunity in Venezuela?” Is Chevron raising Venezuelan output 50%? That is Chevron’s own forecast for its Venezuelan joint ventures, given by chief financial officer Eimear Bonner on 31 July 2026: production up 50% by the end of 2028, to about 420,000 barrels a day. It was not a statement made by the Venezuelan government this week, and the two have been conflated in some coverage. Why are the contracts small and technical? Because the commercial relationship has to be rebuilt. Venezuela expropriated foreign oil assets in 2007 and spent years in arbitration. Reservoir studies establish what is recoverable before capital is committed, and field-level participation agreements limit exposure while confidence is re-established.

Sources: Bloomberg — Venezuela is ready to sign oil deals, minister tells Houston investors; Bloomberg — Venezuela signs deals with SLB and Hunt in a push to boost oil output; Politico — US oil producers and Venezuelan production deals

World.title: SQM Will Spend US$3 Billion by 2028, Most of It on One Salt Flat
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts The number SQM expects capital expenditure of about US$3 billion across 2026 to 2028.

SQM expects capital expenditure of about US$3 billion across 2026 to 2028. Where it goes Chiefly Salar Futuro, the company’s redevelopment of its operations in the Salar de Atacama.

Chiefly Salar Futuro, the company’s redevelopment of its operations in the Salar de Atacama. The partner Codelco, the Chilean state copper company, through the joint venture structure agreed for the salt flat.

Codelco, the Chilean state copper company, through the joint venture structure agreed for the salt flat. The longer figure Salar Futuro itself is described as roughly US$3 billion over seven years, so the two numbers overlap rather than add.

Salar Futuro itself is described as roughly US$3 billion over seven years, so the two numbers overlap rather than add. Why now SQM reported a record second quarter, with lithium sales driving the beat, and raised its outlook.

SQM reported a record second quarter, with lithium sales driving the beat, and raised its outlook. The stated aim More production and a significantly smaller environmental footprint in the Atacama.

More production and a significantly smaller environmental footprint in the Atacama. One thing we could not confirm Reports of a US securities regulator closing a bribery inquiry into SQM without penalty could not be verified.

A record quarter, a bigger budget, and a partnership with the Chilean state that will outlast several governments.

SQM had a good quarter — a record one, on lithium — and used the earnings call to extend its spending horizon. The SQM investment plan now runs to 2028 and totals roughly US$3 billion, and almost all of it is going into one place: the salt flat in the Atacama desert the company has worked for decades and is now rebuilding with the Chilean state as its partner.

The Salar de Atacama, where almost all of SQM’s US$3 billion is going. (Photo internet reproduction)

What the SQM investment plan covers

Management told the second-quarter call that capital expenditure is expected to reach about US$3 billion for the 2026 to 2028 period, mainly to support future growth and cost competitiveness.

The centre of that is Salar Futuro, the redevelopment of SQM’s Salar de Atacama operations, run with Codelco. It is described separately as an investment of roughly US$3 billion over about seven years, aimed at raising production while sharply cutting the environmental footprint of the operation.

Those two figures are not additive. The three-year capex window and the seven-year project budget overlap heavily, and anyone modelling this should treat them as views of the same spending from different angles rather than as separate commitments.

Why Codelco is in the picture

Chile treats lithium as a strategic mineral, and the state has spent the last three years converting that principle into structures. The arrangement between SQM and Codelco is the largest of them: a partnership giving the state a controlling role in the Atacama’s lithium production from the second half of this decade.

For SQM the deal traded control for duration. Its Atacama concessions were due to run out; the partnership extends the operating horizon well beyond that. For Chile it secures a share of the revenue without nationalising an operating business.

The Salar Futuro spending is what that agreement looks like in practice. It is also why the environmental commitments are prominent: brine extraction in the Atacama is politically contested, and the partnership needs local consent it cannot assume.

The quarter behind the decision

SQM’s second-quarter results beat expectations, with record lithium sales volumes and an improved outlook, and the shares rose on the news. Lithium prices have been weak for two years, which makes a record volume quarter the more notable achievement — the company is selling more, not selling dearer.

That is the logic of the capex plan. In a low-price environment, the winners are producers whose costs sit at the bottom of the curve, and Salar Futuro is a cost-and-footprint project as much as a volume one.

Why this matters if you live in Latin America

The lithium triangle — Chile, Argentina and Bolivia — holds the majority of the world’s identified reserves, and the three countries have taken three different approaches. Chile has gone for state partnership, Argentina for tax incentives under RIGI, Bolivia for state control that has produced very little.

This is what the Chilean model looks like when it works: a private operator continuing to run the plant, the state taking a controlling stake and a share of the proceeds, and a three-year capital plan large enough to matter.

The open question is prices. A US$3 billion commitment made during a two-year price slump is a bet that demand recovers before the spending ends. If it does not, the Atacama will still be producing, but the economics of everyone’s lithium plans in the region change.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the SQM investment plan? SQM told its second-quarter 2026 earnings call that capital expenditure is expected to total about US$3 billion across 2026 to 2028, mainly to support future growth and cost competitiveness. The bulk is directed at Salar Futuro, its redevelopment of operations in the Salar de Atacama. Is that the same as the Salar Futuro budget? They overlap. Salar Futuro is separately described as roughly US$3 billion over about seven years. The three-year capex figure and the seven-year project figure are views of largely the same spending, not two separate commitments to be added together. What is Codelco’s role? Codelco, the Chilean state copper company, is SQM’s partner in the Salar de Atacama arrangement, which gives the state a controlling role in lithium production there from the second half of this decade while SQM continues to operate. The deal extended SQM’s operating horizon beyond the expiry of its concessions. Did the US securities regulator close a bribery investigation into SQM? We could not verify that. Reports of a US Securities and Exchange Commission inquiry being closed without penalty in August 2026 could not be confirmed against any primary source, and the claim should not be treated as established.

World.title: Ethiopia Birr Hits Record Low as Central Bank Sells US$500 Million in One Day
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

ETHIOPIA · MARKETS

Key Facts —The record: The birr has weakened about 3.2% this year to near 162 per dollar, a record low, according to Bloomberg. It is the worst performer of the 23 African currencies Bloomberg tracks over twelve months. —The bill so far: The central bank has spent roughly US$2.2 billion defending the currency this year, Bloomberg reports. That figure is the central bank’s own. —Thursday’s sale: The National Bank of Ethiopia said it would sell a further US$500 million on Thursday 20 August, describing the sale as an unscheduled special auction. —The arithmetic: The bank had planned four auctions of US$125 million each this quarter, on 12 August, 26 August, 9 September and 23 September. Thursday’s single sale matches that entire quarterly allocation. —Demand outran supply: At the 12 August auction, banks bid US$470.17 million against an allocation of US$125 million. Participation rose to 28 banks from 14 in June. —Where it cleared: The marginal rate moved from 157.00 to 161.0050 birr per dollar. The weighted average of successful bids moved from 157.00 to 161.7994. —The forecast: David Cowan, chief Africa economist at Citigroup, expects the birr to reach 185 to 195 per dollar by year-end. That is a projection, not a policy target.

The Ethiopia birr has fallen to a record low near 162 per dollar, and the central bank has answered with an unscheduled US$500 million sale on 20 August. That single auction matches the entire amount the bank had allocated for the whole quarter.

What the Ethiopia birr auction reveals

The auctions work in a simple way. The central bank offers a fixed pot of dollars, commercial banks bid a birr price for them, and the highest bidders are served until the pot runs out. That is how the Ethiopia birr’s official exchange rate is now set.

The National Bank of Ethiopia had set out a measured plan for the first quarter of the 2026/27 financial year. Four auctions of US$125 million each, on 12 August, 26 August, 9 September and 23 September, adding to US$500 million.

On 20 August it intends to sell US$500 million in one sitting, and it has called the sale unscheduled and special. The quarterly plan and the single-day sale are now the same number.

It is not the first sale of this size. The bank sold US$500 million at special auctions on 27 January and again on 21 February this year, both outside its regular timetable. What is new is that one day now matches everything it had scheduled for three months.

A central bank that compresses a quarter into a day is not managing a currency. It is defending a level.

Bloomberg reports the bank has already spent roughly US$2.2 billion this year holding the line. The birr has still weakened about 3.2% to near 162 per dollar.

The bidding tells the story more plainly than the rate

At the 25th auction on 12 August, banks submitted US$470.17 million in bids against an allocation of US$125 million. That is a bid-to-allocation ratio of roughly 3.8 times. Only nine of the 28 banks that took part came away with dollars.

In June the same ratio was about 1.6 times. Participation over the same stretch rose from 14 banks to 28.

The clearing levels moved with the demand. The marginal rate went from 157.00 to 161.0050 birr per dollar, and the weighted average of successful bids from 157.00 to 161.7994.

Those numbers describe a market where the official price is set by rationing rather than by clearing. Every auction that ends oversubscribed leaves unmet demand looking for another venue.

What is pushing on the currency

The immediate pressure is the import bill. Higher global oil prices linked to the conflict involving Iran have raised the cost of fuel and fertiliser, both of which Ethiopia buys in dollars.

The same conflict has weighed on remittances from Ethiopian workers in the Gulf, according to Bloomberg’s reporting. That removes one of the country’s steadier sources of hard currency at the moment it is needed most.

Ethiopia floated the birr on 29 July 2024 as the centrepiece of a reform programme backed by the International Monetary Fund. The currency moved sharply in the days that followed and has not found a stable level since.

A float that needs US$2.2 billion of support inside eight months is a managed rate wearing a float’s clothing. That is the tension the reform programme has not resolved.

What outside investors are actually watching

Ethiopia is the most populous country in East Africa and, alongside Kenya, one of the region’s two biggest economies. It is also two years into a four-year International Monetary Fund arrangement worth about US$3.4 billion. The IMF board approved the fifth review on 1 July 2026, releasing about US$464 million and taking total payouts under the programme to roughly US$2.65 billion.

For anyone holding Ethiopian assets, the exchange rate is the transmission channel for everything else. It determines what local earnings are worth in dollars and whether they can be repatriated at all.

David Cowan, chief Africa economist at Citigroup, expects the birr to reach between 185 and 195 per dollar by the end of the year, while also expecting the authorities to stop it crossing 200. That is one bank’s forecast rather than an official projection.

The gap between the auction rate and what importers actually pay outside it is the number that will decide whether the reform is judged a success. Bloomberg puts the street price in Addis Ababa at about 180 birr per dollar, roughly 15% weaker than the official rate. A gap that wide is the clearest sign that a market has not cleared.

The wider East African read

Ethiopia’s difficulty is specific but not unique. Several African economies that liberalised exchange rates in 2024 and 2025 have discovered that the hard part comes after the float, not during it.

Nigeria unified its rates in June 2023 and has spent the years since managing the aftermath. Ghana’s cedi slumped, then rebounded sharply, and its central bank is now managing the swing.

What separates Ethiopia is the thinness of the buffer. Ethiopia went into the float with reserves covering barely two weeks of imports. They have since been rebuilt to about US$5.9 billion, or roughly 2.1 months of import cover, on IMF figures. That is real progress, but it is still a thin cushion for a country this size, and every large auction spends part of it.

That is why a single auction matters more here than it would elsewhere. There is less room behind it.

What would count as evidence either way

The first test is simply whether Thursday’s auction clears, and at what rate. A sale that goes off near the last marginal level would suggest the bank has found a floor.

The second test is the 26 August auction. If the scheduled US$125 million goes ahead as planned, the special sale was a one-off intervention rather than the start of a new run rate.

The third test is slower and more revealing. It is whether importers stop queueing, which is the only durable sign that the official market has become the real one.

Frequently Asked Questions

How far has the Ethiopian birr fallen? The birr has weakened about 3.2% this year to near 162 per dollar, a record low, according to Bloomberg. It is the worst performer among the 23 African currencies Bloomberg tracks over twelve months. How much has Ethiopia spent defending the birr? The central bank has spent roughly US$2.2 billion supporting the currency this year, Bloomberg reports. It said it would sell a further US$500 million on 20 August. Why is the 20 August auction unusual? The National Bank of Ethiopia had planned four auctions of US$125 million each this quarter, totalling US$500 million. Thursday’s single unscheduled sale matches that entire quarterly allocation. What happened at the last scheduled auction? At the 12 August auction, banks bid US$470.17 million against an allocation of US$125 million, with 28 banks taking part. The marginal rate rose from 157.00 to 161.0050 birr per dollar.

World.title: Brazil Court Orders Retailer Casas Bahia to Rehire Workers
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts — The ruling Judge Katarina Roberta Mousinho de Matos, of Brasilia’s 11th Labor Court, suspended the August mass layoffs on August 18, 2026.

— The deadline the retailer has five days to put the dismissed staff back on the payroll, and 48 hours to switch health plans back on.

— The penalty R$500 (about US$97) per day for each worker left out, plus R$10,000 (about US$1,930) for any new Phase 2 dismissal without union talks.

— The headcount the company told the bankruptcy court that about 3,000 jobs went in August, while the CNTC labor confederation counts about 1,900.

— The wider retreat roughly 11,600 jobs and about 355 stores have gone since 2023, including 298 stores closed this month.

A day later. A second judge in Sao Paulo gave the chain only part of the shelter from creditors it had asked for.

Illustrative photo: a Casas Bahia store in Sao Lourenco, Minas Gerais. The chain closed 298 stores in August 2026 before a labor judge suspended the accompanying mass layoffs. (Photo: ZeroTwoAndHiroWW2, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

A labor judge in Brasilia has ordered Casas Bahia, Brazil’s best-known furniture and appliance chain, to reverse its August mass layoffs. The company must put the dismissed staff back on the payroll within five days.

Because it filed for court protection from creditors days earlier, the retailer is now fighting on two fronts at once.

What the Judge in Brasilia Ordered

The injunction came on the evening of Tuesday, August 18, 2026. Judge Katarina Roberta Mousinho de Matos, of the 11th Labor Court of Brasilia, signed it.

She suspended the effects of the collective dismissals and ordered the contracts provisionally restored. In addition, health plans and other assistance benefits cancelled because of the firings must be switched back on within 48 hours.

The court gave the company five days from formal notice to return the staff to the payroll. That clock started once the ruling was served.

Why the Layoffs Were Blocked

Brazilian law treats mass firings differently from ordinary ones. Under a Supreme Court precedent known as Tema 638, a company must talk to the unions before it dismisses a large group.

The judge found that step missing. As a result, she froze the round rather than cancelling it outright.

Leaving the door open for the company to redo the process properly. The rule is about process, not permission.

Unions have no veto, and no collective agreement has to be signed, yet the talks must genuinely happen first.

What Grupo Casas Bahia does. Grupo Casas Bahia S.A., together with its subsidiaries, operates as an omnichannel retailer in Brazil. The company provides consumer electronics, home appliances, furniture, and other domestic items. It also engages in the manufacture, industrialization, and sale of wood-based furniture; ownership and management of equity interests; management of logistics operations; and provision of…

Who Brought the Case

The action was filed by the CNTC, Brazil’s national confederation of commerce workers. It is an umbrella body for retail unions across the country.

The confederation argued that the cuts were pushed through without the bargaining the law requires. Therefore it asked for an urgent order, and it got one the same week.

How Many Workers Casas Bahia Must Take Back

The decision does not name a single headcount. Instead, it covers everyone dismissed on August 13 and 14.

Plus later exits through August 17 that formed part of the same operation. That leaves two competing tallies.

The CNTC counts about 1,900 people cut on those two days. While Casas Bahia told the bankruptcy court that roughly 3,000 jobs went during the August round.

So the true number sits somewhere between the two. It will only be fixed once the company files its own list with the court.

The Fines Attached to the Order

The penalty is not a lump sum. If the company misses the deadline, it owes R$500 a day for each affected worker.

Roughly US$97 at the August 19 rate of R$5.17 to the dollar. That amount is capped, at least for now, at the equivalent of ten months of pay per employee.

Even so, spread across thousands of people it adds up quickly. A second penalty covers fresh cuts.

Any new Phase 2 dismissal made without prior union involvement carries a fine of R$10,000, about US$1,930, per worker.

A Second Courtroom, a Second Ruling

The very next day the story moved to Sao Paulo. On Wednesday, August 19, Judge Taina Maria Leonardo de Oliveira, of the city’s 2nd Bankruptcy and Judicial Recovery Court.

Ruled on the company’s plea for shelter from creditors. She granted the emergency requests only in part.

Crucially, she did not yet admit the reorganization itself, so the full protection the retailer wants is still pending.

What Sao Paulo Granted and What It Held Back

The judge barred the group’s roughly 28,000 creditors from calling in contracts early purely because a recovery request had been filed. Suppliers must also deliver goods already in transit to stores and distribution centres.

In addition, essential contracts must keep running. That list covers water and power utilities, technology and security providers, and the leases on the shops themselves.

She also blocked unusual seizures of receivables outside the normal contract flow. Breaching any of these points carries a fine of R$50,000 a day, close to US$9,700.

The limits matter as much as the grants. She set no end date for the shelter.

Yet ruled that the time used will be deducted from the 180-day freeze the company would get if the reorganization is admitted.

An Inspection Before Anything Else

Before deciding whether to admit the case, the judge ordered an on-the-ground check. A court-appointed administrator must verify that the group really operates as its filing describes.

The report is due within 30 days. Meanwhile, the company has ten days to hand over paperwork it left out of the original filing.

Three Years of Shrinking

August was not the first round. The transformation plan launched in 2023 closed 55 loss-making stores and removed about 8,600 posts.

This month added 298 store closures and, by the company’s own count, about 3,000 more jobs. Taken together, that is roughly 11,600 positions and around 355 shops gone since 2023.

Folha de S. Paulo, working from quarterly filings, puts the staff cut at 11,749 people, or 28 percent of the workforce.

Headcount fell from 41,866 in June 2023 to 30,117 by mid-2026.

The Debt Behind the Crisis

The reorganization filing lists about R$17.3 billion in debt, near US$3.35 billion. It names roughly 28,000 creditors.

The biggest single claim belongs to insurer Zurich Minas Brasil, at R$1.97 billion. An investment fund is next with R$1 billion, followed by Samsung’s Brazilian unit on R$937.6 million.

Household names fill the rest of the top of the list. Electrolux, Whirlpool, LG and Motorola are all owed hundreds of millions of reais.

What the Company Says

The retailer’s response to the labor ruling was short. It told the news outlet Poder360 that it had learned of the decision and was weighing the terms and its next steps.

An appeal remains available. Nothing so far suggests a higher labor court has touched the injunction, so the five-day clock still runs.

What Happens Next

Two timetables now overlap. The labor deadline is measured in days, while the Sao Paulo court’s inspection runs for up to a month.

For staff, the immediate question is pay and health cover. For suppliers and lenders, it is whether the reorganization is admitted at all.

Shoppers with pending orders sit in between. Until the court rules on admission, the company keeps trading under a patchwork of temporary orders.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which court blocked the layoffs?

The 11th Labor Court of Brasilia, part of the 10th Regional Labor Court, or TRT-10. Judge Katarina Roberta Mousinho de Matos signed the injunction on August 18, 2026.

Is the daily fine R$100,000?

No. The labor injunction sets R$500 a day per affected worker, about US$97. A separate Sao Paulo ruling sets R$50,000 a day, near US$9,700, for breaching creditor-protection measures.

Are 3,000 or 1,900 workers going back?

The order does not fix a number. It covers everyone cut between August 13 and 17 in the same operation.

Has the judicial recovery been approved?

Not yet. As of August 20.

Sources: G1; Poder360; O Globo; Folha de S.Paulo; Metropoles; UOL.

World.title: Costa Rica flood emergency keeps 473 schools closed and 1,300 people in shelters
World.content:
If you were thinking of or had plan to go to Caribbean side or in the Northern Zone this week, the heavy rain may have stopped but the disruption has not. Classes remain suspended at 473 schools, and more than 1,300 people are still living in 23 temporary shelters four days after Tropical Wave #33 pushed already-swollen rivers past their banks. Emergency crews are still reaching communities they could not get to over the weekend.

The Education Ministry closure list covers seven education regions. Sarapiquí accounts for 138 schools closed outright, Guápiles for 131 on partial suspension and Sulá for 110, with smaller numbers in Turrialba, Zona Norte-Norte, Limón and Cartago. That is a sharp drop from Monday, when 990 schools were shut. The ministry says the list changes daily and asks families to check its official channels rather than secondhand reports, because a school can reopen and close again within hours.

The rain itself has eased. The National Meteorological Institute expects only isolated showers on the Caribbean coast and variable downpours in the Northern Zone through the morning, with scattered afternoon rain reaching the Central Valley, the Central Pacific and the South Pacific, and possible showers on the Nicoya Peninsula.

The risk that remains is in the ground, not the sky. Soil across the Caribbean and the South Pacific is saturated, which means an ordinary afternoon shower can now trigger a landslide or push a river back up with almost no warning. A hillside that held all season can fail on a rainfall total that would normally pass without incident.

The weekend produced some of the heaviest rain on record. Nine weather stations set 24-hour precipitation records between 7 a.m. Sunday and 7 a.m. Monday, according to preliminary Institute data, with eight of them on the Caribbean slope.

Roxana de Pococí recorded 263.4 millimeters (10.4 inches) in a single day. For comparison, a heavy Costa Rican downpour typically drops around 60 millimeters (2.4 inches) over three hours. The Fundación Neotrópica station in Sierpe de Osa, on the Pacific side, logged 134.6 millimeters (5.3 inches).

Across 48 hours, the Caribbean and parts of the Northern Zone took between 200 and 360 millimeters (7.9 and 14.2 inches). At some stations a single weekend delivered half of what August normally brings in a full month, and monthly totals elsewhere have already reached between 100 and 170 percent of the historical average with almost two weeks still to go.

The National Emergency Commission is still supplying communities it cannot reach by road. A helicopter has been running food deliveries to the indigenous territories of Tayní Cabécar and Alto Chirripó in Limón, and to communities in Sarapiquí, where damaged roads and bridges have cut off vehicle access.

People in shelters are receiving meals, bedding, hygiene kits and medical checks. The count has stayed above 1,300 since Monday and will keep shifting as some families go home and others are evacuated. Route 32, the main link between San José and Limón, was closed Tuesday afternoon after material fell onto the roadway, and the Public Works Ministry scheduled an inspection for first thing Wednesday. Whether it reopens depends on what crews found.

If you need to reach the Caribbean, Route 10 through Turrialba is the alternate and is open to all vehicle types, though it has taken closures of its own during this rain cycle. Check the ministry’s channels before you leave rather than after you are on the road, because the Zurquí stretch can shut again within minutes of a downpour.

Do not drive through standing water, however shallow it looks. Moving water just 30 centimeters (12 inches) deep can float a car, and on a flooded road you cannot see whether the surface underneath is still there. If you have anything booked or scheduled in Sarapiquí, Tortuguero, Cahuita, Puerto Viejo or Guápiles, call ahead. Access varies community by community, and people on the ground will know whether the road to their door is open well before any official list catches up.

The forecast calls for lighter rain in the days ahead. But with the ground this saturated and most of the rainy season still to come, conditions on the Caribbean slope can change a good deal faster than the forecast suggests.

World.title: Brandon Nakashima Saves Three Match Points to Stun Daniil Medvedev at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Brandon Nakashima saved three consecutive match points before completing a dramatic comeback against Daniil Medvedev on Tuesday at the Cincinnati Open. The 27th-seeded American defeated the fourth seed 6-7(3), 7-6(4), 6-1, advancing to the round of 16 after two hours and 51 minutes.

Nakashima appeared headed for elimination when he served at 4-5, 0-40 in the second set. Medvedev had already taken the opening set in a tiebreak and stood one point away from closing the match on three occasions. Instead, Nakashima attacked. He saved the first match point with a forehand approach and volley, survived an 18-shot rally on the second and used serve-and-volley to erase the third. He eventually held serve before forcing another tiebreak.

“Down match points, I was just trying to tell myself to keep fighting for every point,” Nakashima said during his on-court interview. The American carried that momentum into the tiebreak, winning it 7-4 to force a deciding set. Medvedev never recovered. Nakashima broke early in the third and pulled away as the former Cincinnati champion became increasingly frustrated.

Nakashima closed the final set 6-1 to earn his first victory over Medvedev in four career meetings. Medvedev had won their previous encounter in the Brisbane final in January. The result continued an impressive North American hard-court run for Nakashima. The 25-year-old reached the semifinals in Washington before advancing to his first Masters 1000 final in Montreal, where he lost to fellow American Ben Shelton.

Now ranked a career-high No. 22, Nakashima has won 20 hard-court matches this season. Only Jakub Mensik, with 21, has recorded more on the ATP Tour. Tuesday’s victory was also Nakashima’s fifth against a top-10 opponent. It came against a player who has traditionally produced some of his best tennis on hard courts and won the Cincinnati title in 2019.

Nakashima will next face Portugal’s Nuno Borges, who produced another upset by defeating 13th-seeded Andrey Rublev 6-3, 6-4. Borges entered that match having lost all five of his previous meetings with Rublev. The winner will advance to the Cincinnati Open quarterfinals as the tournament moves closer to its August 23 championship match.

World.title: Former Costa Rica Health Minister’s Trial Delayed After Lawyer Leaves Case
World.content:
The trial of former Health Minister Joselyn Chacón has been postponed until October after a court ruled that her attorney had abandoned the defense and the former official missed two scheduled hearings because of a medical condition. The Tribunal of the First Judicial Circuit of San José rescheduled the trial for October 23, 2026. Chacón faces allegations of insult, slander and defamation stemming from a private criminal complaint filed by former lawmaker Francisco Nicolás.

Attorney José Miguel Villalobos, who now serves as a lawmaker for the governing Pueblo Soberano party, had represented Chacón during the case. He submitted his resignation, but the court determined that his departure amounted to abandonment of the defense.

Chacón told the court by email that she did not know Villalobos had withdrawn from the case and said he had not informed her that he would no longer represent her. Villalobos offered a different account. He said he had previously attempted to leave the case, but the court did not accept his resignation. According to the lawmaker, Chacón later asked him to submit the request again so she could find another attorney.

The court temporarily appointed a public defender to protect Chacón’s rights during yesterday’s proceedings. The former minister has since named a new private attorney to represent her when the trial resumes. Nicolás said he plans to send the court records to the Costa Rican Bar Association so the organization can determine whether Villalobos committed any ethical violation. No disciplinary finding has been made against the attorney.

The delay followed a separate dispute over Chacón’s absence from court. When she failed to appear Monday without official medical documentation, the tribunal declared her in rebellion and issued an order for her arrest. Chacón later submitted a medical leave certificate issued by an Ebáis clinic operated by the Costa Rican Social Security Fund, known as the CCSS. The document covered her absences on Monday and Tuesday.

After receiving the certificate, the tribunal canceled the arrest order and directed Chacón to undergo an evaluation by the Judicial Investigation Agency’s Department of Forensic Medicine. The examination is intended to determine whether her condition prevented her from attending and participating in the trial.

The August hearings became the latest in a series of failed attempts to begin the case. Court information indicates that Chacón has presented medical leave documentation on four occasions, while three other postponements involved professional scheduling conflicts raised by her private defense.

The case dates to February 2023, when Chacón was serving as health minister.
