She publicly accused Nicolás, then a lawmaker for the National Liberation Party, of seeking to have the Health Ministry purchase land belonging to a friend. The plot was connected to a CEN-CINAI childcare and nutrition center in Esparza.

Nicolás alleges that Chacón’s statements damaged his reputation. In addition to the criminal complaint, he is seeking ₡10 million in civil compensation. Chacón has rejected the accusations and defended the decisions and statements she made while leading the Health Ministry. The October hearing is expected to include testimony from Chacón and three witnesses.

World.title: Burrell Boom man out on bail after allegedly taking cellphone from friend who was giving him a ride but got stuck in ditch
World.content:
Burrell Boom man out on bail after allegedly taking cellphone from friend who was giving him a ride but got stuck in ditch

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 28-year-old Burrell Boom man is out on bail after being accused of stealing a cellphone from a motorist while he was reportedly assisting him after his vehicle became stuck in a ditch.

Roy Frederick Tillett, a barber and construction worker, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with theft of a black Android cellphone valued at $450, which belonged to a man he knows.

Tillett pleaded not guilty to the charge and denied stealing the phone.

With no objection from the prosecution, the Magistrate granted him bail in the sum of $2,000 plus one surety in the same amount.

As conditions of his bail, Tillett must remain at least 100 yards away from the complainant and must not interfere with him or any other prosecution witnesses.

According to police, the complainant reported that on August 11 he was driving along an unnamed street in Burrell Boom when he picked up Tillett, whom he knew.

The complainant said his vehicle subsequently became stuck in a ditch, prompting him to exit and inspect it. He reportedly left his cellphone between the driver’s and passenger seats while Tillett remained nearby.

The complainant told police that he later asked Tillett to go and purchase something for him. After Tillett left, the complainant noticed that his cellphone was missing.

He reportedly waited for Tillett to return so he could question him about the missing phone, but Tillett did not return.

The man told investigators that no one else had entered his vehicle during that period and subsequently requested court action against Tillett.

Tillett is scheduled to return to court on October 14, 2026.

World.title: Burrell Boom man pleads guilty to possession of cocaine but Judge gives him time served for month already served on remand
World.content:
Burrell Boom man pleads guilty to possession of cocaine but Judge gives him time served for month already served on remand

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Burrell Boom resident who spent nearly a month on remand for possession of 0.13 grams of cocaine walked free from the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday after changing his plea from not guilty to guilty.

Eyon Ramirez, 20, appeared in Court #5 around midday, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug. In sentencing him, the Magistrate took into account the three weeks and six days Ramirez had already spent at the Belize Central Prison and sentenced him to time served.

Ramirez, who had been unable to post bail following his arraignment, expressed relief at being released and said he was happy to be going home. He is expected to celebrate his 21st birthday on Sunday, August 23.

Ramirez was first arraigned on July 24, 2026, following his arrest a day earlier.

According to police, officers conducting motorcycle patrol on Euphrates Avenue near Allenby Street observed Ramirez acting suspiciously and allegedly attempting to evade them. Police said that as officers approached to conduct a search, Ramirez removed a white substance from his pocket and dropped it to the ground before attempting to flee.

Officers reportedly detained Ramirez and recovered the substance, which was later weighed at 0.13 grams and identified as cocaine.

Ramirez was subsequently charged with possession of a controlled drug and remanded to the Belize Central Prison, where he remained until Wednesday’s court appearance.

World.title: Cop accused in Kevin Depaz Caye Caulker murder receives 145 pages of disclosure
World.content:
Cop accused in Kevin Depaz Caye Caulker murder receives 145 pages of disclosure

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police Constable Lionel Rodolfo Urbina, who is on interdiction and remanded on charges stemming from the 2025 stabbing death of 19-year-old Kevin Matthew Depaz on Caye Caulker, returned to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday.

Urbina was brought from the Belize Central Prison under a special security escort and appeared unrepresented in Court #3, where he was provided with 145 pages of disclosure, including seven DVDs containing evidence in the case.

The matter was adjourned to October 21, 2026, when Urbina is expected to appear in the San Pedro Magistrate’s Court for the commencement of his preliminary inquiry. He was further remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Urbina was arraigned on January 22, 2026, on one count of murder in connection with Depaz’s death, as well as two counts of attempted murder and two counts of use of deadly means of harm in relation to injuries allegedly inflicted on Neesean Allen and Julian Canul. Reports identified Urbina as a 20-year-old police constable when he was charged.

The charges arose from a violent altercation on Caye Caulker during the early morning hours of June 30, 2025. Depaz, Allen and Canul became involved in a confrontation with off-duty Police Constables Urbina and Darneak Swasey after an earlier incident near Munchies Fast Food on Luciano Reyes Street. Depaz suffered a stab wound to the abdomen and later died at the Caye Caulker Health Centre, while several others involved in the confrontation were injured.

Following an investigation and directives from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Urbina was charged in January. Swasey was not charged with Depaz’s murder.

Urbina remains on remand awaiting the preliminary inquiry.

World.title: Why Belize keeps speaking on Palestine, the century behind yesterday’s statement
World.content:
Why Belize keeps speaking on Palestine, the century behind yesterday’s statement

By Horace Palacio:

Yesterday, from Belmopan, the Government of Belize issued a statement about violence in a land more than twelve thousand kilometers away. It condemned escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian civilians in the West Bank, called on Israel as the occupying power to protect the population, and reaffirmed that the occupation itself is unlawful and must end.

And somewhere in Belize, somebody read that and asked the honest question. Why does a small country with potholes to fix keep raising its voice about a war on the other side of the world?

Today I will answer that question properly. First the facts of this moment, then the century of history behind them, told fairly, and finally why this quarrel touches Belize far more directly than most Belizeans realize.

Start with what is happening right now, because the numbers are staggering. United Nations officials told the Security Council this month that the West Bank has reached a breaking point. Settler violence stands at the highest levels since UN monitoring began twenty years ago, more than 1,400 documented attacks this year across 260 communities, an average of six attacks every single day, dozens of Palestinians killed, roughly 3,800 driven from their homes in 2026 alone, among them more than a thousand children. UN investigators describe a repeating pattern, an outpost rises beside a Palestinian village, the harassment begins, the wells and grazing lands are cut off, the attacks come, and when the families finally flee, the land is taken. Israeli lives have been lost in this spiral too, and Belize’s statement mourned all civilian victims, as it should.

But none of this began this year. To understand it, you must walk back a century, and you must walk fairly, because this is the story of two peoples and one land, and each carries a wound the other rarely sees.

The Jewish people trace three thousand years of history, faith, and longing to that land, and by the late 1800s, fleeing massacres and hatred across Europe, a movement arose to rebuild a Jewish homeland there. In 1917, Britain, then conquering the region from the Ottomans, promised support for that homeland in a territory whose population was overwhelmingly Palestinian Arab, people rooted in those hills and orchards for countless generations. One land, promised in different ways to two peoples. Nearly everything since flows from that.

Then came the Holocaust, six million Jews murdered in Europe, and with it an unanswerable case for refuge. In 1947 the United Nations voted to partition the land into two states, one Jewish, one Arab. Jewish leaders accepted. Arab leaders rejected what they saw as the carving up of their homeland. War followed. In 1948 Israel declared independence and survived invasion by its neighbors, and in that same war some 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from their homes, a catastrophe they call the Nakba, creating a refugee people whose descendants number in the millions today. One event, two memories, a state born and a homeland lost, both true at once.

The hinge of everything came in 1967. In six days of war, Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza. And here is the plain meaning of the word that fills every news report, occupation. It means the Palestinians of those territories have now lived for nearly sixty years under a military authority they did not elect and cannot vote out, while Israel began moving its own civilians into the captured land, the settlers, whose communities now hold hundreds of thousands of people. International law is not vague here. Moving your population into occupied territory violates the Geneva Conventions, and in July 2024 the International Court of Justice, the world’s highest court, ruled that the occupation and the settlements are unlawful and must end. Belize made formal submissions in that very case, and the court’s opinion is the foundation of yesterday’s statement.

There were moments of hope. In the 1990s, the Oslo Accords brought mutual recognition and a promised path to a Palestinian state beside Israel. That hope bled out through an assassin’s bullet that killed Israel’s peacemaking prime minister, through terror bombings that shattered Israeli buses and cafes, through settlement growth that ate the map faster than negotiators could draw it, and through failed summits and a second uprising. Gaza spiraled into its own tragedy, an Israeli withdrawal, a Hamas takeover, a blockade, and war after war.

Then October 7, 2023. Hamas fighters stormed southern Israel and killed about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and dragged roughly 250 hostages into Gaza, the deadliest single day for Jews since the Holocaust. Israel’s response engulfed Gaza in a war in which Gaza’s health authorities report tens of thousands killed and whole cities pulverized, a war that brought genocide proceedings before the ICJ, a case in which Belize formally moved to intervene last year. A fragile ceasefire finally took hold in late 2025. But while the world watched Gaza, the West Bank burned hotter each year, and that is the fire yesterday’s statement addresses.

Now, Belize’s record, and note something remarkable about it. This is one of the very few foreign policy questions on which red and blue have stood in one line. It was the Barrow government that recognized the State of Palestine in 2011. It was the National Assembly, in 2022, that passed resolutions on the character of the occupation. It was the Briceño government that suspended diplomatic ties with Israel in November 2023 over the bombardment of Gaza, that argued before the world court, that welcomed the 2024 opinion, and that filed to intervene in the genocide case in 2025. Fifteen years, two parties, one consistent voice. Whatever else divides Belmopan, this has not.

Why? Here is the answer, and it sits closer to home than Jerusalem. It sits on our own western border.

Belize is a small nation living beside a larger neighbor that has claimed, in our lifetimes, a vast portion of our territory. We did not answer that claim with an army we do not have. We answered it with law, taking the dispute to the International Court of Justice, the same court, the same law, the same principles now being tested in Palestine. The deepest rule of the modern world order, written in blood after the Second World War, is that territory shall not be acquired by force. That rule is not an abstraction to Belize. That rule is Belize. It is the legal ground beneath every square mile of this country.

So understand what is truly at stake when settlements devour occupied land and the world shrugs. Every time force creates facts and law fails to undo them, the shield that protects every small nation rusts a little more. If occupation can be normalized there, annexation can be normalized anywhere, and the countries that should tremble first are not the great powers. They are the small ones whose only armor is the rulebook. When Belize stands at the United Nations and insists that international law must govern, it is not meddling in a distant quarrel. It is paying the premium on its own insurance policy.

And there is something older than law in it too. We are a people who know what it is to be colonized, to have our land promised over our heads, to win nationhood against the appetite of the powerful. A nation with that memory recognizes the story when it sees it, and loses something of its soul the day it looks away.

Yesterday’s statement called for the protection of all civilians, Israeli and Palestinian alike, and for peace grounded in law, justice, and mutual security, two peoples, two states, side by side. That is not radical. That is the world’s own stated solution, endorsed again by more than 150 nations, waiting only for the courage to enforce it.

Small countries cannot send armies, Belize. We send principles. And in a world where might keeps testing the fence, a small nation’s loudest weapon is its refusal to accept that might makes right.

Yesterday, Belmopan fired that weapon again.

It should never holster it.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Higher light bills as BEL adds 1.5 cents per Kilowatt-hour in August
World.content:
Higher light bills as BEL adds 1.5 cents per Kilowatt-hour in August

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Electricity customers across Belize will pay more on their light bills this month as Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) applies a new Cost of Power Adjustment (COPA) of 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour, following a final ruling by the Public Utilities Commission (PUC).

The adjustment is the first under a new regulatory sandbox introduced by the PUC to monitor BEL’s actual cost of purchasing power. BEL reported that its actual power costs over the past six months were 4.3 cents per kilowatt-hour higher than the reference cost approved by the PUC.

However, customers will not be required to cover the full difference at once.

Under the new system, monthly COPA adjustments are capped at 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour. For August, customers who are not enrolled under the Social Rate will therefore pay an additional 1.5 cents for every kilowatt-hour consumed. The charge will appear separately on electricity bills and is not subject to GST.

The PUC said the adjustment will be reassessed monthly based on verified information provided by BEL, meaning future COPA charges could increase, decrease, remain at zero or result in a rebate.

World.title: International News: Colombia quake losses estimated at $9.6 billion
World.content:
International News: Colombia quake losses estimated at $9.6 billion

By Zoila Palma: Colombia’s President Abelardo De La Espriella has estimated that the economic losses from last week’s powerful earthquake could reach 30 trillion pesos, or approximately $9.6 billion.

The preliminary assessment includes damage to buildings and infrastructure across affected areas, Reuters report.

De La Espriella said around 24.5 trillion pesos in losses were linked to buildings, while another 5.5 trillion pesos involved infrastructure. “Just imagine the scale of the disaster,” the president said.

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake caused widespread damage across western Colombia, including in the major cities of Cali and Pereira.

The disaster has reportedly killed 280 people, injured more than 4,000 and left another 143 people missing.

The earthquake represents the first major crisis facing De La Espriella, who took office only days before the disaster.

World.title: 30th Anniversary of National Pesticide Training & Certification Programme 1996 – 2026
World.content:
30th Anniversary of National Pesticide Training & Certification Programme 1996 – 2026

The Pesticides Control Board (PCB) has been dedicated to training and awareness-raising in pesticide life-cycle management since 1988 when the PCB Secretariat was established, and a nationwide awareness campaign launched in anticipation of the Pesticides Control Act, Chapter 216 of the Laws of Belize, coming into effect. The Pesticides Control Act, which came into effect on 31 December 1988, allowed for the phased implementation of the provisions dealing with the certification of users of restricted use pesticides.

On 17th August 1996, the Certified Users Regulations, S.I. No. 112 of 1996 came into effect. The Regulations require users of Restricted-Use Pesticides to be able to extract information from the label to follow dosage, application and precautionary directions; understand general principles of safe and effective pesticide use, storage and disposal; differentiate pesticides according to use and hazard; accurately and safely prepare the mixture to be applied; calibrate and maintain a knapsack sprayer, and understand responsibilities toward fellow workers and the public.

The Pesticides Control Board (PCB) has been dedicated to training and awareness-raising in pesticide life-cycle management since 1988 when the PCB Secretariat was established, and a nationwide awareness campaign launched The PCB’s National Pesticide Training and Certification Programme was thus launched in 1996, targeting an initial 10,000 farmers for training and certification in the first two years of programme implementation.

The Training and Certification Programme has evolved over the years and is currently implemented by a cadre of five inspectors/trainers. The training modules in pesticide life-cycle management are adaptable to different target groups and training approaches.

The programme is carried out nationally on an ongoing basis, with training sessions carried out routinely at centralized locations, and by request from partners and stakeholders.

From 2020 – 2025, almost 6,000 Certified Applicator licenses were issued to persons who were trained and certified as farm and trade applicators under the PCB’s National Pesticides Training and Certification Programme.

The Pesticides Control Board takes great pride in showcasing its flagship programme and its dedicated team of trainers who continue the legacy of PCB pioneers who laid the foundation for the PCB’s enduring mission in responsible pesticide management.

World.title: International News: Traffic in Strait of Hormuz slows as uncertainty over waterway persists
World.content:
International News: Traffic in Strait of Hormuz slows as uncertainty over waterway persists

By Zoila Palma: Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed today as uncertainty continued over the status of the key waterway following a blockade during the Iran war.

Vessel-tracking data showed that many shipowners remained reluctant to use the strait amid conflicting signals about whether it has fully reopened to shipping, Reuters report.

Kpler data showed that six commodity vessels crossed the strait on Tuesday by 0258 GMT, down from nine the previous day and below the 10-day daily average of 11. The vessels included an empty very large crude carrier that traveled along the Omani side of the waterway, as well as two tankers entering the strait and two medium-range fuel tankers and a post-Panamax vessel exiting.

The uncertainty follows conflicting statements from U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran over the status of the waterway. Trump said Tuesday that no talks were underway with Iran and insisted the Strait of Hormuz was open, while Iran maintained that the waterway remained closed to shipping.

The Strait of Hormuz previously handled about one-fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.

World.title: No more moos
World.content:
Moo Moo was injured in a hit and run along Walks Road in Spanish Town, St Catherine. Naphtali Junior

AFTER days lying in the sun as residents did their best to provide the care she needed, Moo Moo’s story has come to a heartbreaking end.

The injured cow, who captured the hearts of residents on Walks Road in Spanish Town, was euthanised by the Veterinary Services Division on Wednesday after the professionals determined her injuries were too severe.

Reports are that the cow was injured in a hit-and-run incident on August 11. Residents said they made several reports and calls to animal-related facilities, but were unable to get assistance for the animal. Gabriel Hamilton and Nicholas Thomas became the beloved animal’s primary caregivers, staying with her until her final moments.

The animal’s owner has not come forward.

Dr Sophia Ramlal, director of veterinary services in the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining, confirmed that the cow was euthanised using chemicals on Wednesday at approximately 10:15 am after examinations revealed that her injuries were significant and she could not be treated back to health.

“We could determine from the physical examination that both her right front leg and her right hind leg were broken. She was therefore unable to stand and unable to walk around. It is my information that this accident occurred approximately one week ago. However, the ministry became aware of this yesterday (Tuesday),” said Ramlal.

She added that a physical examination could not confirm the cow was pregnant, given its position on the ground.

Ramlal said the euthanasia was conducted by a team comprising members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), the Jamaica Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (JSPCA), and the National Solid Waste Management Authority (NSWMA). She said the actions were carried out in keeping with provisions under the Cruelty to Animals Act.

“Provided that the JCF is advised by either a justice of the peace or a registered veterinarian that the injuries that the animal has suffered, in this case a cow, are so severe that the animal should be put to sleep, then that process can occur,” she explained.

“We wanted it to be done humanely. We wanted to make sure that we dealt with it as professionally and expeditiously as we could, and her carcass was moved right after she was put down,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Responding to comments on social media requesting that the cow be harvested for beef, Ramlal explained that because chemicals were used, Moo Moo’s remains are not fit for consumption.

“The intent is not for this cow to be salvaged for meat because, given the extent of the injury, [her] health status… is generally unknown. There could be a generic sepsis, and it could be that the meat is not what we consider healthy for eating, so this cow was disposed of and is not safe for consumption,” she said.

Nicholas Thomas said he was saddened by Moo Moo’s passing, but happy she is now pain-free.

“I can’t explain the feeling. I just have to focus on the bright side. Now I can get more sleep, and I just have to try not to cry when I go out there. Sometimes I was up with her all night, around 10 or 11 o’clock, giving her water and just making sure she was alright until morning. I’m gonna miss her,” said Thomas about his beloved Moo Moo.

He was among residents who thought the cow looked pregnant and he had hoped any calves she had could be saved.

“It hurt me, but the bright side is that she’s resting now,” Thomas told the Observer.

Though heartbroken that Moo Moo did not make it, Moo Moo’s other caregiver Hamilton agreed that the actions of the veterinary division was the most humane outcome as it relieved the cow from suffering.

“When I was reaching out for help initially, I knew that this would probably be one of the interventions, but that would be determined by a veterinarian’s assessment. To not see her suffering anymore, a piece of my heart is happy with it, but it’s a life lost, so it’s never a happy day. I know in general Jamaicans don’t look at it that way; they more look at her as livestock, something to eat, or raise. But with animals, when you’re going to eat them, you kill them before you eat them so they are not suffering,” she stressed.

“I don’t like to see animals suffering. I’m just hoping that this will bring awareness to Jamaican people that while they are roaming on the road, we must be the ones to look out for them. It’s not the other way around. I think humans don’t really know how to co-exist with animals and that’s an issue,” she added.

Stressing the need for better treatment of animals, Hamilton extended thanks to the vet services division, Thomas, and other residents who assisted in Moo Moo’s care before her sad end.

World.title: HEART in high schools
World.content:
HARRISON… wants it mandatory for high school graduates to have skills certification

MOUNTAIN SPRING BAY, Trelawny — Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon says she will be pushing to have the skills-focused HEART/NSTA Trust programme, now restricted to participants over 17 years old, more deeply integrated into high schools across the country. She has asked teachers for their support as the strategic shift is made.

“I will be working to change that legislation so that we can have HEART working more in the schools, and therefore we can get more support for TVET (technical and vocational education and training) in our schools,” revealed Morris Dixon on Wednesday.

“That’s a big change! So when I do it I want to hear you supporting me in public that this is something that is important for our schools,” the education minister cajoled, Wednesday, while addressing the final day of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association’s (JTA) 62nd Annual Conference which was held over three days at Ocean Coral Spring resort in Trelawny.

Established by late former prime minister and Jamaica Labour Party Leader Edward Seaga in 1982, HEART’s mandate was to provide the country’s workers with the skills needed to boost productivity. Traditionally there have been clear lines drawn between academic and vocational studies, with the latter often regarded as a second option. In recent years, however, there has been a push to change that perception, and it is an issue Morris Dixon has spoken of in the past.

“With all the changes happening globally, TVET is the area that is going to take the world forward. That’s where we’re going to have jobs. And that’s where I need your help with telling parents that your child wanting to be a plumber is a good thing. I want you to be able to tell your parents that if your child wants to do construction, that’s great,” she said Wednesday.

The minister highlighted a global shortage of skilled practitioners, including construction workers, plumbers, and electricians.

“TVET has to be more centrally integrated, even in traditional high schools. It has to be, and you and I agree on this one,” she said to the more than 250 educators in attendance.

Beyond students leaving high school with Caribbean Examinations Council and City and Guilds qualifications, Morris Dixon said it is equally critical for them to be armed with certification in a specialised skill area.

“That’s a fundamental change in the system, but it’s something that I’m committed to working with, and I hear the [JTA] president is also interested in that area,” said the minister.

“That is something I’ll be coming back to the JTA on, to help me in championing that change in our system, because it’s important that we have more skills certification in our high schools,” Morris Dixon added.

It may not be a hard sell as JTA President LaSonja Harrison made similar comments during her investiture ceremony Monday night.

“Isn’t it high time that all children leaving high school do so with certification in a skilled area? If we mean our population any good, that needs to become mandatory,” said Harrison.

She also suggested that Government reallocate a portion of the revenue earned from the three per cent payroll tax on businesses, the HEART Trust levy, to assist with upgrading and maintaining technical and vocational schools.

“This only makes sense, to my mind, because these institutions — oftentimes in collaboration with HEART — ensure their students graduate with said certification. I am not just questioning the Government, I’m positing possible solutions as well,” the JTA head said Monday.

“Another option is [that] the monies allocated to provide AI chatbots, via Jamaica Learning Assist, can and should be rerouted to support this,” Harrison added.

World.title: Jamaica lists 60 public beaches with free access
CXC success
World.content:
Sixteen months after announcing a pilot for its Caribbean Targeted Education Certificate (CTEC) in mathematics to tackle “the perennial under-performance of students” in the subject, the Caribbean Examinations Council (CXC) on Tuesday reported an 88 per cent pass rate among the 2,535 candidates who sat the exam in the May-June 2026 sitting. A total of 2,230 candidates passed.

Dr Wayne Wesley, CXC registrar and chief executive officer, made the disclosure during the live results ceremony from Anguilla, saying the results were proof that the region has “overwhelmingly accepted CTEC”.

“I am pleased indeed, and I am proud to announce that of these 2,535 candidates who wrote CTEC module one in the mathematics pilot examinations, 88 per cent achieved acceptable grades, and across the entire Caribbean only one candidate received the lowest grade. It simply means that most candidates are benefiting from the approach. Measured against a generation in which barely one in three candidates succeed in a typical sitting, this achievement represents a remarkable turnaround,” Wesley said.

Acknowledging, however, that “a module is not a whole subject”, the CXC registrar pointed out that “the full qualification still requires completion of every module at the full standard”.

“But that is precisely what these results demonstrate. When learning is assessed in focused, achievable stages, our students do more than cope; they excel, they engage, persist, and succeed. The May-June mathematics pilot proves that the modular approach works for students, for classrooms, and for the region. This landmark result belongs to the young people who earned it,” Wesley stated.

CTEC, the new qualification which was unveiled by CXC in April 2025, is at the same standard of Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) and Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) and utilises the same syllabus.

“For years in mathematics — the subject that is foundational to every vocation in life — only about a third of our candidates have achieved acceptable grades in a typical sitting. Behind that statistic are hundreds of thousands of young people who sat in our classrooms for five years and walked away with nothing in hand to show for what they did learn. Not because they learn nothing, but because our instrument of assessment was an all-or-nothing event. One subject, one sitting, one verdict. If the verdict went against you, the system did not recognise you and stayed silent about your progress,” Wesley noted in explaining the motivation behind CTEC.

“I described CTEC as a game-changer, and I promised then that we are witnessing the beginning of the end of the Caribbean Examinations Council as we know it. Today we keep that promise and we make history in Anguilla by announcing that the achievement of the highly successful CTEC pilot in mathematics in the May/June 2026 examinations and, with the approval of our board of governors, CXC is pleased to officially launch the Caribbean Targeted Education Certificate,” the CEO said.

“At CXC we hold to the position that competence is competence, no matter how long it takes to achieve and no matter how the route and… no matter the route by which it comes. This is how things and times have changed. This is how we have to meet this generation of learners where they are,” he added.

Wesley contended that “an assessment model built in the [20th] century cannot be expected to adequately serve a 21st century generation”, but said “CTEC is assessment redesigned for learners without lowering by a single degree the standard to which we hold”.

“When we were designing CTEC we asked ourselves, would the region embrace it? Today we have proof of concept from a region that has overwhelmingly accepted CTEC. When we invited the region to pilot CTEC mathematics module 1, more than 2,500 candidates stepped forward as pioneers across 15 territories, and 42 centres from Jamaica to Belize, from Barbados to the Cayman Islands and Anguilla, which was among the first countries to sign on to the pilot. Principals told us that their students were excited about the pilot examinations,” he said.

Wesley said the modularised examination format will now be applied to four other subject areas going forward, given the success of the maths module pilot.

“This is a new day for our Caribbean learners on the strength of this CTEC mathematics pilot. The Caribbean Examinations Council is declaring to our students this simple truth: What you know counts. We hear you. We see you. Your learning has been seen, measured, and certified. You are not at the end of the road. You are on your way up the staircase,” he said.

Telling policymakers across the region that “CTEC is yours to embed in your national education strategies, in your workforce and TVET planning and second chance programmes”, Wesley said CXC’s team was ready to work with the various ministries of education across the region and will be visiting territories in the weeks ahead to do exactly that.

CXC also said the 2,535 candidates who were involved in the pilot will continue to enjoy doing the other modules free of cost.

The candidates have a four-year period to complete it and will receive CSEC certification at the end.

World.title: Saving Moo Moo
World.content:
Nicholas Thomas, a resident of Spanish Town, feeds the cow he affectionately calls Moo Moo. (Photo: Napthali Junior)

Driving along Walks Road in Spanish Town, in the vicinity of Crescent Primary School, motorists may have noticed a cow lying motionless on the side of the road in the blazing sun, in the same spot for days. That cow is affectionately called Moo Moo by community members who have been taking care of her since she was injured in an accident more than a week ago.

When the Jamaica Observer visited the area Monday, police officers were seen feeding the injured cow grass and offering her water as community members looked on. Moo Moo ate slowly, pausing between bites as she gulped down water from a Dutch pot, seemingly desperate to rehydrate after days exposed to the summer heat. She remained largely immobile with most of her legs tucked beneath her body as though to protect them from further harm.

Reports from the policemen, Constable Dwight Lewis and Leighton Taylor, are that they were passing the area on Monday when they saw the cow and stopped. Moo Moo is believed to be pregnant and was injured during a hit-and-run accident. The owner has not yet come forward, and the accident has not been reported.

In the meantime, residents have stepped in.

A registered nurse who frequents the area, Gabriel Hamilton, said she spotted the cow about a week ago and became concerned when she noticed the animal was immobile.

“I came into the community, and I was asking around. People were not sure whose animal it is. I got closer to her, and I realised that her front right leg was injured, and I saw some blood in her abdominal area as well. The members of the community also told me that she’s pregnant, and I was like, ‘No, this cannot be’,” said Hamilton, visibly distressed as she recounted the interaction.

An animal lover who almost pursed a career as a veterinarian, she said she immediately sprang into action, calling Hope Zoo, the Jamaica Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (JSPCA), the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) and even her friend who is a trained veterinarian. Members of the community said they also made several calls to animal-related facilities, but no one has come to help.

Determined to ensure that the animal survived, Hamilton said she and other members of the community formed a pact to take care of Moo Moo. She said she entrusted community member Nicholas Thomas to be the cow’s primary caregiver, promising to compensate him for his efforts to keep Moo Moo alive. She had noticed that Moo Moo had lost weight and she was concerned about her nutrition.

Thomas said he was happy to officially take on the role, noting that he was already providing some level of care to the animal.

“When she ready for food she say, ‘Moo, moo’ and so I call her the name Moo Moo and she just accept everything with love,” he said, laughing.

He then bent down to rub the cow’s head, later jumping with joy as he thanked the news team for stopping by to highlight the story. He said he is optimistic that Moo Moo will survive, urging anyone who can help to do so.

Constable Lewis said he has reported the incident to his supervisor, and they are working to get a member of the agriculture team on location to transport the cow and get it medical attention.

“It’s part of our duty to serve, protect, and reassure, so we are reassuring the cow that help is on the way, and we are trying to get through to see if there is any owner so the owner can come and get her. The owner might not be sure as to its whereabouts. The owner might realise that the cow is not back, but as to the actual location of the cow, the owner might not be sure, so with the help of the media, probably the owner can get in touch and then speak to the Spanish Town police,” Constable Lewis told the Observer.

Constable Taylor, who farms as a hobby, said he loves animals and had to stop to help Moo Moo.

“We just want to make sure that she stays alive until the relevant persons come. We wish we could give her some shelter, but it’s out of our hands because we can’t even lift her up, so we just a try we best to make sure she stays alive,” said Taylor.

“Everybody who is passing can give a hand because we can’t stay here the whole day with her, but each person that is passing can give an eye. I realise a lot of persons help out because we come here and see a pot with water, so that’s good. It could’ve been my animal, so it’s good to see everybody helping out,” added Taylor.

World.title: RECOVERY AHEAD OF SCHEDULE
World.content:
JAMAICA could return to pre-Hurricane Melissa levels of economic output as early as the April-to-June quarter of 2027, significantly sooner than previously expected as the year-on-year contraction in the economy narrows and reconstruction gathers momentum.

The Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) said Tuesday that the current trajectory suggests the economy could regain the level of output recorded before Melissa within 1.5 to two years of the hurricane, compared with an earlier expectation that recovery would take about three years and extend into fiscal year 2028/29.

“Note, however, that full recovery — to include rebuilding efforts and replacing housing stock, public infrastructure and livelihoods — will be over a more extended period, possibly three to five years,” PIOJ Director General Dr Wayne Henry said at the institute’s quarterly economic briefing.

The improved outlook comes even as preliminary PIOJ estimates show that real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted 2.9 per cent in the April-to-June quarter compared with the corresponding period of 2025, marking a third-consecutive quarter of year-on-year decline.

The economy contracted 7.1 per cent year on year in the October-to-December 2025 quarter and 4.1 per cent year on year in January-March 2026.

The PIOJ, however, rejected suggestions that Jamaica is in a recession, pointing instead to the sequential improvement in economic activity following the hurricane-induced collapse in the final quarter of 2025.

“Yes, we can confirm that there is not a recession. We are not in a recession,” Senior director of the PIOJ’s Economic Planning and Research Division James Stewart told the Jamaica Observer.

Stewart said a recession also appeared unlikely for the remainder of the year.

While output in the first quarter of 2026 remained below the corresponding period a year earlier, seasonally adjusted real value added an increased 3.3 per cent compared with the hurricane-hit October-to-December quarter.

“Following three consecutive quarters of quarter-over-quarter growth during the first nine months of 2025 the economy experienced a sharp setback in the October-December 2025 quarter as Hurricane Melissa triggered a 7.3 per cent decline in real value added relative to July-September 2025,” Henry said.

“Importantly, the latest GDP release from Statin [Statistical Institute of Jamaica] confirms that the economy has begun to recover from the shock. The seasonally adjusted real value added for January-March 2026 increased by 3.3 per cent compared with the October-December 2025 quarter, signalling a rebound in economic activity,” he added.

The PIOJ, in its latest review of economic performance, said the April-to-June downturn largely reflected the lingering effects of Hurricane Melissa, which disrupted production, employment, domestic demand, and business and consumer confidence.

During the review quarter the goods-producing industry declined by an estimated 6.4 per cent as key sub-industries, including agriculture and mining and quarrying, recorded significant contractions.

Agriculture fell 17 per cent as hurricane damage across major crop-producing parishes was compounded by drought conditions associated with the El Niño phenomenon.

Mining and quarrying, on the other hand, contracted by 23.9 per cent, largely due to a 30.8 per cent decline in aluminium production as technical challenges linked to hurricane damage continued to weigh on operations.

There were, however, signs of resilience in other productive activities as manufacturing grew by an estimated one per cent while construction expanded 0.3 per cent, supported by higher civil engineering activity.

The services industry contracted by 1.7 per cent, with most industries declining. The exceptions were financial and insurance activities, up 1.9 per cent; wholesale and retail trade, repair of motor vehicles, and installation of machinery and equipment (WRTRIM), up 0.2 per cent; and public administration and defence, up 0.1 per cent.

Accommodation and food service activities, one of the larger service industries, however fell 12.2 per cent, reflecting weaker tourism activity. Preliminary data show stopover arrivals for April and May falling 19.6 per cent to 382,745 visitors, while visitor expenditure declined 17 per cent to US$578 million.

For the January to June period or first half of the calendar year real GDP is estimated to have contracted by 3.5 per cent, with the goods-producing industry down 6.8 per cent and services down 2.4 per cent.

Despite the weaker headline numbers, PIOJ Director General Dr Wayne Henry said the underlying trend points to an economy recovering from a significant one-off shock rather than entering a prolonged downturn.

Henry also pointed to developments in the labour market as another positive indicator, saying the pace of recovery reflects the resilience of Jamaica’s underlying economic fundamentals despite widespread disruption caused by the hurricane.

The PIOJ, while maintaining a negative short-term outlook, said it expects the rate of contraction to narrow as more industries recover. The institute forecasts a contraction of 0.5 per cent to 1.5 per cent in the current July-to-September quarter, followed by growth of one per cent to three per cent for fiscal year 2026/27.

“Economic growth is expected to be driven by gradual recovery in all industries, due to an expectation for fairly robust growth in the latter half of the fiscal year,” Henry said.

He said the outlook is supported by the low-base effect from Hurricane Melissa’s impact in the latter half of fiscal year 2025/26, faster recovery across most industries, increased reconstruction activity, favourable weather conditions, and the potential resolution of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

A rise in capital expenditure under the Public Sector Investment Programme is also expected to support the recovery. Spending increased 55.8 per cent to $13.7 billion during the April-to-June quarter, boosting public investment and reconstruction activity.

“This momentum is expected to continue over the short to medium term as reconstruction activities intensify and the implementation of recovery projects accelerate,” Henry said.

World.title: FUTURE KINGS!
World.content:
Jamaica’s players celebrate during the CWI Rising Stars Under-19 men’s three-day cricket final against Barbados at Arnos Vale Stadium in St Vincent on August 1, 2023. (Photo: CWI Media)

Jamaica Cricket Association (JCA) President Dr Donovan Bennett says that while the Kingsmen ownership continues to find its footing with the Jamaican franchise in the Caribbean Premier League (CPL), his eyes remain fixed on the developmental aspect of their partnership.

For two years Jamaica was without a franchise in the region’s premier Twenty20 cricket competition, but that changed when the Kingsmen Sports Enterprise landed a successful bid.

The move also coincided with the return of the competition to Jamaica, which last hosted a CPL match when the now-defunct Tallawahs defeated Barbados Tridents in September 2019.

But amidst the buzz as the freshly branded Jamaica Kingsmen prepared to host their fourth and final home match of the 2026 season at Sabina Park late on Tuesday, Bennett noted that grassroots plans are in the pipeline.

“Certainly [hosting the games] has helped to rekindle interest in cricket. My [goal] now is to get everybody on board — both the [Kingsmen] franchise and the [Jamaican] Government — in our developmental programmes,” he told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

In February 2026 the Observer had reported that the United States-based Kingsmen group was committed to supporting grassroots development.

Kingsmen Sports Enterprise representative Faisal Mirza had said that one of the Fawad Sarwar-owned organisation’s priority is to pump resources into developing Jamaica’s young talents.

“…We definitely want to invest in grassroots and again reintegrating grassroots cricket and school cricket into the Jamaican ecosystem. Driving more of the youth into cricket… so that homegrown talent can once again sort of elevate to the levels of… the greats like Dre Russ [Andre Russell], Rovman [Powell] and Chris [Gayle] and all these legends whose shadows are often arched even beyond the game itself right,” Mirza said.

Bennett said on Tuesday that he looks forward to the investment and insisted the raw talent is available in Jamaica for players to matriculate.

“The Kingsmen are smart people. They not only want to help Jamaica’s cricket for Jamaica, they want to help Jamaica’s cricket for the Kingsmen also,” the JCA boss said.

“We have some very good youngsters around. I’m very excited about five or six Under-19 youngsters who, with the proper type of developmental programmes in place, can go very far.

“I’ve already spoken to the Kingsmen and they are very interested in our age-group programmes, and we’ve spoken to the Government who have promised to help, and also to a few sponsors who we are trying to engage,” he said.

He said he is already rubbing his hands at the prospect of implementing plans to help shape the future of Under-13 age-group players.

“We started our Under-13 programme last year and that needs to continue. We already have got invitations from both Guyana and Trinidad for our Jamaica Under-13 team to participate in tournaments there in December so we need to get busy as soon as the CPL is finished. In Jamaica — and we see other territories doing it as well — is to place the emphasis on the ground level,” Bennett said.

— Sanjay Myers

World.title: NCB resets consumer lending after delinquency spike
World.content:
NCB Financial Group Chief Executive Officer Robert Almeida says the group paused lending through recently introduced unsecured consumer products for about three months while it tightened its credit models. The affected loan book has since been relaunched and is growing with a lower delinquency rate, as NCB seeks to convert its larger deposit base into prudent new lending.

NCB Financial Group Limited (NCBFG) paused lending through recently introduced unsecured consumer products for about three months after delinquencies rose, then relaunched them with tighter credit models, Chief Executive Officer Robert Almeida said.

Almeida told the Jamaica Observer in an interview last Friday, following NCBFG’s quarterly investor briefing, that the affected loan book was growing again with a lower delinquency rate. He did not identify the products, disclose the size of the portfolio or provide delinquency rates before and after the changes.

“Consumer retail, and really unsecured consumer retail, is where we were seeing the spike in our current delinquency profile,” Almeida said.

“We took a pause for about a quarter while we tightened up those models, figured out where the weaknesses were, and then we relaunched. That loan book is now growing again, and it is growing with a lower delinquency rate.”

The intervention came during a wider contraction in NCBFG’s loan book. Gross loans and advances fell by $25.27 billion, or 3.9 per cent, to $615.57 billion at June 30 from $640.84 billion a year earlier, according to the group’s unaudited nine-month financial statements.

Almeida said the consumer-loan pause was one of several reasons for the decline. Scheduled repayments exceeded new lending during the period, while the group became more cautious following Hurricane Melissa. Management’s earlier concentration on improving basic service and attracting deposits also slowed lending, he said.

While loans declined, customer deposits rose by $67.72 billion, or 8.4 per cent, to $874.04 billion. Gross loans were equivalent to 70.4 per cent of deposits, according to a Business Observer calculation, down from 79.5 per cent a year earlier.

The movement left NCBFG with a larger pool of deposit funding relative to its loan book, but also increased the pressure on management to put that money to work without taking on excessive credit risk.

Almeida said the group was not deliberately reducing its credit exposure and wanted to reverse the decline in lending. NCB was becoming more active in motor-vehicle financing and would increase its focus on mortgages and larger corporate transactions, he said.

The delinquency spike in the newer consumer products was unrelated to the $10.67 billion in bad loans that NCBFG wrote off during the nine months to June, Almeida said. The write-offs were nearly three times the $3.75 billion recorded in the corresponding period last year.

Almeida said the write-offs covered older problem loans across the portfolio that had already been provided for.

“It included a bit of everything, because really we weren’t writing off as quickly as we should,” he said.

Removing the loans and corresponding provisions from the balance sheet therefore did not create a fresh charge against current profit. The write-offs, together with improved collections, recoveries and lower classified exposures, helped reduce non-performing loans by $4.7 billion, or 16 per cent, to $24.1 billion. The non-performing-loan ratio improved to 3.91 per cent from 4.49 per cent.

Group-wide credit impairment losses fell by 36 per cent to $4.37 billion. Almeida said current credit costs were increasingly concentrated in retail lending after several large corporate exposures produced more uneven charges in earlier periods. He said the experience with the newer consumer products had led NCBFG to tighten its underwriting.

The group’s June-quarter profit recovered from the March period, although much of the improvement came from unrealised gains on listed foreign equities rather than a comparable increase in recurring income.

Consolidated net profit rose by 57 per cent from the preceding quarter to $8.24 billion but was little changed from $8.25 billion in the corresponding period last year. Profit attributable to NCBFG shareholders increased by 30 per cent sequentially and 8.4 per cent year on year to $6.08 billion.

Gains on foreign-currency and investment activities totalled $5.74 billion, compared with a $2.01-billion loss in the March quarter — a swing of $7.75 billion.

Almeida said the foreign equities were listed and liquid, making the gains realisable, although their value remained exposed to market movements. He said averaging the March and June quarters produced what he regarded as recurring attributable profit of about $5 billion to $6 billion a quarter.

He expects that range to rise to between $6 billion and $7 billion “relatively quickly” as NCBFG works towards a return on equity of 15 to 20 per cent and a cost-to-income ratio below 60 per cent.

Those targets remain some distance away. NCBFG reported an annualised return on equity of 8.57 per cent and a nine-month cost-to-income ratio of 70.4 per cent. Its June-quarter cost-to-income ratio was approximately 66.7 per cent, based on a Business Observer calculation.

Sheree Martin, interim chief executive officer of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited, told the investor briefing that many processes at the bank remained manual, meaning efficiency improvements would be partly incremental. She said the bank was working to make its operations faster, simpler and more customer-centred, while increasing revenue to support its existing cost base.

For the nine months, net profit attributable to NCBFG shareholders fell by 30 per cent to $13.28 billion, largely because the prior-year period included a one-off gain from the sale of the group’s Netherlands insurance brokerage. NCBFG said attributable profit would have increased by 38 per cent after excluding that gain.

The group must now turn its growing deposit base into new loans while preserving the tighter credit standards introduced after the consumer-lending setback.

“The good news is, when you’re bringing in the deposits, you build up a stronger capacity to lend,” Almeida said. “Now we have to realise and utilise that capacity to grow the loan book.”

World.title: LAYING THE GROUNDWORK FOR AI-POWERED CYBERSECURITY
World.content:
While AI is a powerful tool for attackers, it is also a powerful asset for cybersecurity. Rene van Haaster, vice president EMEA North, Elastic

There is, thankfully, another side to the story. While AI is a powerful tool for attackers, it is also a powerful asset for cybersecurity. Organizations are leveraging AI to reduce their mean time to detect, respond and recover, and to stay ahead of advanced attacks.

The EU’s Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI not only outlines a coordinated strategy for responding to AI-driven attacks, but also proposes a blueprint for structured access to advanced AI models for the use of IT security teams working within public authorities and private companies.

Adapt and survive

This is an important step forward but, in today’s AI-fueled threat landscape, there are three areas that EU organizations need to consider if they want to keep hackers in check. In short, they must adapt to survive.

The first is control and sovereignty. This is particularly important in Europe, where technological sovereignty has become an increasingly strategic objective.

Organizations need the ability to understand where their data has been created, moved and stored. This is central to their ability to retain meaningful control over the technologies they depend on. In practice, this means avoiding architectures that lock them into specific providers or limit their ability to integrate new capabilities and retaining the freedom to move data in, between, and out of vendors and service providers as their needs evolve. Vendor lock-in is a procurement concern, and one that many organizations seek to escape from.

World.title: Former PM Fillon suspended from top French honor over fake jobs conviction
World.content:
François Fillon arrives at the Court of Appeal for the review of his sentence for corruption over a 'fake jobs' scandal, at the Palais de Justice courthouse in Paris, on April 29, 2025. | Bertrand Guay/AFP via Getty Images

PARIS — Former French Prime Minister François Fillon has been suspended for 10 years from the Légion d’honneur, France’s highest order of merit, after being found guilty of providing his wife with a fake job in which she was paid a salary using taxpayer money.

The decision to suspend Fillon was published Thursday morning in the French official gazette. It was approved by President Emmanuel Macron after being recommended by the body tasked with handling disciplinary measures for the Légion d’honneur.

The fake jobs scandal emerged during the campaign for the 2017 presidential election and cost Fillon a shot at the presidency, as he was a front-runner in the contest before the allegations emerged.

World.title: Russian overnight strikes kill at least 13 in Ukraine
World.content:
A person stands next to cars and buildings damaged in a Russian strike on Kyiv. | Roman Pilipey/AFP via Getty Images

Russia unleashed a barrage of missiles and drones across Ukraine early Thursday, killing at least 13 people and wounding dozens more.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the hours-long attack struck Kyiv and the surrounding region as well as Odesa and Chernihiv, damaging apartment buildings, a children’s hospital and a school in the capital. Twelve people were killed in Kyiv and another in the surrounding region, he said, with around 40 injured.

“Unfortunately, while Moscow is investing in ballistic missiles and escalation, such strikes do not always receive the response they should from the world,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. “As long as Ukraine does not have enough anti-ballistic defense, Russia will not consider peace seriously.” U.S.-made Patriot interceptors “cannot yet be replaced,” he added.

World.title: Labour’s Farage donor crackdown hits a Downing Street roadblock
World.content:
A domestic donations cap will not be in the elections bill when it returns next month.

Labour MPs want a cap on political donations to stave off Nigel Farage’s big-money backers. Andy Burnham is set to disappoint them.

Downing Street will not include a universal domestic cap on political donations in Britain when the elections bill returns on Sept. 2, two officials briefed on government thinking said. But both the officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss policy considerations, did not rule out returning to the issue again in the future.

“We’re prioritizing cracking down on foreign interference and crypto billionaires as part of this piece of legislation,” one of the officials said, referencing existing proposals in the elections bill from Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer to cap overseas donors and ban cryptocurrency donations.





That’s despite mounting pressure to act from the British PM’s own MPs as they fret about Farage, whose rise has been aided by a flurry of cash from individual donors — and hints from Burnham himself that he is minded to move ahead.

There is currently no limit on the amount individual donors based in the U.K. can give to a political party. Donations above £11,180 must be reported to the Electoral Commission watchdog.

Burnham told transparency campaigners before becoming prime minister that he supported a cap to “guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation.”

A Liberal Democrat supporter holds up a donation bucket at a party conference in 2021. | Chris J Ratcliffe/Getty Images

While indicating a wider review of political funding would be required before setting a firm figure, Burnham said his “gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k” for the upper limit.

Following Burnham’s arrival in No. 10 Downing Street in July, officials in Whitehall had been waiting for a signal that they should start work to include a donation cap in the Representation of the People Bill — the official title of the elections bill.

But the two officials quoted above said using that bill as the vehicle for a cap could delay plans also included in the legislation to give 16-year-olds the right to vote at the next general election.





A third British official acknowledged the Sept. 2 date, when the elections bill returns, is a “crunch point,” and suggested ministers could “kick the can” and commit to considering action when the bill gets to the House of Lords.

A Labour MP pushing for a donations cap said the arguments being put forward for not going ahead with a donations cap are “bullshit,” adding: “They are scared of the unions.”

Complicated landscape

A POLITICO analysis of how a £500,000 donation cap would have hit the main political parties’ finances over the last three years demonstrates the trade-offs Burnham would face in pushing ahead.

The analysis draws on publicly-available Electoral Commission returns for Westminster’s main political parties between Jan. 1 2023 and Dec. 31, 2025.

It shows a £500,000 ceiling would have curbed 55 percent of Reform UK’s reported private donations over the past three years — amounting to some £12 million — suggesting Nigel Farage’s party would have taken the greatest hit of any of the parties in proportional terms over the period.

But the data also shows there is potential peril for Labour in slamming a lid on funding — particularly if cash from trade unions, which represent some of the party’s major backers, is included.

A £500,000 cap over the same period — with no union exclusion — would have wiped out 47.4 percent of all private donations to Labour, or around £34 million in funding.





An exemption from the cap for unions would leave Labour’s war chest significantly stronger. Labour would have kept hold of £12 million of that money over the same period, which included the donation-rich run-up to the 2024 general election.

The GMB trade union has already urged Labour MPs not to back a cap due to concerns it will damage the labor movement’s historic relationship with the party.

Parliamentary pressure

Opting for a cap with or without a union exemption carries significant political risk for Burnham. Capping unions alongside individual donors and corporates would dent Labour’s finances and strain relations with the movement seen as foundational to the party’s identity.

But exempting them from any cap would bolster Farage’s narrative that changes to election rules are part of an intentional establishment campaign to halt his party’s progress.

Burnham’s predecessor, Starmer, already proposed an annual £100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas.





The measure could create a major hurdle for crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, who has donated over £12 million to Reform UK despite being based in Thailand.

But MPs are already putting pressure on Burnham’s new government to go further.

Several amendments pushing for domestic caps set at various amounts — up to £1 million — were proposed when the bill was introduced earlier this year. A proposal from Labour MP Stella Creasy, which would mirror the £100,000 cap on overseas donors, gained the most support.

A donations bucket featuring Nigel Farage at a UKIP conference in Margate, Kent in 2015. | Ben Stanstall/AFP via Getty Images

At the time, the amendments were aimed at demonstrating political appetite for a long-running campaign to limit the sway of mega-donors, but MPs and campaigners had hoped Burnham’s previous comments had indicated he was gearing up to act.

One adviser working the parliamentary push for a donations cap said MPs could back down if the government suggests its own cap — regardless of the size of it.

“Our preferred outcome is the government come forward with their own individual donation cap,” the adviser said. “Whatever the level is we will support it.”





Supporters of a cap also pointed to Creasy’s amendment, drafted with assistance from Transparency International UK, as a potential middle-ground for the knotty union problem. Rather than a blanket policy, Creasy proposes that affiliation fees — an annual political levy usually paid by unions on a per-member basis — would be exempt from the cap, while other donations would be included.

POLITICO’s analysis shows that approach would lessen the blow on Labour’s finances — while not providing unions a complete carve-out.

In 2024, GMB gave Labour £2 million in total — of which £1.1 million was affiliation fees.

Under Creasy’s carve-out for unions, the £1.1 million in affiliation fees would go directly to Labour.

Only the remaining £900,000 would be subject to the cap, wherever it is set — meaning a far gentler loss to Labour.

“The loophole must be closed to prevent mega-rich donors who have the potential to harm democracy — as the government has accepted is possible — that means they can continue to donate just because they claim a U.K. postcode,” Creasy said.





POLITICO’s analysis suggests that the Creasy amendment’s proposed cap — £100,000 — would have eaten into the donation income of leading parties had it been applied over the last three years.

In 2023, a £100,000 cap would have deprived the then-governing Conservative Party of more than £26 million — around 54 percent of all its declared donations.

Labour would have lost between £11 million and £16 million, depending on how the rules were applied to unions — a loss of between 50 percent and 70 percent of its declared donations.

In 2024, both Labour and Conservatives would have lost higher sums of cash as election campaign fundraising hit its peak, although the losses remain similar in percentage terms.

Other parties would have faced similar hits, with the Liberal Democrats losing around 20 percent of their £9 million declared donation income, while around 40 percent of Reform UK’s £3 million of declared funds would have been ineligible.

Analysis of last year’s data suggests a £100,000 cap would have been devastating for Farage’s outfit given its reliance on mega-donors.

Of the £18.8 million declared in donations for 2025, more than £15 million would be lost under Creasy’s plan — around 80 percent of Reform’s total declared donations.





With campaign spending hitting record highs at the 2024 election, even a lenient cap would have had a substantial impact on the country’s major political parties. But successive polls have found public support for the measures.

In January, YouGov’s biannual tracker showed that 67 percent of Brits backed a donations cap of £50,000 or less, with support for the current, unlimited system dropping from 21 percent in 2020 to just 13 percent at the start of this year.

World.title: Zelenskyy’s rival Fedorov overplays his hand with election push
World.content:
Zelenskyy still commands broad support as a war leader, and his allies pointed out that, regardless of public frustration, there are limits to how much he can reveal about the inner workings of the state when national survival is at stake.

Fedorov’s emergence as a rival to Zelenskyy was accelerated by his shock dismissal as defense minister last month. The 35-year-old built up a strong following for spearheading Ukraine’s success in using new technologies — from cyberattacks to drones — to damage Russia.

His ejection from office sparked immediate protests, with thousands of people taking to the streets, calling for his reinstatement or for Zelenskyy to properly explain the decision to fire him.

In his address on Tuesday night, Fedorov delivered a thinly veiled criticism of Zelenskyy’s management style, referring to his peremptory approach to hiring and firing.

“People cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made. Why some reforms move forward while others are blocked. Why decisions needed on the frontlines today spend months circulating through government offices,” Fedorov said.

“It is dangerous when society develops the feeling that the main criterion for an appointment is not professionalism, results, or the ability to transform the country, but personal loyalty to the system,” added the former minister, who had himself been viewed as a Zelenskyy loyalist for seven years.

World.title: Russia runs out of petrol at seven in 10 stations as fuel crisis worsens
World.content:
Petrol was available at fewer than three in 10 petrol stations across Russia on Wednesday, the latest sign that a second wave of fuel shortages is hitting harder than the first, with queues forming at pumps in Moscow for the first time.

 

The monitoring app Gdebenz put nationwide petrol availability at 28% of filling stations on Wednesday, down from 41% a week earlier.

Fuel restrictions — including limits on the volume sold per customer, QR-based rationing and odd-even number plate schemes — were in place in nearly all regions as of last Saturday, according to Benzinmap, which tracks restrictions and prices nationwide.

Gazprom Neft filling stations in Moscow set a temporary cap of 40 litres per fill-up. Tatneft capped petrol at 50 litres and diesel at 60. By Wednesday, the Yandex Fuel service showed AI-92 petrol available at just one in 10 stations in the capital.

The crisis is the direct result of Kyiv's sustained drone campaign against Russian oil infrastructure in a bid to weaken its war machine amid Moscow's ongoing all-out invasion of Ukraine. By early July every major refinery in Russia had been struck at least once.

In the first two weeks of August alone, nearly a dozen more facilities were hit, including Yaroslavnefteorgsintez in Yaroslavl, two refineries in Bashkortostan and export infrastructure at the port of Ust-Luga.

Russian Forbes calculated that damaged refineries now account for 54% of total national refining capacity. Daily petrol output fell to between 75,000 and 80,000 tonnes in July, against summer demand of 115,000 to 120,000 tonnes — a daily deficit of roughly 35%.

Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged the shortage at the end of July, describing it as "non-critical". He repeated the phrase on Wednesday.

"There are no critical consequences from such attacks, there have been none and there cannot be any. But they do, of course, cause us damage; that is obvious, we understand it, we see it and we know it," Putin said.

Disagreements over imports further the crisis

Russia's position as one of the world's largest oil exporters has not shielded it from the shortages.

In July Moscow banned petrol and diesel exports to protect domestic supply. It has been importing fuel by rail from Belarus — shipments that surged 25-fold year on year between January and July — Kazakhstan and for the first time Morocco, when a Lukoil-supplied cargo of approximately 30,000 tonnes of AI-92 was loaded at Tangier and shipped to Murmansk.

Much of the imported fuel has not reached consumers: according to Russian industry sources cited by the portal InfoTEK, large volumes of Indian and Moroccan petrol are stuck at Murmansk because suppliers want between 110,000 and 130,000 roubles per tonne, while the state regulator is demanding a price below 78,000 roubles**.**

A further supply gap is expected in September when Belarus's Novopolotsk refinery undergoes scheduled maintenance.

Belarus supplied a record 212,000 tonnes of petrol and 162,000 tonnes of diesel to Russia in July. It now processes Russian crude on a tolling basis and is Moscow's most important external fuel source. Both of Belarus' refineries — Novopolotsk and Mozyr — have a combined export capacity of roughly 2 million tonnes per year, a fraction of what Russia needs.

Retail petrol prices rose 7.4% in the first half of 2026 to an average of 70 roubles per litre, and diesel by more than 12%, according to official data. Residents in some regions say prices have exceeded 100 roubles per litre (€1.02).

The Kremlin has ordered the Federal Antimonopoly Service to tighten price controls; the agency said on Wednesday it had opened 41 cases against oil companies for violations.

The crisis has forced Russia to reintroduce fuel grades that it banned in the 2010s. On 5 August the government authorised the production, import and sale of Euro-2, Euro-3 and Euro-4 petrol for almost a year.

High-sulphur fuel below the Euro-5 standard can degrade modern engines and produces significantly higher levels of air pollutants. Trading in the lower grades started on the St Petersburg exchange on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, authorities are prosecuting people who have complained publicly about the shortages.

In Volgograd, authorities detained five residents after they recorded a video message to the head of the Russian Investigative Committee Alexander Bastrykin, complaining that officials filled up without restrictions while ordinary drivers faced rationing.

One received five days' administrative arrest, while another was fined. A Perm resident who staged a solo picket over petrol access was also fined.

World.title: Why swimming in the Rhine is allowed in Switzerland but banned in Germany
World.content:
It is 32 degrees in Basel. On the bridge people are eating ice cream, while below it swimmers keep surfacing as they drift along in the Rhine. In Basel you are allowed to swim in the river, despite international freight shipping and other leisure activities.

 

"Part of the river in the city centre is marked out with buoys," Tim Edler tells Euronews. Swimmers, leisure users and shipping all share the same stretch of water here. Edler is co-founder of Flussbad Berlin, an association that wants to make the Spree in Berlin safe for swimming. He was recently in Basel for the Swimmable Cities European Forum. The aim of this network is to make urban waterways accessible again and clean enough for bathing.

And in Basel that is already reality, "one of the city's central features", as Edler puts it. The Swiss city is widely regarded as the Mecca of river swimming in major cities. "For many people who live and work here, the Rhine is an important part of their everyday lives," says Conradin Cramer, president of the Basel cantonal government, speaking to SRF.

River bathing is not a gift of nature

In mid-August around 4,500 people showed how it is done. Edler also took part in the Rhine swim, an annual event in Basel. The approximately two-kilometre course runs downstream from Kleinbasel to the Johanniter Bridge. Safe bathing is made possible by clear rules and good information, explains Christoph Bosshardt, head of Basel's location marketing, speaking to SRF.

Clean water alone is not enough. "Showers, steps, entry points, rescue plans and clear rules are just as important," Bosshardt tells the Swiss media company. In Basel the infrastructure along the Rhine has been systematically expanded over many years.

Swimmers in the Rhine in Basel. Copyright 2006 AP. All rights reserved.

After a major fire in 1986 at a Basel chemical factory warehouse, not only chemicals but also tonnes of toxic fire-fighting water flowed into the Rhine. What followed was an ecocide – and a rethink about how the river should be used in future. Basel does not have a clean, swimmable Rhine by chance; it has worked towards it over decades. Edler also says: "This is something you can achieve through persistent, focused change."

Why the Rhine is swimmable in Basel but not in Cologne or Düsseldorf

Edler, who also wants to introduce swimming in Berlin's Spree, sees the core problem in the way waterways are managed. "The most important prerequisite that exists in Basel is not water quality, riverbanks, ports or facilities; it is the willingness to allow people to use the river on their own responsibility," says Edler.

Because in Basel too people are well aware that the Rhine has strong currents and, as a fast-flowing river, entails risks. The city and the Basel section of the Swiss Life Saving Society (SLRG) provide maps showing the safe areas.

On the website (source in German) of the City of Basel you can find information on water level and temperature. The water should be at least 18 degrees Celsius, you should always swim with others, and you should not leave the marked swimming areas. So in Basel there is a clear awareness that river swimming involves dangers.

The swimmers in the river float along with their so-called Wickelfisch float bags. Copyright 2006 AP. All rights reserved.

"The authorities and politicians are not there to shield people completely from these dangers, but should instead create the conditions that allow them to deal with them in an appropriate way," Edler believes. For him, concrete information and clear rules are a better option than bans.

Basel lies where Switzerland, France and Germany meet. Here the Rhine even marks the immediate border. If you were to swim a few hundred metres further from Basel, "then you swim into France, where it is banned, and across the river in Germany it is banned as well," Edler tells Euronews. It is, of course, the same river, but it is perceived differently.

Why is river bathing failing in Germany?

In Germany, the Rhine is still a long way from becoming a giant public swimming pool. Almost 500 kilometres north of Basel lies Cologne. Here, and in neighbouring Düsseldorf, bathing and swimming in the Rhine are strictly prohibited throughout the city area. Anyone who ignores this faces fines of up to 1,000 euros.

The bans have been in force in these major cities since late summer 2025. Cologne cites numerous fatal bathing accidents as the reason. "The Rhine is particularly dangerous because you cannot see the whirlpools and suction effects, which are caused among other things by ships," the city explains. Düsseldorf and other riverside cities have issued similar bans.

Edler, however, asks why swimming is so dangerous in the first place. The Rhine in particular has been dedicated to shipping, with the riverbed modified in places. To that end, so-called groynes or training walls have been built – gravel banks or stone walls jutting into the water. It is here in particular that currents develop with a suction effect towards the navigation channel.

"If people fall into the water from one of these groynes that stick out into the river, they are automatically in an area of deadly whirlpools," Edler also warns.
