The H5 bird flu has been confirmed in seven birds involved in six different “bird flu events” on the NSW South Coast.

There have been 11 bird flu events reported in NSW, which may involve multiple birds.

A greater crested tern. Fairfax media

The latest events involve greater crested terns and giant petrels near Narooma and Merimbula.

“These new events are very disturbing, but we’re continuing to prepare for further impacts of bird flu,” Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said in a statement this afternoon. “We are undertaking surveillance and we are working closely with wildlife groups to share as much information as possible.”

World.title: Government must get tough to protect our future prosperity
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are three irrefutable facts in the blame game over which side of politics is responsible for our trillion dollar debt (“Government debt to hit $1 trillion today”, August 20). The first is that John Howard and Peter Costello paid back the Hawke/Keating-era debt, leaving Australia debt-free when they lost office. The second is that the Coalition under Morrison/Frydenberg had little choice when COVID hit but to pump money into the economy to stop total collapse. The third is that it is Labor’s responsibility to track a path back to surplus by cutting expenditure and waste, and improving productivity. What we see at the moment is just the opposite – subsidies are handed out every day, the renewables obsession continues unabated (and uncosted), the public service remains bloated, unions are taking over workplaces, laws and regulations are stifling innovation and economic activity, and working from home is becoming a right. Labor has been in power for more than four years now. Despite booming mining revenues, all we have to show for it is forecast deficits as far as the eye can see. Labor is responsible for our future prosperity and it is failing to deliver by making the hard choices needed. Pity our children and grandchildren. Ian Morison, Forrest (ACT) Appropriate response I am a Sydney Swans supporter and am outraged by the behaviour of the players implicated in the latest scandal (“Swans fans devastated by sexual assault allegation”, August 20). But I fail to see how this degrades the so-called culture of the club. It is not the club’s fault that these men made such stupid decisions. I think the real culture of the Sydney Swans is shown by the leaders of the club, who have come down hard on these players. In doing so, they have recognised that winning a trophy is much less important than allowing such behaviour to be swept under the carpet. John Rome, Mount Lawley Photo: Megan Herbert You grasp the effects of poor choices by adult men when you realise you’re wearing a Sydney Swans jersey and quickly take it off before you pick your grandchild up from daycare. Mark Palmer, Inverell As legendary Australian rugby league coach Jack Gibson once famously warned his players: “Nothing good happens in a bar after midnight.” Geoff Goodfellow, Moss Vale Passing the buck



If the government manages to remove 240,000 people from the NDIS I assume they will all be picked up by the new scheme the government plans to implement – which will also be paid for by either individual states or the Commonwealth (“States have more work to do on NDIS, says Butler”, August 20). This will just shift the cost from the NDIS onto a different platform. How is this making any difference for people who require help? I was never any good at maths, but even I can see this doesn’t add up. Monica Turik, Mona Vale Leaders’ poor example Greg Baker poses the question at the heart of ethics: “What is the right thing to do?” (Letters, August 20). Many letter writers have suggested that parents should instil values and schools endorse them. Less has been mentioned of the examples set by our leaders. How telling, then, that the government and opposition together endorsed such limited curbs on the gambling industry despite the well-known potential to cause harm and the population begging for reform. How might that decision adversely affect not only children, but all Australians? If we can’t trust our elected representatives to bring about legislation that most constituents strongly believe in, how can any government require anyone else to behave ethically Barbara Watt, Frenchs Forest Doesn’t pass the test Among the thousands of students who sat for the selective high school examinations, successful applicants have just received the good news (“Selective school offers out as gender quotas take effect”, August 20). However, many who were offered places in a selective high school will instead opt for a private school scholarship, which, according to the article, was always their primary goal, while others who accept their offers will be committing to a long-distance daily commute for the next six years – a round trip of about 110 kilometres a day in one case! Neither of these outcomes – using a selective placement to secure a place in a private school, or having students travel across regions to school – seems desirable to me. Irene Buckler, Glenwood Akshaya Valluri made it into Penrith High School but does not know if she will accept her offer. James Brickwood Double standard



Three Scots College teenagers are charged with sexual assault and released on bail to their parents. In a parallel universe, three teenagers from south-west Sydney, also charged with sexual assault, are remanded in custody (“Private school students allegedly raped girl in Sydney home”, August 20). It will be interesting to watch these studies of crime and punishment as they unfold. It may be as socially and morally revealing as Dostoevsky’s classic. Rowan Godwin, Rozelle Gunning for change Tracy Blackburn’s “sandstone curtain” jibe at city people sipping lattes from eco-friendly cups is not only patronising; it rather gives away the contempt behind her argument (“Farmers take aim at state’s gun ownership restrictions”, August 19). I run a farm in regional NSW and the graziers near me manage perfectly well with one or two firearms for various legitimate purposes – foxes, feral cats, injured large animals, wild pigs and deer. They know their firearms are tools and that a smart person does not need excess tools. Ms Blackburn might also remember that many of those supposedly clueless latte-sipping city people she disparages are the doctors, nurses and teachers who leave the city to fill essential positions in rural and regional communities. They don’t need a lecture about life on the land – rural Australia needs them. And the latte sneer is increasingly tired. I see plenty of local farmers and graziers happily sipping lattes from reusable cups. Perhaps Ms Blackburn could join them, take a soothing sip and reconsider the notion that common sense stops at the sandstone curtain. Farmers deserve to be heard in the gun debate. But so do others, without the sneering city-versus-country caricature. Vivien Clark-Ferraino, Duckmaloi Unite on gambling reform Instead of supporting the government’s pathetic modifications to the recommended new gambling laws, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor could have worked with Anthony Albanese to get all of Peta Murphy’s anti-gambling reforms passed into law and collected lots of much-needed public brownie points (“Husband of late MP Peta Murphy gives his verdict on Labor’s gambling reforms”, August 20). We heard both parties praising Murphy’s proposals when they were introduced to parliament but when it came to the crunch each party backed off, frightened to lose millions from the gambling lobby. We know that the gambling industry is all-powerful and has our politicians seemingly under its control, but if our two main parties had worked together they could have got all Murphy’s reforms through both houses of parliament. It could have been as easy as that, and would have had the public’s support. Christine Shale, Mosman Decades of pollution



Lead pollution in the soil near homes and schools around Broken Hill was known about 40 years ago (“‘Potent’ toxin found above guidelines in soil at 10 childcare centres”, August 20). I included the issue when teaching environmental medicine to postgraduate students at the time. There is an immense slag heap that borders part of the town and every time the wind blew, it would spread lead-contaminated dust over the whole town. The poorer families’ houses collected more dust, exposing them more. The government has dragged its heels in preventing this pollution and remediating the town, and is still doing so after all this time. Why isn’t BHP cleaning it up? It’s their mess. John Frith, The Entrance Lead has been found over national thresholds at 10 childcare centres in the NSW outback town. Artwork: Stephen Kiprillis Empty nests In her article about housing people in need, Julie Power writes about the utilisation of vacant properties pending development, demolition or upgrades (“The empty homes that could help solve Sydney’s housing crisis”, August 20). There is another measure that, without laying a brick so to speak, could deliver more housing, address the cost of living for those struggling to meet mortgage payments and tackle the loneliness epidemic among older, single people. The cost to the government would be negligible. Britain’s Rent a Room scheme allows homeowners to earn up to £7500 a year tax-free (about $15,000) from letting out furnished accommodation in their homes. I would love to see this scheme adopted in Australia. Jill Robinson, Randwick Congratulations to Toga for their outstanding initiatives in finding vacant properties for the homeless, whether short or long term. I have often wondered about the seemingly empty hotel accommodation that I pass in Sydney. Irene Thom, Vaucluse Renters struggle The budget tax increases were to force investors out of existing housing and into new construction (“Renters in crossfire of battle over tax reforms”, August 20). The idea was for reduced prices of existing property to assist first home buyers while increased investor demand would increase prices for new stock, thereby stimulating supply. Renters who can never buy will inevitably face increasing rents from declining old stock and higher rents on new. If I were now forced to sell a house that a neighbouring family has rented for over 20 years, it would almost inevitably go to a well-financed owner-occupier. My tenants could not afford it and they would lose their home. William S Lloyd, Denistone



Danger of censorship I spent 14 years working as a humanitarian worker in Bangladesh, Myanmar and Cambodia. I saw what happens when governments and institutions restrict access to information and make certain ideas too dangerous to discuss. I returned to Australia assuming that freedom of expression and access to information were deeply embedded in our public institutions. That is why I find the reported removal of How to Sell a Genocide from Waverley library so disturbing (“Sydney council pulls book critical of Israel from library shelves”, August 19). People have every right to find a book offensive, including this one. But that cannot be the test for whether a public library makes a book available. The NSW Parliament has just strengthened the Library Act to protect libraries’ freedom to collect and make available material. Yet Waverley library has reportedly removed this book following a complaint. We should be very careful about becoming comfortable with censorship simply because, on this occasion, we happen to dislike the book being removed. A public library should expose us to ideas we disagree with, not protect us from them. Stav Zotalis, Waverley Waverley library has removed How to Sell a Genocide from its shelves. . I imagine Adam Johnson is hoping to have further bans imposed on his book. The free publicity and controversy would really boost sales. Banning certainly helped popularise To Kill a Mockingbird, Catcher in the Rye, Ulysses , Harry Potter, The Satanic Verses, Lady Chatterley’s Lover and many others. Paul Doyle, Glenbrook I’d like to let fellow readers and librarians know that I’ve phoned my local library in Marrickville Adam Johnson’s book How to Sell a Genocide has not been “removed”. I just thought all the readers from Waverley and surrounds might like to know. Antoinette Riley, Marrickville Memory loss As I age, I am conscious of memory loss and wonder how well I am doing. Having listened in recent days to the evidence of numerous ICAC witnesses, all of whom are much younger than me and can hardly recall anything about important work matters just a few years ago, I have decided to stop worrying. Michael Georgeson, Balmain

World.title: ‘No limits’: Carroll offers royal commission extra resources to weed out corruption
World.content:
Premier Ben Carroll has promised to give the newly established royal commission into the building industry whatever additional time, funding and power it needs to rid the state’s construction sector of criminals and corruption. Former South Australian chief justice Chris Kourakis was named commissioner on Thursday with broad terms of reference and powers that extend into the executive government, allowing him to call politicians and advisers alongside public servants, union leaders and building firms. Loading This could include Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews, as well as senior advisers such as those whom The Age last month revealed had sought to warn Allan in writing about lawless CFMEU tactics, cost blowouts and the reported infiltration of organised crime on taxpayer-funded projects. Brushing aside concerns about the modest $50 million starting budget and 12-month reporting deadline for the inquiry, Carroll said he would set “no limits” on Kourakis completing his work.



“If the royal commission needs more time or money to do its job, it need only ask,” Carroll told The Age. “My door is open.” The royal commission’s terms of reference The extent to which corruption, criminal conduct or serious misconduct has occurred on Big Build projects, including any such activity undertaken by the CFMEU, construction companies, subcontractors and labour hire companies

Whether the government and government agencies adequately adhered to their roles and responsibilities in the oversight and governance of Big Build projects

The causes, preconditions and impact of corruption, criminal conduct and serious misconduct on Big Build projects, including whether government procurement, oversight, policies or legislation contributed to its prevalence

The actions of construction companies and Victorian government authorities, including Victoria Police, in responding to or mitigating the risk of corruption, criminal conduct or serious misconduct on Big Build sites

Measures that could be implemented to tackle future corruption, and whether Victoria can recoup misappropriated funds lost to Big Build wrongdoing The deadline for Queensland’s commission of inquiry into the CFMEU and construction misconduct was extended for 18 months and will now report December 2027. Its budget was also boosted to $95 million. The announcement of a royal commission was welcomed by business groups and integrity advocates but criticised by former CFMEU boss John Setka, who resigned from the union in 2024 hours before the first story in this masthead’s Building Bad investigation series was published. On Thursday, Carroll confirmed details of the inquiry he promised when becoming premier three weeks ago, and also pledged to introduce legislation to parliament next month to bolster the powers of Victoria’s anti-corruption watchdog.



The move, which comes after two years of reporting by The Age on corruption and organised crime on construction sites for government infrastructure, was Carroll’s first commitment after replacing Allan. Ben Carroll unveiled the terms of reference for the royal commission on Thursday. Joe Armao “It is clear – and I want to acknowledge the role of both investigative journalism and whistleblowers – that there was grift, there was thuggery, there was misogyny, and there was violence on taxpayer-funded construction sites,” Carroll said on Thursday. “I have zero tolerance for that. We are giving this royal commission the broadest, most extensive, wide-ranging powers. Full transparency; nothing is off limits.” Kourakis’ inquiry will be tasked with exploring the extent of corruption, criminal conduct or serious misconduct that has occurred on major public and civil projects, or which is related to these projects.



For corruption and misconduct that is found to have occurred, the royal commission will investigate the causes and impacts behind this behaviour alongside the role of government, the circumstances that allowed it, and whether any changes to policy had contributed to the problem. Related Investigation

Building Bad Building Bad One of the items on the commission’s term of reference is “whether the executive government of Victoria, and/or delivery authorities adequately adhered to their roles and responsibilities in the oversight and governance of major construction projects”. This will provide a level of access to the political side of government not often seen through public inquiries, with Carroll saying he would give Kourakis the powers and resources he needs when asked if the commission could access cabinet documents and unsigned ministerial briefs. In July, The Age obtained a secret briefing to Allan that outlined many of the issues exposed in the Building Bad series but which was written almost a year beforehand in June 2023.



The document was addressed to Allan but does not bear her signature, and was signed off by four high-ranking infrastructure and transport public servants. An official source confirmed at the time that Allan had been briefed on the report’s contents, but the former premier said she had no knowledge of it. One of the impacts the royal commission will explore will be waste, misdirected funds and inflated costs, providing an avenue to consider the estimate by integrity expert Geoffrey Watson that CFMEU misconduct may have added $15 billion to the cost of the Big Build. Contractors and agencies will be examined to determine whether they properly responded to corruption risks. Lawful industrial action and action under health and safety laws are not within the scope of the inquiry. Carroll did not say whether hearings would begin before the election, leaving that at the discretion of the commission.



Kourakis served as South Australia’s chief justice from 2012 until his retirement from the bench earlier this year. He was previously the state’s solicitor-general from 2003 to 2008. In a move similar to that of Queensland’s Fitzgerald Inquiry, Carroll will also create a special prosecutor in September to work alongside the inquiry. Royal commissions can make adverse findings but don’t have the power to lay charges, which the prosecutor will be empowered to do through special legislation. Kourakis will advise on whom to appoint to the role, and they will be provided with funding and resources to work with both the commission and law enforcement agencies. Carroll said the prosecutor wouldn’t wait for the final report to act and bring people or organisations to account even as the commissioner continued their inquisitorial process.



The government will also introduce legislation next month giving new powers to the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission to pursue taxpayer funds to subcontractors and labour hire firms, known as follow-the-dollar powers. The definition of corrupt conduct will also be expanded so IBAC can pursue so-called “grey corruption” after calls from successive commissioners. Under the narrow definition of corrupt conduct that has restricted IBAC’s reach since its establishment in 2012, it can currently investigate only behaviour that constitutes a serious criminal offence. Carroll denied establishing the royal commission was driven by self-interest with the state election looming and voters concerned about corruption in the Big Build. “This is about the future of our state and valuing taxpayer dollars,” he said.



“I will let others judge about this exercise, but I can tell you very clearly, and I can tell all every single Victorian, this is about them. “This is about doing what is right for Victoria and Victoria’s future, and that is what’s driven me every single moment of this process.” Special Minister of State Ingrid Stitt with Premier Ben Carroll during Thursday’s announcement. Eamon Gallagher Carroll said the inquiry would be a legacy for his government and bring about lasting change. When asked whether his predecessor had turned a blind eye to corruption in the sector, the premier said the government needed to be “curious, and not incurious” about what had occurred.



“Everyone’s been reading the papers. Every single Victorian has been having conversations. Integrity is non-negotiable,” he said. Allan refused to set up the inquiry despite pressure from integrity advocates, the opposition and her own MPs after two years of reporting by The Age, The Australian Financial Review and 60 Minutes on organised crime and corruption in Victoria’s Big Build. Loading Known as Building Bad, that investigation has uncovered serious allegations of organised criminal infiltration of taxpayer-funded construction projects, violence and drug use on worksites, payments to so-called “fixers” such as underworld figure Mick Gatto, and concerns the government presided over a culture where builders were encouraged to give in to demands from the increasingly lawless CFMEU. As recently as Thursday, this masthead revealed that the former national vice president of the Mongols outlaw bikie gang is being investigated by police over allegations he offered inducements to officials still serving in the CFMEU in return for their support of his business.



Before Labor’s leadership change, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson had promised the Coalition would order its own royal commission if it were to claim power in November. She released her proposed terms of reference earlier this month, setting the stage for a political fight over Carroll’s commission. Shadow attorney-general James Newbury on Thursday labelled the inquiry a “cover-up commission” and said an inquiry set up by the Coalition, rather than Labor, was the only way to understand the final cost to taxpayers. But his chief criticisms were that it should guarantee that Allan or Andrews provide evidence and that the CFMEU is the only union named in the document. It will be up to Kourakis to decide whether to call the former premiers and investigate other unions, but the terms of reference do not limit his ability to do so. Former CFMEU secretary John Setka dismissed the royal commission as a witch hunt and questioned what it would achieve.



“I’m surprised the Liberals didn’t write the terms of reference,” he told The Age. “It is just going to be another witch hunt – a circus, a lawyer’s picnic and lobster back on the menu.” CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby said they would fully co-operate with the commission, but that misconduct was not confined to one organisation. “If this royal commission is serious about uncovering the truth, it must follow the evidence

wherever it leads,” he said. “That means examining the conduct of developers, head contractors, subcontractors, labour hire operators and anyone else who has profited from unlawful or unethical behaviour.”
