The move, which comes after two years of reporting by The Age on corruption and organised crime on construction sites for government infrastructure, was Carroll’s first commitment after replacing Allan. Ben Carroll unveiled the terms of reference for the royal commission on Thursday. Joe Armao “It is clear – and I want to acknowledge the role of both investigative journalism and whistleblowers – that there was grift, there was thuggery, there was misogyny, and there was violence on taxpayer-funded construction sites,” Carroll said on Thursday. “I have zero tolerance for that. We are giving this royal commission the broadest, most extensive, wide-ranging powers. Full transparency; nothing is off limits.” Kourakis’ inquiry will be tasked with exploring the extent of corruption, criminal conduct or serious misconduct that has occurred on major public and civil projects, or which is related to these projects.



For corruption and misconduct that is found to have occurred, the royal commission will investigate the causes and impacts behind this behaviour alongside the role of government, the circumstances that allowed it, and whether any changes to policy had contributed to the problem. Related Investigation

Building Bad Building Bad One of the items on the commission’s term of reference is “whether the executive government of Victoria, and/or delivery authorities adequately adhered to their roles and responsibilities in the oversight and governance of major construction projects”. This will provide a level of access to the political side of government not often seen through public inquiries, with Carroll saying he would give Kourakis the powers and resources he needs when asked if the commission could access cabinet documents and unsigned ministerial briefs. In July, The Age obtained a secret briefing to Allan that outlined many of the issues exposed in the Building Bad series but which was written almost a year beforehand in June 2023.



The document was addressed to Allan but does not bear her signature, and was signed off by four high-ranking infrastructure and transport public servants. An official source confirmed at the time that Allan had been briefed on the report’s contents, but the former premier said she had no knowledge of it. One of the impacts the royal commission will explore will be waste, misdirected funds and inflated costs, providing an avenue to consider the estimate by integrity expert Geoffrey Watson that CFMEU misconduct may have added $15 billion to the cost of the Big Build. Contractors and agencies will be examined to determine whether they properly responded to corruption risks. Lawful industrial action and action under health and safety laws are not within the scope of the inquiry. Carroll did not say whether hearings would begin before the election, leaving that at the discretion of the commission.



Kourakis served as South Australia’s chief justice from 2012 until his retirement from the bench earlier this year. He was previously the state’s solicitor-general from 2003 to 2008. In a move similar to that of Queensland’s Fitzgerald Inquiry, Carroll will also create a special prosecutor in September to work alongside the inquiry. Royal commissions can make adverse findings but don’t have the power to lay charges, which the prosecutor will be empowered to do through special legislation. Kourakis will advise on whom to appoint to the role, and they will be provided with funding and resources to work with both the commission and law enforcement agencies. Carroll said the prosecutor wouldn’t wait for the final report to act and bring people or organisations to account even as the commissioner continued their inquisitorial process.



The government will also introduce legislation next month giving new powers to the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission to pursue taxpayer funds to subcontractors and labour hire firms, known as follow-the-dollar powers. The definition of corrupt conduct will also be expanded so IBAC can pursue so-called “grey corruption” after calls from successive commissioners. Under the narrow definition of corrupt conduct that has restricted IBAC’s reach since its establishment in 2012, it can currently investigate only behaviour that constitutes a serious criminal offence. Carroll denied establishing the royal commission was driven by self-interest with the state election looming and voters concerned about corruption in the Big Build. “This is about the future of our state and valuing taxpayer dollars,” he said.



“I will let others judge about this exercise, but I can tell you very clearly, and I can tell all every single Victorian, this is about them. “This is about doing what is right for Victoria and Victoria’s future, and that is what’s driven me every single moment of this process.” Special Minister of State Ingrid Stitt with Premier Ben Carroll during Thursday’s announcement. Eamon Gallagher Carroll said the inquiry would be a legacy for his government and bring about lasting change. When asked whether his predecessor had turned a blind eye to corruption in the sector, the premier said the government needed to be “curious, and not incurious” about what had occurred.



“Everyone’s been reading the papers. Every single Victorian has been having conversations. Integrity is non-negotiable,” he said. Allan refused to set up the inquiry despite pressure from integrity advocates, the opposition and her own MPs after two years of reporting by The Age, The Australian Financial Review and 60 Minutes on organised crime and corruption in Victoria’s Big Build. Loading Known as Building Bad, that investigation has uncovered serious allegations of organised criminal infiltration of taxpayer-funded construction projects, violence and drug use on worksites, payments to so-called “fixers” such as underworld figure Mick Gatto, and concerns the government presided over a culture where builders were encouraged to give in to demands from the increasingly lawless CFMEU. As recently as Thursday, this masthead revealed that the former national vice president of the Mongols outlaw bikie gang is being investigated by police over allegations he offered inducements to officials still serving in the CFMEU in return for their support of his business.



Before Labor’s leadership change, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson had promised the Coalition would order its own royal commission if it were to claim power in November. She released her proposed terms of reference earlier this month, setting the stage for a political fight over Carroll’s commission. Shadow attorney-general James Newbury on Thursday labelled the inquiry a “cover-up commission” and said an inquiry set up by the Coalition, rather than Labor, was the only way to understand the final cost to taxpayers. But his chief criticisms were that it should guarantee that Allan or Andrews provide evidence and that the CFMEU is the only union named in the document. It will be up to Kourakis to decide whether to call the former premiers and investigate other unions, but the terms of reference do not limit his ability to do so. Former CFMEU secretary John Setka dismissed the royal commission as a witch hunt and questioned what it would achieve.



“I’m surprised the Liberals didn’t write the terms of reference,” he told The Age. “It is just going to be another witch hunt – a circus, a lawyer’s picnic and lobster back on the menu.” CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby said they would fully co-operate with the commission, but that misconduct was not confined to one organisation. “If this royal commission is serious about uncovering the truth, it must follow the evidence

wherever it leads,” he said. “That means examining the conduct of developers, head contractors, subcontractors, labour hire operators and anyone else who has profited from unlawful or unethical behaviour.”

World.title: Premier ‘did his own research’ on gun buybacks, committee hears
World.content:
NationalNSWGun control Premier ‘did his own research’ on gun buybacks, committee hears Anthony Segaert August 20, 2026 — 6:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW Premier Chris Minns has admitted the government’s gun buyback scheme will result in some gun owners reimbursed for less than what their weapons are worth on the market. Minns told the NSW upper house’s budget estimates committee on Thursday the government had no plans to change a “special exemption” allowing primary producers and sport shooters to own no more than 10 firearms, a portion of the policy that has attracted fierce criticism from farmers. NSW Premier Chris Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese address the media on the gun buyback scheme. The state government announced on Monday it would join the federal government’s national gun buyback scheme – the only state to do so – and Minns has declared he was willing to make it an election issue. Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane this week labelled the buyback “half-baked” and a “very expensive solution to the wrong problem”. The scheme, first announced after December’s Bondi Beach terror attack, is the largest buyback scheme since the one that followed the Port Arthur massacre in 1996, and will result in gun owners being paid between $450 and $1000 in exchange for their firearms.



Upper house Nationals member Sarah Mitchell told the premier that many gun owners would be left thousands of dollars out of pocket by the scheme because the value of their weapons was much higher than what the government was offering to pay. Minns said he had done “my own research” on the recommended retail price for some firearms and “in many of the instances, it’s below the compensation that we’re asking for”. Related Article Guns Farmers take aim at state’s gun ownership restrictions “The schedule is such that in some instances it will be below the recommended retail price for the resale for the resale value, but it’s not in every instance,” he said. Minns said the government had put in a special exemption cap for farmers and sporting shooters to hold 10, not four, guns, because it “wanted to reduce the net number of guns in the community”.



“We had to make a considered decision,” he said. “It’s not four, which is the general licence condition for guns, and we believe that this is the appropriate number in regional communities. Otherwise, it may get to the point where there’s no point in having the reform or the change.” He did not answer questions from Mitchell about why the government decided 10 was an appropriate cap. “We listened obviously to the farming community, and we believed that in agriculture, as was the case for sporting shooters, there needed to be a special exemption, not the minimum four, but it couldn’t be an infinite number,” he said. “Many disagree with us, but at the end of the day, there needed to be a figure because if the figure was so astronomically high, it would make the whole policy redundant and not worth pursuing in the first place.” He later added: “You deserve a straight answer. We’re not going to change the policy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Wellington residents march on parliament in bid to get rising water bills lowered
World.content:
Hundreds gather in Wellington to protest new Tiaki Wai bills Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Some Wellington residents are fed up and stressed by the prospect of rising water bills as they marched on parliament in a bid to get the organisation to lower costs.

And a former Wellington mayor-turned MP, who turned out to the protest, admitted his was among councils which could have invested more in water infrastructure in previous years.

About 300 people turned up in central Wellington on Thursday to raise concerns about their water bills in a cost of living crisis, as part of the Stop Tiaki Wai group.

Water bills were increasing by 13.3 per cent on average across the region this year, and were projected to reach over $6000 per year in a decade.

A sign at Thursday's protest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Lower Hutt resident AJ said that's shocking.

"The people are fed up, you can't get blood out of a stone can you?"

She said her first water bill was about $500 for the quarter.

"I came out here today, because the cost of living is through the roof, and this is just one more bill that people have to find money to pay - and people can't find that money anymore."

Mary Head, an Upper Hutt resident and pensioner, said she's frustrated about the way her water bills were being calculated.

"There's only my husband and I at home, and the amount of water we use, is negligible to say a family - and yet we are paying the same or more of a family of six or eight," she said.

Mary Head at the protest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Tiaki Wai said in its first years' of operation, the way water services would be calculated was taken from councils' rates bills.

In Upper Hutt, Porirua and Lower Hutt water bills were being calculated through a combination of a fixed rate and property value.

In Wellington city, most people's bills were based on property valuation, board chairperson Will Peet recently told RNZ.

The entity has said it wants to move to a single-pricing model in the future, as well as install water meters.

But Head said the indicative costs Tiaki Wai had put out for that so far - at half-a billion dollars for the programme - were ridiculous.

Protest organiser Guy Nunns admitted he can't actually stop Tiaki Wai - which was set up under the government's Local Water Done Well policy.

Protest organiser Guy Nunns. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Nunns said he would be paying his bill this year - but suggested he would encourage people to not pay their bills if the costs don't change.

That's not something Wellington City Councillor Karl Tiefenbacher, who was among the crowd at parliament, agreed with.

"I don't think that really works. To be fair I am against the fact we have no rates cap on top of Tiaki Wai - I think that's the issue."

He asked what the point of rates caps against councils were, if there was none against water entities.

"I think water is the biggest issue we have. I think this protest actually represents what is wrong with our society at the moment, and that's that it's becoming unaffordable."

When asked whether he thought spending was needed to upgrade failing pipes and water plants, Nunns said "no one" was happy with the current state of infrastructure.

Attendees at the protest on Thursday. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"We have always paid for water infrastructure in our rates, people have not necessarily understood that, they'll be understanding it now - but at $2200 a year, and until recently I was the sole occupant of the property, that's not realistic."

New Zealand First MP and former Wellington city councillor and mayor Andy Foster was also at the protest.

He was asked whether the council he led between 2019 and 2022 did enough to invest in pipes during its years in power.

He said his council set in motion more investment and was heading in the direction of a CCO for infrastructure, but also said more could have been done.

"We were going to fix it, so long term, yes, there was under-investment in infrastructure, but that is true of pretty-well every council in the country."

Tiaki Wai said it needed to spend $25 billion dollars across three decades to fix the regions old failing water treatment plants and pipes.

Stop Tiaki Wai protest attendee, Bridie McGill with her sign. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Officials said there's a major crisis point at Seaview, where a crucial outfall pipe was leaking into the harbour and the Waiwhetū stream.

They also said about 100 kilometres of pipe at the point needed to be replaced each year.

In a recent interview with RNZ, Brewster urged anyone facing hardship to contact the organisation, saying Tiaki Wai had policies in place to help those who were really struggling to pay bills.

But he said debt collection would have to be pursued for those who were refusing to pay for no reason.

"If you are refusing to pay the bill and not contacting us then we, we would unfortunately, we would have to pursue that.

"Because at the end of the day there is an obligation to pay the bill, if nobody pays their bill we've got no money to fix the system."

Attendees march to Parliament. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said on Thursday, he respected the rights of Wellingtonians to join the protest and express their views.

But he urged the protesters to respect those working at Tiaki Wai trying to upgrade the region's infrastructure.

World.title: Ombudsman shines light on 'coercive and unlawful treatment' at Wakari Hospital
World.content:
A Wakari Hospital patient with intellectual disabilities was almost constantly locked in their bedroom for at least 18 months in conditions the Chief Ombudsman says amounted to prolonged solitary confinement.

Inspectors for the Ombudsman visited the inpatient unit for adults with intellectual disabilities in Dunedin in March.

Last month, Chief Ombudsman John Allen shared the findings, saying inspectors observed some of the worst practices they had witnessed and some treatment amounted to torture.

Health New Zealand confirmed plans to close the ward on the same day, while the Ministry of Health said it would launch an independent investigation that would consider if allegations of human rights abuses should be referred to the police.

John Allen released a longer summary of the concerns and urgent recommendations on Thursday, detailing observations under the heading "punitive, coercive and unlawful treatment".

Inspectors detailed a model of care that appeared to prioritise containing and restricting patients to minimise the immediate risk of physical harm, with little attention given to providing meaningful rehabilitation or person-centred care, the report said.

The ward has faced significant criticism before, with a previous ombudsman calling it "a disgrace".

Dunedin's Wakari hospital inspected under crimes of torture Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

But the March inspection was triggered by an innocuous visit to check on a refurbishment Health New Zealand said would be underway from mid-2025, which would require patients to be relocated.

During an unannounced visit in October 2025, Ombudsman staff members discovered the refurbishment remained largely in the planning phase and patients had not been moved out.

They became "very concerned" about patients seen living in restrictive environments, flagging this with ward management and government agencies before sending an information request to Health New Zealand.

In December 2025, Health New Zealand confirmed a high level of restrictions remained at Ward 10A.

It prompted that four-day announced visit in March.

"We became very concerned about the conditions and treatment experienced by tāngata whaikaha (whaikaha means 'to have strength, to have ability, otherly abled, enabled')," the report said.

"We were concerned that the practices of the ward were extreme, fostered institutionalisation, risked traumatising tāngata whaikaha and may have constituted abuse."

Inspectors observed that one patient was locked in their bedroom "almost unceasingly" with extremely limited contact.

"We were very concerned that the physical arrangements were increasing the institutionalisation of this tāngata whaikaha, which had persisted for at least 18 months," the report said.

"We considered these arrangements may amount to prolonged solitary confinement."

The attempts to expose the patient to the ward also appeared to be very limited.

"At the time of the inspection, their bedroom door was being unlocked and left open for 90 seconds each day (rather than 30 seconds previously)," the report said.

The Ombudsman said it expected coercion was not used to modify behaviour and tāngata whaikaha had choice where possible.

Instead, the report outlined a pattern of staff incentivising good behaviour so patients could have their basics needs met including losing access to the toilet while in seclusion, being told they would only be able to see a dentist if their behaviour stabilised, or not being allowed to buy things with their own money unless they complied with staff directions.

"We were highly concerned about the potential use of punitive, coercive and unlawful practice on the ward."

Chief Ombudsman John Allen Supplied

Inspectors found patients might not have consented to some of the medication and sedatives they were given, including intramuscular injections.

This is not legal except in limited circumstances.

A bariatric EVAC mat was used to restrain and move patients, resulting in friction burns for some patients, despite the Ombudsman saying the United Nations' Special Rapporteur on Torture had raised concerns about the use of similar restraints and how they should only be used for legitimate medical reasons.

"In our view, moving a tangata whaikaha to a seclusion room is not a 'legitimate medical reason' envisaged by the Special Rapporteur," the report said.

Helensburgh Cottage, which was meant to help people to transition to care providers in the community, had remained empty since the pandemic despite the Ombudsman noting it appeared to be a better environment to provide care.

Staff told inspectors that it was not being used due to staffing pressures.

While detailing facts about Ward 10A, the Ombudsman noted that previous inspection reports found the physical environment was not fit for purpose - a description the former District Health Board also used.

The Ombudsman's concerns were detailed to senior staff at Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health after the visit, before urgent recommendations were made.

Allen did note that the relevant agencies had taken swift action in response to the concerns and recommendations.

The Ombudsman's recommendations included:

Health New Zealand urgently improving the "conditions of detention" by ending all prolonged isolation and improving physical living arrangements, activity and care.

Ending the use of bariatric EVAC mat to restrain and move tāngata whaikaha.

Urgently take measures to ensure the individual safety and rehabilitation of all tāngata whaikaha on Ward 10A.

The Ministry of Health making sure an independent investigation was undertaken.

Immediately reviewing the medications prescribed to tāngata whaikaha on Ward 10A, to ensure that all medication is lawfully prescribed and administered.

Immediately implementing a model of care in Ward 10A that focusses on tāngata whaikaha well-being and rehabilitation.

Health New Zealand previously said it was taking the allegations made by the Chief Ombudsman and others very seriously.

"We take patient safety and care very seriously and want to acknowledge the patients, their families, and our staff, all of whom we are supporting during this period of change," a spokesperson said.

"Our focus remains on ensuring the safety, dignity, and rights of the current patients, while strengthening oversight and reviewing practices."

Health New Zealand planned to undertake a wider review of forensic intellectual disability services nationally, and said it had already enhanced clinical oversight, reviewed patient care and rehabilitation plans, strengthened approaches to reducing seclusion, and strengthened governance arrangements.

World.title: National MP Greg Fleming breaks ranks, criticises Budget tax change
World.content:
A first-term National MP has criticised a tax change the government has introduced, saying a plan to cap the donation tax credit has "zero" logic.

Maungakiekie MP Greg Fleming said work was underway to "fix" the cap, but the minister responsible said that was not the case.

Fleming was speaking at a charity sector political hui in Wellington on Thursday, when he was asked about the logic behind the $100,000 donation cap limit.

"Zero," he responded. "I've no problems with being quoted publicly on saying I think it was an error."

At the Budget, the government made changes to the charity tax credit rules, which would mean no more tax credits once donors give more than $100,000 to charities.

Individuals could claim a third of their charitable donations back as a tax credit, as long as the value of their donations did not exceed a third of their annual total taxable income.

The $100,000 cap will affect about 350 donors when it is introduced next April, but they represent about 10 percent of donations claimed or about $103 million.

In a regulatory impact statement, the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) said the government spent about $350 million a year on tax credits.

IRD took the view that there was no conclusive evidence the credits actually lead to more giving, and that there was a risk of bad actors and misuse, such as those claiming the credit in advance of the funds being applied to charitable purposes or deriving a private benefit from the donations.

When the cap was announced in May, Revenue Minister Simon Watts said it would ensure the donation tax-credit scheme remained financially sustainable and would also limit tax-planning risks that arose when a donor made a gift to a charity they controlled themselves.

The charities sector has expressed concern that the cap may make would-be donors consider dialling back their donations at a time the sector was already struggling - a view Fleming appeared to agree with.

Fleming said he understood why the cap had been brought in, but there were a "myriad" ways to fix the misuse of donor-advised funds, without introducing a cap.

He said the cap was a "sledgehammer to crack a walnut" and further changes would be made.

"I'm advocating really, really hard for this and I can assure you that work is underway to to fix that," he said.

Watts said Fleming's comments were not correct and the government's position had not changed since the Budget.

"These changes resulted from IRD concerns that, in some cases, the tax credit was being misused for tax planning purposes," he said. "The change does not come into effect until 1 April 2027 and only affects donations over $100,000.

World.title: Nursing graduate applies for more than 100 jobs without success
World.content:
Nursing graduates who have applied for hundreds of jobs and have not found work say it's devastating to hear there's a shortage of nurses.

The nurse's union says Aotearoa's health system is falling into a deeper crisis, with emergency departments and wards bursting at the seams.

It follows revelations that Health New Zealand has hired just 54 full-time equivalent nurses in the past two years.

Nursing graduates struggle to find work while hospitals in crisis Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The situation is driving some graduates to consider making the move to Australia... joining their course mates who have already left.

After finishing hundreds of unpaid placement hours in Auckland, Megan completed her Bachelor of Nursing late last year.

In Aotearoa, new nurses have to apply for graduate positions, some do this through Te Whatu Ora's application system called ACE.

Others apply directly to private hospitals, community organisations and primary care.

But since graduating in March, Megan has applied for more than 100 nursing jobs and hasn't had any luck.

"I feel like I've failed, or there's something that I'm not showing in my application. I didn't realise it was going to be this hard to get a job."

Megan told Checkpoint she's getting by on the Jobseeker benefit while she continues to look for work.

If she can't find work soon, she's eyeing up Australia and said she may be forced to give up on nursing entirely.

"If I don't get a job I'm either likely going to have to re-study something else, or go into a completely different workforce.

"The running joke at the moment is that I become a flight attendant, which I don't really want to, but I've got to get a job somewhere."

Megan said it doesn't make sense how hard it is to find work because of reported shortages and staff burnout.

"We see constantly that the hospitals are understaffed and people are dying.

"Going into an election year, how can you promise us as nurses, new grads and even the public that the hospitals are going to be staffed?"

Hearing stories of graduates not being able to get work has students worried too.

Eden Sandhu is in her final year of studying nursing at Ara Institute of Canterbury.

But seeing nurses the year above missing out on jobs has made her anxious.

"Like thinking that there's no guarantee of securing a graduate position is just draining.

"We're told that there's a shortage, but all of us still experience anxiety that people aren't getting jobs, will there be a position for me when I graduate?"

To get their degrees, nurses have to complete hundreds of hours of on-the-job training, which is not paid.

Eden Sandhu said she had sacrificed so much financially to become qualified and worried about the future.

"[It's] a huge a worry because I've got a family and a mortgage... it's not okay to have graduates coming through having to consider after three years, to find something else."

Moving to Australia is something that's been on Eden's mind over the past few months.

"I think if New Zealand focused on supporting the students through placement, offering paid placements, upping the amount nurses are paid for the incredible stress levels they carry.

"Focussing on how to keep nurses here and not have such a terrible environment that people need to shoot off, that would change how I feel about leaving," she said.

"I would want to stay, I do want to stay, but unfortunately [if I don't find a job] I can't."

Dawn Blyth, the Nurses Organisation's National Student Unit co-leader, is also in her final year of study.

People in her cohort have already applied to Australia's graduate programmes.

"I graduate in November... we understand that jobs aren't guaranteed anywhere in any climate.

"But what is really hard to understand is how can we be saying that our country is so short of nurses... when there isn't the funds to put those nurses into jobs."

Health New Zealand national chief nurse Nadine Gray told Checkpoint they were offering a similar number of roles to last year to keep a mix of experienced and graduate nurses.

She said they were supporting all graduate registered nurses into employment, but this might not happen immediately, and they had never been able to employ every graduate nurse.

World.title: Former Alliance candidate Mary O’Neill sentenced for harassment of Napier neighbours
World.content:
A former local government and parliamentary candidate has been warned she could end up in prison if she does not stop harassing her neighbours.

Mary Jelena O'Neill, 62, was sentenced in the Napier District Court on Thursday for a single charge of intentional damage.

The offending happened in Napier, but O'Neill appeared via an audio-visual link from Dunedin, where she now lives.

The charge, which was proven against her at a judge-alone trial this year, was laid after O'Neill hired a contractor to cut back trees on the property of her neighbours on Napier's Bluff Hill.

However, Judge Russell Collins said the heart of the matter was not the physical damage caused but a "cynical act of harassment" towards the neighbours.

O'Neill has a previous history of harassing the same neighbours - including four breaches of a protection order in 2021 - and other people, dating back to a charge of threatening behaviour in 2015.

Court documents from 2021 say she made "false and damaging" accusations of sexual misconduct about one of her neighbours to the authorities and on social media.

She also once threw a rock at an AA serviceman who had been called out to fix a neighbour's car, then drove towards him, stopping about 60cm away.

Judge Collins stopped short of imposing a custodial sentence on O'Neill, saying she had "complex needs" and her claims about the neighbouring family were "delusional".

Instead, he imposed a maximum term of two years of intensive supervision by a probation officer.

The supervision includes conditions that O'Neill lives at the Dunedin address and does not go near her former house or neighbour's house on Napier Hill.

She will also need to do any counselling thought necessary.

She is not allowed to contact her victims or post anything about them on social media.

Judge Collins warned O'Neill that if she breached her intensive supervision, or reoffended, "I doubt that you would avoid a term of imprisonment", or at least an electronically monitored sentence such as home detention.

O'Neill stood unsuccessfully as a candidate in the Hawke's Bay Regional Council elections in 2019 under the name Jelena Jordan.

She was previously an Alliance Party candidate for Parliament in 2011 and 2014.

This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Woman and child seriously assaulted during Northland break in, man arrested
World.content:
A woman and her child were injured in an assaulted during an alleged break in at a Northland property.

Police have arrested a 38-year-old man following what they called a "violent aggravated robbery" in Kaikohe at 7am on Thursday.

Detective Senior Sergeant Aaron Crawford said police were called to a report of a man allegedly carrying a gun, breaking into a property on Williams St.

A woman and her child were inside, Crawford said, and the pair were "seriously assaulted" before a man fled in a car he stole from the home.

The police Eagle helicopter found the car a short time later in Ōmāpere.

Crawford said the man police believed was involved attempted to run and allegedly tried to steal another car by assaulting another person.

Police intervened, Crawford said, and took him into custody.

A gun and items police believed belonged to the home of the woman and child had since been found, he said.

The woman was taken to hospital in a serious but stable condition, Crawford said, and the child had minor injuries.

"Both are understandably shaken," he said.

The 38-year-old man was in custody and Crawford said charges were pending.

Police wanted to hear from anyone who saw what happened on Williams St or any sightings of a yellow Suzuki Swift travelling west on SH12 towards Whirinaki, Kouto Loop Rd and then Opononi and Ōmāpere.

They also wanted to hear from anyone who saw a man acting "suspiciously" in the Ōmāpere area on Thursday morning.

Information could be provided online at 105.police.govt.nz, or by calling 105 and using the reference number 260820/5258.

World.title: Mother of man murdered in Auckland Prison wants accountability from Corrections
World.content:
Mother of inmate stabbed to death wants corrections held accountable Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The mother of a man who was murdered in Auckland's maximum security prison wants the Corrections Department held accountable for his death.

Blake Lee was shanked to death by another inmate, in an exercise yard inside Auckland Prison at Paremoremo in March 2020.

A Coronial inquest into his death at the Auckland District Court heard details about Lee's transfer to the prison, just hours before he was murdered.

For Lee's mother, Teresa Absolum, it was the good things about her son she tried to remember.

"It's obviously very painful listening to the evidence as it brings feelings of sadness and anger at the way Blake died up," she said.

"I am trying to remember all the good things about my son."

Lee was killed in the prison yard, shortly after his transfer from Whanganui prison to Paremoremo.

The man responsible for his murder, Siuaki Lisiate, was a senior member of the Crips gang, while Lee was an affiliate of the Mongrel Mob.

In 2020, there was no set policy on where gang members should be placed in the prison.

Paremoremo's prison director at the time, David Pattinson, was asked if it was practical to separate rival gang members inside.

"Not unless we built a bigger jail," he said.

Photographs taken of Paremoremo's prison director at the time, David Pattinson, had to be blurred. Finn Blackwell / RNZ

"It would be difficult, there are principles around the style of people that comes together, what influence they can have on the rest of the prisoner group.

"We work hard to maintain a safer environment."

He was question by Susan Gray, the lawyer representing Lee's mother, about the risk of letting a newly transferred prisoner into the yard with different gang members.

"He enters into the yard, he greets people in the yard, they greet him," Pattinson said.

"He acts with confidence in that space, he looks comfortable in that environment, and unfortunately others intervene to change that for him."

Pattinson said at that point in time prior to the attack, it looked like a good decision to offer Lee the opportunity to exercise.

Two years prior, Lisiate had attacked double murderer Graeme Burton with a shank while both men were doing time in Paremoremo.

Gray asked Pattinson about Lisiate's violent past.

"You would agree, surely, that Mr Lisiate had a history of extreme violence," Gray asked.

"I don't disagree with that," Pattinson replied.

Lee's mother told RNZ she wanted to see members of rival gangs separated in prison.

"I would like Corrections to be accountable for my son's death but also for gang members from different gangs never to be mixed," she said.

But Pattinson told the lawyer representing Corrections, Claire Paterson, the murder was not gang related.

Blake Lee died at Auckland Prison in Paremoremo. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"A lot of work was done by Corrections in the aftermath of this tragic incident," Paterson said.

"Was there any evidence found that this was in fact a gang related incident," she asked.

There was no evidence to support that, Pattinson said.

That was despite an earlier High Court memorandum from Lisiate himself, describing gang tensions behind bars as ever-present.

Pattinson said if Lee was transferred to Paremoremo again today, he would likely be put in the same unit.

Later in the day, the inquest heard from the current prison director, Stephen Parr.

He said the protocols in place today would prevent Lee from being placed into a mix on the day of his arrival.

Parr spoke about the shank Lisiate had, saying it was not uncommon for makeshift weapons to be made from items in the prison environment.

"The screening procedures in place were then and are now considered appropriate, however, no procedure is foolproof nor immune to human error," he said.

"It is unfortunate that these procedures were not completed to the required or expected standard on that day."

Parr said he was not in a position to definitively say whether correct scanning procedures would have detected Lisiate's shank.

"Staff acted in accordance with the process that was in place at the time in placing Mr Lee in the yard with that mix of gangs," he said.

World.title: NZ Cricket boss Geoff Allott says $7.3 million deficit forecast 'not good enough'
World.content:
New Zealand Cricket has announced a preliminary deficit of $7.3 million for the last financial year and is planning on slashing the broadcast schedule for the final T20 Super Smash season as part of cost-cutting measures.

The preliminary deficit announced on Thursday by NZ Cricket (NZC) is significantly higher than the budget forecast deficit of $1.8m for the financial year ending 31 July 2026.

In a media release, New Zealand Cricket (NZC) primarily attributes the difference to the organisation budgeting for revenue from a multi-year domestic broadcast contract, which had already been received in previous financial years.

It said a reduction in income following changes to NZC's partnership with sponsor Dream11, prompted by changes to India's gambling laws, together with an increase in the organisation's overall costs, also contributed to the deficit.

NZC chief executive Geoff Allott acknowledged the situation was disappointing, but believed the game was still in good financial health.

"As an organisation we accept that this financial performance isn't good enough, nor is it sustainable," he said.

"It's important that we own this updated budget deficit and immediately put in place the necessary steps to adjust and ensure it doesn't happen again."

The NZ Cricket boss said the coming financial year was set to be more prosperous.

"With net projections forecasting a surplus in excess of $10m, driven largely by the broadcast and commercial revenue generated by the in-bound tour by India.

"That being said, we are acutely aware that as a business our financial model over a four-year cycle is typically lumpy, so we need to be prudent to ensure the long-term sustainability of cricket."

Less than half of the matches in the 2026/27 Super Smash season will be broadcast. photosport

The final financial position may differ from the preliminary figure as the $7.3m deficit remains subject to completion of NZC's annual audit expected in early November.

Allott confirmed a range of measures NZC had undertaken in response to the updated budget deficit, including a full review of internal financial processes, and a reassessment of budgets for the coming financial year.

Allott said a reduction to the broadcast schedule for the final season of the T20 Super Smash was also on the cards, following consultation with the Major Associations and the NZ Cricket Players Association.

Plans are underway for a proposed T20 franchise League for the 2027-28 season to replace the Super Smash competition.

Allott said just 24 of the 64 matches this summer would be broadcast across 12 double-header match-days, including the finals.

Allott said NZC was currently in discussions to ensure the proposed 24 matches remained free-to-air in New Zealand, following the conclusion of TVNZ's broadcast rights agreement last season.

"The loss of Super Smash title sponsor Dream11, coupled with the FY26 budget deficit, meant this was the most financially responsible decision for the competition.

"Our support and commitment to the community game, as well as the players and fans, remains a key priority and we're confident that we are taking a considered and responsible approach in the circumstances."

World.title: Swans sponsors pull support in wake of allegations
World.content:
A number of brands associated with the Sydney Swans have suspended their activities with the club in the wake of a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault in Melbourne on Monday.

Five Swans players, Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon are linked to the police investigation.

The players are yet to be formally interviewed or charged and it is not suggested that any of them are being accused of sexual assault.

Sponsors Colgate, Volkswagen and Telstra have confirmed to the ABC that they have "suspended" or "paused" their activities with the players involved.

Other sponsors, including QBE and realestate.com.au, have released statements condemning any abuse or violence against women but have stopped short of withdrawing their support for the club.

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich expressed a "sincere apology for the distress this incident has caused the wider community," in a statement released on Wednesday afternoon, naming "members, supporters, commercial partners, Academy families, staff members, athletes, their partners and families".

'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident Five Sydney Swans players stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards issue an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

"Our thoughts remain with everyone affected, particularly the women involved. All women deserve to feel safe and respected," the statement read.

"We understand and share the hurt that many of you we will be feeling. To say we are disappointed is an understatement.

"We know that moving forward as a club will take time.

"Every member of our community will process this in their own way, and we do not take your trust or support for granted.

"We are committed to doing the work required to uphold the values, standards and culture we expect of everyone at the Sydney Swans."

Andrew Pridham (right) and Matthew Pavlich have apologised to parties affected by the allegations. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

A number of club sponsors have expressed concerns, but added that they would not comment on the matter while the police investigation was ongoing.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson told the ABC.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

A spokesperson for realestate.com.au noted that the company was "deeply concerned" by the allegations and would await the findings of police investigations.

Meanwhile, Australian Red Cross Lifeblood has pulled out of a match-day activation ahead of this Sunday's double-header.

"Given the serious nature of the current investigations involving Sydney Swans players, we've decided to step back from planned match day activities with the Sydney Swans this Sunday," the statement read.

"We have shared our concerns directly with the club and we are in regular communications with them.

"As ongoing investigations are being conducted by the relevant authorities, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further at this time. Our focus remains on encouraging people to donate blood and plasma to help ensure patients across Australia receive the lifesaving treatments they need."

Police are investigating an alleged sexual assault that took place at the Pullman Hotel on Monday morning. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

All five of the players have been suspended by the Swans for the rest of the AFL season.

The bans are separate from the police investigation and are related to the players' decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women to their hotel, for which they have apologised.

Volkswagen Group Australia said it too was aware of reports and would pause its activities with all the players involved.

"Volkswagen Group Australia has clear values and expectations for the organisations and individuals associated with our brands," the statement read.

"We do not tolerate violence, assault, intimidation or abusive behaviour of any kind."

"In light of the allegations that have been reported, we have paused our activities with the players involved."

On Wednesday, Telstra said it was "deeply concerned" by the incident and that players "who are also Telstra Ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing".

Heeney and Warner have both represented the telecom in activations and s this season.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time," Telstra said in a statement.

Colgate Palmolive said it had "suspended" its personal partnership with Heeney "pending completion of the investigation."

The company said in a statement that it is "aware of reports regarding an investigation by Victoria Police" and that the company "take these matters very seriously."

Heeney's children's book pulled from shelves

Isaac Heeney's publisher has "paused the promotion" of his two books, as well as the publication of a third. (Instagram: Isaac Heeney)

Heeney's publisher, Allen & Unwin, has paused publication of the third book in his Little Isaac Footy Fever series, Super Swan, which was due to hit shelves in November.

"Allen & Unwin is aware of reports relating to Isaac Heeney and a Victoria Police investigation, and that his employer has exercised sanctions under club policy and his terms of employment," a statement read.

"We view this matter seriously and believe that the women involved deserve respect and support.

"We have paused promotion of his two books and the publication of his third book, while the police investigation is under way. We are unable to comment further while the matter is in the hands of the police."

Gleebooks, Readings and Big W have all confirmed Heeney's books have been removed from stores nationally.

"In line with our policy for all such matters, we removed Isaac Heeney's books from our shelves as soon as we were aware of his involvement in the allegations," a spokesperson for Gleebooks said.

Big W said it has paused all sales of the book "pending the outcome of this matter."

"BIG W regularly reviews its range of products to ensure it aligns with our values and community expectations," a statement read.

"We have decided to pause all sales of Little Isaac Footy Fever books in our stores and online."

Booktopia continues to stock the book but said it would "continue to assess the situation".

"We're working closely with the publisher regarding their plans and will continue to assess the situation," Booktopia said in a statement.

"We appreciate the sensitivity and will carefully consider any decision, together with the publisher, in due course."

Amazon and Dymocks have not responded to requests for comment.

World.title: Raiders and Broncos are still reckoning with the legacy of a classic
World.content:
There are some defeats so cruel a team cannot survive even if it doesn't kill them and some triumphs that never leave a team even if they go on to greater glories and sometimes, if we're lucky, both things happen at the same time.

That's what Canberra and Brisbane are both reckoning with ahead of their match tomorrow night, the first meeting for the two clubs since last year's double-extra time semi-final that ended with Broncos winning 29-28 in the 94th minute.

It's scheduling malpractice on the NRL's part that we've had to wait so long for a sequel, which now has a direct-to-video quality when it could have been a blockbuster.

Walsh grabs the Sun to light up Brisbane's season Brisbane and Canberra went to the great beyond in their golden point finals match and it was Reece Walsh who led the Broncos to the promised land.

Perhaps they hoped this match would have finals implications but history didn't say it was likely.

Canberra and Brisbane are two of the NRL's great boomtowns — the Raiders haven't made the top four in consecutive seasons in 30 years and the Broncos haven't done it in 20.

Each club has spent 2026 trying to come to terms with what happened to them, both on that day and since, and both have struggled to carry the weight of what came next.

It was match where Canberra's wave broke and broke hard just as Brisbane's was beginning to crest.

That crest became a tsunami in the weeks to come, as part of a series of matches that can stand equal with any in NRL history.

The Raiders win was their greatest escape, as they came from 16-points down with 15 minutes remaining in a game that defied belief even as it was happening.

The Panthers win in the preliminary final was their most cathartic as they exorcised the demons of their 2023 grand final loss with their best all-round performance of the finals.

The win over Melbourne in the decider was their most glorious, capping as astounding a run to paradise as any team has ever had. They will almost certainly win more grand finals in the future but they will definitely never win one like that again.

After a 20-year drought, it was the premiership of a lifetime, great enough that even a fanbase as varied, voracious and expectant as the Broncos was able to forgive their rough start to life as champions.

But a start was all they could forgive because they cannot forget. Their eyes had seen the glory and the coming of Reece Walsh and they basked in the memories of Brisbane reaching a level of brilliance, ferocity and belief that made them a terrible and wonderful sight to behold.

Brisbane finished off the run of a lifetime to win the 2025 premiership. (AAP: Mark Evans)

Such play would never be sustainable over a full season because you cannot spring your way through a marathon, but in 2026 they've barely got out of a jog and the turn against them has been harsh, swift and brutal.

A spate of injuries in the early part of the season exposed the top-heavy nature of their roster and despite a few brave efforts to start they eventually tipped right over and head to Canberra with 12 losses in their last 13 games.

Old heads like Ben Hunt and Adam Reynolds look like they went on a year too long and younger ones, like Ezra Mam, have shown the ability to replace them but not the maturity or consistency.

After a year where he went from a train and trial deal to playing Test and Origin football and the winning try-scorer in the grand final, Gehamet Shibasaki has looked a lot more like the journeyman he was than the premiership hero he became.

The departing Payne Haas has been strong but not the superhuman we have come to know and with him leaving for Souths and Reynolds retiring it will be a new look Bronco next year — maybe for better, maybe for worse but certainly for different.

It has been a listless premiership defence from the Broncos. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

It's clear that victory has defeated them in a way Canberra, Penrith and Melbourne never could. The merciless march of time is a forever war, but for Brisbane the guns fell silent because they had no more worlds left to conquer.

That has brought them here, where the chance of going from premiers to wooden spooners is somehow possible which is made all the more maddening because the qualities they showed in that golden September still lurk within even if they rarely show themselves.

That sole win in their last 13 starts was against the might of Penrith, away, on a waterlogged track they wouldn't let racehorses run on with Walsh again leading the way.

It has been a difficult and stop-start season for their fullback, who has a boundless energy that is sometimes too great for concentration to control.

His struggles was best typified by his last act for the year — Walsh threw a pass that was intercepted and taken the length of the field by Alofiana Khan-Pereira for a try, but only because he battled hard to get into position despite suffering a serious ankle injury only moments before, one which ended his season prematurely.

Losing Walsh means the remote possibility of Brisbane going from first to last must be entertained. This is a team who have been waiting for this season to end for some time now and they are heavy outsiders for Friday against a Canberra team who have plenty to play for.

The reason for the Raiders motivation is not so much their finals hopes, which are desolate enough they're relying on Wests Tigers to win another game, but because of the home farewell to Josh Papali'i, the club's most capped player and modern day favourite son.

It will give the Raiders a north star to aim for, something Brisbane stopped looking for a while ago.

The visitors are waiting for this season to end while the home side wish it could keep going — Simi Sasagi, their best player this year, has a tenderised shoulder but has kept playing because he wanted to suit up with Papali'i as many times as he could.

Canberra will mark Josh Papali'i's final home match on Friday night. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The veteran prop is the best player the Raiders have ever had who has not won a premiership and as a shining example that greatness can be possible in Canberra he's an important symbol for a team that has to continually prove itself to sceptical outsiders.

His achievements mean Papali'i is a living piece of club history and blood and tears will mix together to make it a sentimental day, as so many days are for Canberra because this a club that rides their emotions like no other.

After a difficult season, which began in the shadow of the finals loss to Brisbane and the defeat to Cronulla which followed, this is a retreat into their own hearts and that's the place they always feel strongest.

Last year, their premiership hopes could not have been more brutally buried unless Brisbane had thrown them a shovel, pulled out a gun and told the Raiders to start digging.

That bled into 2026 as Canberra took a long journey from minor premiers last year to second last a few months ago before settling back into the middle of the pack they know so well but after last year it was hard not to want for more.

Canberra have failed to match last year's minor premiership victory. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

This is a team with the second-longest premiership drought in the league and chances to end it are hard to come by.

It has given this year a lost quality, typified by the "self-entitled and undisciplined" football that Ricky Stuart believes cost them at the start of the season, when they fell into a four-match losing streak from which their finals chances never really recovered.

Throw in the loss of Jamal Fogarty, his replacement Ethan Sanders going through the peaks of valleys so many young halfbacks must endure, an injury run that seemed restricted solely to second rowers and a serious ill-suitedness to the set restart madness that engulfed the early parts of the year and it became overwhelming.

Their fall has not been as hard as Brisbane's but neither is it from such a towering height, which paradoxically increases the pain instead of softening the blow. The Broncos, at least, have what came after that day in the capital.

The Raiders have more to play for than the Broncos on Friday night. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

There's a chance that being up 28-12 with 15 minutes left, or the stolen moments before the full-time siren penalty that allowed Walsh to level the scores is as good as it gets for Canberra for a while.

That, like the seconds before Jamal Fogarty's extra time try was correctly chalked off the board even as Channel Nine had literally started the countdown to cut to the overdue 6pm news with the club's song ringing through the stadium, erroneously heralding a victory which never arrived, could be as close as they'll come to the promised land for some time.

A win against the Broncos tomorrow won't exorcise those demons any more than a loss would compound them. The blood is still on the blade but it has dried. What came before hangs over the match, but enough time has passed that it does not loom.

Canberra will celebrate the past as Brisbane wait for the future to arrive and both will continue to grapple with the legacy of a game that reaches far beyond one autumn afternoon.

Both teams, to some extent, have set themselves on fire as they tried to pass the torch from then to now and in different ways they are still running on it's fumes even a year later.

For the Broncos it is intoxicating in a way they'll always remember. For the Raiders it's just toxic in a way they cannot forget.

They are both of them haunted, one by what was and one by what might have been.

World.title: Storm enforcer Kamikamica forced into medical retirement after stroke
World.content:
Tui Kamikamica's bid to captain Fiji at the World Cup and play on next year is over, after he was forced into medical retirement following advice from specialists.

Kamikamica's career had been hanging in the balance since he suffered a stroke in March, leaving him needing heart and brain surgery.

The 32-year-old had hoped to return for the Storm this year, before being driven on by a potential comeback for Fiji in October at the World Cup.

But recent medical advice prompted him into retirement, bringing an end to a 142-game NRL career that included being in the squads for the 2017 and 2020 premierships.

"I'm incredibly proud of everything I've been able to achieve in the game, representing Storm and captaining my country," Kamikamica said.

"Melbourne Storm has been a huge part of my life for the past 10 years.

"I'm so grateful to the club, my teammates, coaches, staff and everyone who has supported me and my family throughout my rugby league career.

"To play for Storm and captain Fiji are memories I'll cherish forever.

"I want to thank everyone at Storm for believing in me and giving me the opportunity to play at the highest level."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Kamikamica had been inducted as a life member of the Storm this week, before telling teammates that he was no longer able to play on.

The prop also played 23 Tests for Fiji, and was part of the side that reached the semifinal against Australia at the 2017 World Cup.

"Tui has given an enormous amount to Melbourne Storm over the past decade," Melbourne CEO Justin Rodski said.

"[Kamikamica] leaves the club with the respect and admiration of everyone who has had the privilege of working alongside him.

"He has been an outstanding player, teammate and leader, but above all else, Tui is a wonderful person who has always put his teammates and the club first.

"His contribution to our two premiership teams in 2017 and 2020, his leadership within our playing group and his commitment to representing Fiji are all testament to the character of the man."

Kamikamika's retirement comes at the end of what has been a tough year for the Storm off the field, including coach Craig Bellamy's own health battles.

The Storm are still unsure whether Eli Katoa (pictured) will be cleared to return to the field. (AAP: Darren England)

Melbourne is still gathering medical opinions on Eliesa Katoa's future, which is likely to be assessed further in the next month.

Both Katoa and the Storm still hope he will be able to return to the field, after three head knocks in the space of 90 minutes with Tonga last year led to seizure activity and bleeding on the brain.

Katoa must initially return to minimal-contact training as a first step, before anything beyond that is fully considered.

The Tongan international remains contracted until the end of next year, with the Storm also facing the tricky balance of planning its 2028 roster and salary cap.

Katoa had been close to the best second-rower in the NRL last year, with his absence desperately felt at the Storm in this season.

AAP

World.title: 'Fair bit of anger across the whole AFLW' after Swans players allegation
World.content:
As the fallout continues with focus on the Sydney Swans men's AFL team, the club's women's team has been thrust into an unfair spotlight and become another unwilling casualty.

This was a week when the Swans AFLW team was given equal billing to the men's team with a double-header on the SCG, at a club that is very public in celebrating its inclusive values.

Swans players issue apology Five Sydney Swans players stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards issue an apology.

Instead, the club's respect for women has been brought into question, with the women's players and women in the football community left feeling hurt and angry by the actions of the men's players.

The club has suspended five of its men's players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — for the remainder of the 2026 season for breaching club behavioural standards.

The five players are linked to an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, where the Swans were staying after their win over Essendon on Sunday night.

It is not suggested that they are being accused of sexual assault, and no-one has been arrested or charged in relation to the alleged incident.

Sympathies across the footy space remain, first and foremost, with the alleged victim, including everyone spoken to for this story.

While finding it difficult to talk about anyone outside of the woman at the centre of this story, AFLW pioneer Chyloe Kurdas told ABC Sport it had been a "horrendous" week for many women in the footy space.

Sydney started its season on a high after a round one victory against Adelaide. (Getty: Mark Brake)

"As women, we live with the fear of sexual assault every day, and so this is not just something that only the Swans AFLW team will be feeling. There will be a fair bit of anger across the whole AFLW system," Kurdas said.

Diversity and inclusion leader Rana Hussain, who has worked across multiple sports including within AFL clubs, said sexual violence was not an abstract issue for women, as many were feeling this story deeply.

In Australia, one in five women have experienced sexual violence over the age of 15, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, and Hussain said: "Even for those who haven't, most women understand its prevalence and have spent their lives learning to navigate and mitigate that risk.

"So these players are likely carrying this both as employees of the Sydney Swans and as women. And now they have to pull on the jumper, represent their club and potentially answer questions about something they had absolutely nothing to do with," Hussain said.

"We need to be really careful that the women of the Sydney Swans aren't asked to carry the cultural and emotional labour of this moment.

"Too often when these issues arise, women are leaned on to explain why it matters, what respectful culture should look like and what needs to change.

"They can love their club and represent it proudly while still asking difficult questions of their leaders about what the club's values actually mean when they are tested. Standing the players down is an important first step, but for the people inside that organisation, the work doesn't end there."

Sydney Swans will be put under an unwanted spotlight this weekend. (Getty: Mark Brake)

The ABC has spoken to sources in and around the AFLW program, who are not able to speak on the record, but conveyed their deep hurt.

One source close to the women's program said there were strong feelings of hurt, anger and humiliation following the actions of the men's players.

The double-header between the programs is the first in the club's history, with the women running out on the SCG for premiership points on Sunday before the men's game.

While the club will continue to build enthusiasm for the AFLW game against Essendon, the Swans players will have an undesired added layer of attention in what was originally a celebration.

Swans women's players and coaches have yet to comment publicly on the matter. However, that will likely change when they are obliged to do media post-game on Sunday.

Star player Chloe Molloy has already been questioned by media on her way into Swans HQ this week.

"The women, through no fault of their own, there'll be a spotlight put on them because of poor behaviour from men," Kurdas said.

Swans say players 'in serious breach' The Sydney Swans say the players allegedly linked to an incident at a Melbourne hotel "are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

"We don't know what allegedly has happened. But running out there, flying Sydney Swans' flag and playing your role for the club, when you don't know if the boys that play would have your back and play their role for you?"

At a press conference on Wednesday, Sydney CEO Matthew Pavlich said his club's women's team was "deeply disappointed" in the five male players suspended for breaches of club standards and that the club was "supporting them as best they can".

Earlier this week, former AFLW All Australian and now commentator for Seven and Triple M Kate McCarthy questioned how much the AFL space was doing to engage truly and include women and girls in footy spaces safely.

The post was praised by current AFLW players, including GWS' Tilly Lucas-Rodd, while Lions star Jade Ellenger commented: "This is what using a platform for change looks like, so well said."

In a lengthy post, McCarthy wrote in part: "The AFL says it wants women and girls to feel that football belongs to them. That has to mean more than having an AFLW competition or getting women through the gates.

"It means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated, and how our industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise."

World.title: De Minaur suffers US Open seeding blow after Cincinnati boilover
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has missed out on a top-four US Open seeding after crashing out in the fourth round of the Cincinnati Masters.

De Minaur had the chance to climb into the world's top five with a deep run at the final Masters 1000 event before the season's last grand slam in New York.

But the Australian number one delivered a flat performance to fall 6-3, 6-4 to rising Frenchman Arthur Fils in just 82 minutes on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

De Minaur dropped serve once in each set and was unable to break the 21st seed at all.

The world number eight's exit means de Minaur is certain to be seeded in the top eight at Flushing Meadows, still ensuring the Australian does not run into a higher-ranked player until at least the quarterfinals.

But with Carlos Alcaraz still injured, de Minaur could have snatched a US Open top-four seeding and been guaranteed to avoid heavyweights such as Jannik Sinner and Alexander Zverev until at least the semifinals.

Australian qualifier Chris O'Connell plays his fourth-round match in Cincinnati later on Thursday against American sixth seed Taylor Fritz.

AAP

World.title: 'Have they brought value?': McIlroy fires shot at returning LIV Golf stars
World.content:
Masters champion Rory McIlroy believes it could be a "tough road back" for LIV Golf players who may be eyeing a return to the PGA Tour and questioned what value they would even offer the US-based circuit.

McIlroy, speaking to reporters ahead of this week's BMW Championship, needed a brief moment to reflect before answering a question on whether the possibility of players returning from LIV Golf brings value to the PGA Tour.

"I mean, I would argue, have they brought value to LIV? You know?" McIlroy said at Bellerive Country Club in St Louis, Missouri.

"I think the PGA Tour's in a really good spot."

Australia's Cameron Smith is among the LIV Golf cohort that is yet to return to the PGA Tour. (Getty Images: Jamie Squire)

LIV Golf is wrapping up its 2026 season this week near Indianapolis and said earlier this month that it had secured a lead investor that will provide a funding boost as it prepares for a future without backing from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

It remains unclear, however, whether major champions ⁠Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm, two of LIV Golf's biggest draws, will stay on with the rebel circuit beyond this season or seek a return to the PGA Tour.

Brooks Koepka took advantage of a limited-time Returning Member Program in early 2026 to rejoin the PGA Tour after leaving LIV Golf last December.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Koepka's return came at a cost, with the five-time major winner facing a five-year forfeiture of potential equity in the PGA Tour's Player Equity Program, representing an estimated $50–85 million loss depending on his performance and tour growth.

DeChambeau, Rahm and former British Open champion Cameron Smith were also eligible to return under the same Returning Member Program that closed on February 2 after a three-week application window.

McIlroy said he was pretty certain that any additional returning players would not be welcomed back straight away.

"If they were offered this returning member program back in February, the one that Brooks took, then, yeah, maybe. But that has sort of come and gone," he said.

"And I think it was said at the time that the deal that they might get going forward, if they do decide to come back, isn't going to be as good as the one that Brooks got. So, yeah, I would say it's going to be a tough, tough road back."

Reuters

World.title: Socceroos star Circati seals $33m transfer move to Portuguese giants
World.content:
Young Socceroo Alessandro Circati has become the latest Australian international to be snapped up in a money-spinning European transfer, as he hails his move from Parma to Benfica as a "privilege".

Following Lucas Herrington's move from the MLS to become Australia's only Premier League player at Hull City, and Nestory Irankunda joining Benfica's great rivals Sporting from Watford, Circati has been signed by the Portuguese giants for a reported 20 million euros ($33 million).

With Nishan Velupillay's move from Melbourne Victory to third-tier German club FC Ingolstadt 04 also completed on Wednesday, World Cup Socceroos are clearly the flavour of the month, with other reports linking top clubs with Norwich striker Mohamed Toure.

Circati's move from the Italian top-flight Serie A to Portugal's Primeira Liga has been in the pipeline for a while, with the 22-year-old having signed a five-year contract through to 2031 with the Lisbon-based double European champions.

"To all the Benfiquistas, yeah, I can't wait to play in front of you all, and win as many titles as we can. It's a huge honour. It's a privilege. I'm over the moon, couldn't be happier," Circati said in a message to the fans on the club's website.

"I think it's a reward for many years of hard work. I'm so happy to be here, and I can't wait to play for Benfica."

The Italian-born Circati will play at the world-famous Estadio da Luz — the Stadium of Light — and sounded just a little awe-struck as he added: "I can't wait. I've just had a look at it now. It's amazing, and I'm very, very excited to play."

Socceroos forward Nishan Velupillay (right) is also moving to a new club, joining Germany's FC Ingolstadt 04. (Reuters: Albert Gea)

Asked about adapting quickly to his move, he added: "I think I'm very adaptable. I think you can play me in either role of the centre-back, in a back-four or a back-three.

"I'm sure it's going to take a bit of time to adapt, but I'll try and make it as fast as possible with the help of my teammates and staff. But I'm sure I'll fit in just fine."

The lad who came through the ranks at Perth Glory and, after completing a trial with Parma in 2021, returned to his Italian roots to join them, has made swift and impressive progress in Serie A, last year being a stand-out for the northern club as they finished 12th.

Circati also played in all four of the Socceroos' World Cup matches, with 17 international appearances now under his belt and one goal to his name.

Parma paid tribute to his time at the club in a statement, saying: "Alessandro made a total of 96 appearances for Parma, including 37 in Serie A, scoring two goals and playing a key role not only in the club's 2023/24 Serie B title triumph but also in securing survival over the following two seasons.

"President Kyle J. Krause, CEO Federico Cherubini and the entire Parma Calcio family would like to sincerely thank Alessandro and wish him every success in the next chapter of his career."

World.title: FIFA vice-president withdraws support for Infantino after 'final straw'
World.content:
More national football federations and FIFA officials have withdrawn their support for the football body's president, Gianni Infantino, after the exit of chief operating officer Kevin Lamour, which one FIFA vice-president described as the "final straw".

FIFA said on Tuesday (AEST) that Lamour had left the organisation. It came weeks after he publicly criticised Mr Infantino's plan to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other tournaments.

His exit prompted Hungary's Sandor Csanyi — one of eight FIFA vice-presidents and a member of the FIFA Council — to withdraw his support for the embattled Mr Infantino, who is under pressure from three confederations to resign.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"The final straw was the unexpected dismissal of Kevin Lamour," Mr Csanyi wrote in a letter to Infantino, seen by Reuters.

"Kevin performed his duties to a high professional and ethical standard and, as a highly competent executive, made a significant contribution to the transparent operation of the organisation.

"The fact that his dismissal was prompted by his criticism of the above-mentioned initiative — an initiative that you yourself ultimately acknowledged to have been misguided — points to serious shortcomings in professional judgement, ethical standards and leadership."

FIFA did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr Lamour had said staff had been "deceived" over the plan, which he described as the project of one person.

Other FIFA vice-presidents who have attacked Mr Infantino's conduct are UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin, AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al-Khalifa, and CONCACAF president Vittorio Montagliani.

'Extremely worrying'

Dejan Savicevic has labelled recent developments at FIFA under Infantino's tenure "extremely worrying". (Getty Images: Gualter Fatia)

Montenegro's Dejan Savicevic, a FIFA Council member since 2017 and president of the country's football association, said they had also withdrawn their earlier letter of support for Mr Infantino's candidacy.

Mr Infantino is up for re-election in March and is seeking a fourth term until 2031.

Mr Savicevic wrote a letter to FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström outlining his concerns.

"The recent developments within FIFA are extremely worrying and have shown a serious lack of communication and transparency not only to the member associations … but also to the internal members, FIFA Council included, and structures which should hold the foundations of FIFA," he wrote.

"The proposals put forward exposed concerning vulnerabilities regarding governance, not only at the political level but also within the FIFA administration.
